## 口译与施压：《臺湾漫游录》作家杨双子德国新书活动卷入政治争议的前前后后

图像来源，Orina Zhao/BBC News Chinese

图像加注文字，杨双子（中）近日巡回德国宣传其得奖作品《臺湾漫游录》的德文版，包括在首都柏林举行朗读会。

*       *   Author, 赵鲁阳
    *   Role, BBC中文特约记者
    *   Reporting from, 柏林报导

*   Published 1 小时前

*   阅读时间: 5 分钟

台湾作家杨双子近日在德国多地出席《臺湾漫游录》德文版宣传活动，近日在慕尼黑文学馆举行的场次陷入政治风波。

台湾驻慕尼黑代表处称，中国驻慕尼黑总领事馆曾要求取消杨双子的活动，并表示愿意出资、另行安排中国作家取而代之，引发外界关注北京方面是否有施压。

慕尼黑文学馆馆长塔妮娅·格拉夫（Tanja Graf）回应BBC中文查询时，否认有关说法，表示馆方从未被要求取消杨双子的活动，形容“被当作工具”令她感到不适。

同一场活动也因为口译问题引发热议，杨双子发言期间涉及台湾、中国及历史政治的表述，遭大幅压缩。口译其后承认当天确有遗漏，但否认自我审查。

## 慕尼黑活动曾否遭北京施压？

杨双子的小说《臺湾漫游录》今年5月获国际布克奖（International Booker Prize），出版了20多种语言的译本，德文版于10月面世，杨双子先后在德国慕尼黑、柏林、汉堡及法兰克福等地出席新书活动。其中10月1日慕尼黑文学馆举办的活动，因为口译效果不佳引发争议，事件其后进一步延伸至政治层面。

BBC中文于10月6日向格拉夫求证，她的回覆与中央社此前引述赵彦清的说法完全相左。

她表示，文学馆从未被要求取消杨双子的活动，也未收到以中国作家取代她的要求。她也否认曾向任何人作出相关表述，并形容有关说法“相当荒谬（quite absurd）”，因为该馆对于活动举办权拥有绝对的自主权。

慕尼黑文学馆于1997年开幕，经费来自市政府资助、场地租金、活动收入及私人捐款等。负责营运的基金会强调其独立性，市政府与私人创办方在基金会中享有同等代表权。

格拉夫说，馆方曾收到中国驻慕尼黑总领事馆的联络，对方希望在11月安排一个由中国作家代表团组成的活动，但由于文学馆未来六个月的活动已经排满，加上馆方只安排德语出版作品的活动，因此她只能拒绝。

她强调，文学馆未来会继续邀请来自世界各地、包括台湾在内的作家。“我们依然深信艺术与文学的力量。但这种显然被当作工具利用的经历，并非令人愉快的体验。（But the experience of being apparently instrumentalized is not a very pleasant one.）”

图像来源，Anadolu via Getty Images

图像加注文字，《臺湾漫游录》刚于5月获颁国际布克奖，杨双子与英文版译者金翎（右）出席了在伦敦举行的颁奖礼。

## 中国领馆批“虚假新闻”

BBC中文致函中国驻慕尼黑总领馆，发言人回覆称，“对杨双子女士在慕尼黑文学馆的活动毫不知情，从未就此与馆方进行过联系，也从未提出要求取消活动”，“对于相关报道针对我馆的虚假新闻，我馆感到遗憾和愤慨”。

发言人证实，总领馆曾于9月中旬拜访文学馆，但因文学馆行程已满，无法安排中国代表团于11月举办文学活动，“我馆未提出过资助这一活动的想法”。

中方声明重申，“台湾是中国领土不可分割的一部分，坚决反对任何利用文化交流从事台独分裂活动的行经”。

BBC中文同样致函并致电台湾驻德国代表处慕尼黑办事处，至截稿前未获回覆。

## 口译争议：省略“中国”、“拉上拉鍊”

除有关活动是否受到政治施压的争议外，10月1日的活动也因现场口译表现受到关注。

当晚，杨双子在慕尼黑文学馆介绍《臺湾漫游录》德文版，活动由《南德意志报》（Süddeutsche Zeitung；《南德日报》）记者马凯（Kai Strittmatter）主持，德文版译者白嘉琳（Karin Betz）参与对谈。

据中央社报道，赵彦清表示，口译员曹昌振（Chang-Chen Tsao）未能完整传达杨双子的发言，也没有将部分德语对谈内容翻译给她，令她难以判断何时可以参与讨论。他还称，口译员在活动开始前曾向杨双子表示，部分政治议题无法翻译，但没有解释原因。

BBC中文观看活动录影后发现，部分涉及台湾、中国及历史政治的表述未被完整翻译，口译员现场没有做任何笔记，出现反复和杨双子核对、打断其发言的情况，杨双子一些较长发言遭大幅压缩。在其他德语嘉宾发言时，口译员也未向杨双子完整传递。

例如，杨双子谈到《臺湾漫游录》这本历史小说与当代台湾的关系时，谈到“台湾有一个这么强大、有侵略性的国家在身边，有些台湾人也认为，被中国侵略也没关系，我想要对这些人说，有关系”。

口译员随后将有关内容概括为，“台湾有一个很大的邻居，紧邻着一个大国。这种威胁显而易见，而我希望这种威胁变得清晰可见”。其中并未直接提及“中国”，也没有翻译杨双子所说的“有些台湾人认为被中国侵略也没关系”。

《南德意志报》记者马凯随后追问，杨双子所说的“邻居”是否指中国。口译员随后笑了笑，并用手指做出将嘴巴“拉上拉鍊”的动作。

杨双子谈到“台湾历史叙述自主性的重要性”，以及她选择以食物、旅行和女性等主题书写这段历史，是因为这些元素能够跨越时间，与当代台湾人产生共鸣，因此成为她创作这部小说的重要切入点。

不过，口译并未完整传达她这一段较长的发言。翻译过程一度中断，曹昌振与杨双子不断确认原意，马凯也介入协助厘清，现场观众随后发出笑声。

活动中有关中国对台湾进行“资讯的认知作战”的讨论，也未获完整准确翻译。杨双子讲述了很多关于台湾通过的法律和台湾主权探索之间的矛盾，前后讲述长达5分钟，但口译员将相关表述处理为“假新闻”（fake news），且大幅省略，没有完整传达原意。

[跳过 Facebook 帖子](https://bbc.com/zhongwen/articles/cmd7q5glg9llo/simp#end-of-facebook-content)

告知: BBC 不对外来网站内容负责

结尾 Facebook 帖子

## 口译员否认自我审查

慕尼黑文学馆馆长格拉夫向BBC中文表示，馆方是根据另一名口译员的推荐聘请曹昌振，对方与《臺湾漫游录》德文版译者白嘉琳相识。

她指出，口译员当晚似乎难以应付活动的要求，未能准确传达杨双子表达中的细微差别。有时杨双子发言数分钟，口译员却只翻译了一句话。她还提到，口译员没有携带纸笔，也没有做笔记。

格拉夫说，现场说中文的观众对口译质素感到失望，但没有人在问答环节公开表达不满。她同时表示，德国观众整体反应积极，活动结束后的签书队伍很长。

曹昌振书面回覆BBC中文查询，承认当天的口译有疏漏与不足，愿反省道歉，但他强调“绝对没有”因为个人政治立场，刻意删除、淡化或回避杨双子谈到中国、中华民国或台湾政治处境的内容。

对于把嘴巴“拉上拉鍊”的动作，他解释，活动一开始时，有人询问台湾政治等问题，主持人表示希望先回到小说本身，政治问题稍后再谈，“我是在那个情境下做出了拉上拉鍊的动作”，而不是出于自我审查“不敢谈中国”，希望外界不要赋予“根本不存在的政治意图”。

曹昌振也在声明中介绍，自己是中文和德文教师，有20多年教学经验，曾任[中国流亡作家廖亦武](https://bbc.com/zhongwen/trad/world/2011/07/110714_germany_china_writer)的口译。

BBC中文亦就口译争议联络杨双子，其经纪人表示杨双子行程繁忙，且相关问题难以在简短篇幅内充分回应，婉拒了采访邀请。

## 德国巡回活动继续举行

视频加注文字，在国际布克奖结果揭晓前夕，杨双子带BBC中文记者走过小说登场的场景，也是她的家乡——台中。

慕尼黑活动争议后，《臺湾漫游录》的德国宣传行程仍在继续。

根据出版方春山出版社在社交媒体发布的资讯，慕尼黑活动当天约300个座位座无虚席，另有80多张线上直播票售出，现场售出80多本德文版书籍。有读者带来韩文、英文及中文等不同语言版本，请杨双子签名。

杨双子10月4日在柏林举行的德文版朗读活动同样吸引不少读者。该活动由德台协会邀请举办，现场座无虚席，口译工作则由长期驻德的台湾记者林育立负责。

《臺湾漫游录》以1938年日本殖民统治下的台湾为背景，讲述日本女性青山千鹤子与台湾女性王千鹤之间的故事。两人沿着台湾铁路旅行、品尝当地美食，并在旅途中经历文化交流与情感变化。小说透过两名女性的关系，探讨殖民权力、语言、身份认同及台湾历史的叙述方式。

该书获得2026年国际布克奖，出版多种语言译本。小说中，台湾女性王千鹤担任日本女性青山千鹤子的口译员。杨双子也曾以“翻译的翻译”形容自己与历史、语言及文化之间的关系。

title: EU sends envoy to Beijing as rising exports from China raise economic anxiety
summary: BRUSSELS -- The European Union is bracing for a confrontation with China as a trade deficit exceeding $1 billion a day heightens anxiety over potential job losses and pushes the bloc’s political leaders to take a more aggressive approach to
content:
BRUSSELS -- The European Union is bracing for a confrontation with China as a trade deficit exceeding $1 billion a day heightens anxiety over potential job losses and pushes the bloc’s political leaders to take a more aggressive approach toward its second-largest trading partner.

The European Commission’s top trade envoy, Maroš Šefčovič, will be in Beijing Thursday for a two-day meeting with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao. The goal is narrowing the EU’s 360 billion euro ($410 billion) trade deficit with China. Earlier this year, he [gave Beijing a deadline](https://apnews.com/article/eu-china-trade-meeting-0b2afb981360117cb617052a2987ac98) of October to provide meaningful results in doing so.

Politicians and economists across the 27-nation bloc consider China’s massive subsidies and exports a major threat to core industrial sectors from steel foundries to car factories. China diverted many of its exports to the EU and other markets after the [U.S. raised tariffs](https://apnews.com/hub/tariffs).

In a debate Tuesday in European Parliament in Strasbourg, lawmakers overwhelmingly expressed anxiety alongside defiance over trade with China. On Wednesday, they voted 454 to 86 on a resolution to toughen up on China that centered on a call for “economic reciprocity and a proportionate EU response if China does not open its markets.”

Ahead of the vote, Hilde Vautmans, the Belgian lawmaker who led the resolution, said that “Europe has economic power, it’s time we used it.”

Despite the seeming European unity this week, it remains unclear what the EU can or is willing to do. It has already rolled out trade [measures against Chinese steel imports and e-commerce small parcels](https://apnews.com/article/eu-china-trade-steel-ecommerce-quotas-tariffs-e181c15226f44d6a2f782d4800fa837e).

France’s High Commission for Strategy and Planning in February called for swift action, like 30% tariffs on many of China’s exports, and a devaluation of the euro against the Chinese currency. Sales of German autos are [plummeting in China](https://apnews.com/article/cars-china-economy-europe-sales-d156bfb9548c6d1c7e08ccb906963959), but China is also poised to [gobble up market share](https://apnews.com/article/european-union-electric-vehicles-tariffs-china-b56ef6eff5e8970bf3a9d3304fbdbaa5) in Europe by undercutting European automakers on price thanks to heavy state subsidies. There have already been [mass layoffs](https://apnews.com/article/volkswagen-job-cuts-plants-oliver-blume-8ebf1cc6693a06d06b12fac5693c8333) at major manufacturers like Volkswagen.

A letter by France and Germany, a copy of which was seen by The Associated Press, called for a sweeping rethink of the EU’s China policy. Among other actions, it proposed making it easier for the European Commission to use the bloc’s so-called “trade bazooka,” the [Anti-Coercion Instrument](https://apnews.com/article/eu-us-tensions-trade-tariffs-greenland-e30b341ce1c6d95a168067dd4348586b). This is a never-used-before raft of measures for blocking or restricting trade and investment from countries found to be putting undue pressure on EU member nations or corporations.

Yet not all EU nations agree on such tough measures. Spain, the eurozone’s fourth-largest economy, has been [less adversarial toward China](https://apnews.com/article/spain-china-xi-jinping-iran-trump-war-d53d0157078c1aabc4f022f8553ea8d7?utm_source=app&utm_medium=iOS_share&utm_campaign=copy_link) in recent years. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has visited Beijing four times in three years.

The European Policy Centre in Brussels said in June that European battery producers, solar panels, steel, electric vehicles, chemicals and machinery are already hemorrhaging jobs and capacity and called for a trade investigative body modelled on Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the phenomenon another “ [China shock](https://apnews.com/article/china-trade-exports-tariffs-trump-germany-edd7a75a090afca912b4650bcceb562d) ” for Europe, similar to what happened in the U.S. in the early 2000s when hundreds of thousands of factory jobs in the American heartland were wiped out.

The EU’s ailing economy requires both a domestic overhaul and a more aggressive foreign trade policy, especially with China, said Tim Rühlig, a China analyst at the European Union Institute for Security Studies, the bloc’s internal think tank.

Rühlig also said that European businesses and political leadership bear some blame.

“It’s clear that just protecting yourself from China is not the future,” Rühlig said. “But to have a chance of making yourself ready for future technologies and to remain competitive in the coming 15-20 years, you have to protect yourself.”

It is impossible to disengage completely with China as the EU did with Russia following its invasion of Ukraine, Rühlig said, but there is robust momentum now to reset trade relations with Beijing.

“Where do we make ourselves independent or at least more diverse? And where do we still work with the Chinese?” Rühlig asked.

## Popular Reads

This week in Beijing, when asked about the letter penned by France and Germany, a spokesperson at China’s Ministry of Commerce said that the countries should refrain from encouraging the EU to resort to protectionist measures.

“Protectionism cannot enhance competitiveness, and decoupling or cutting off supply chains will only harm others without benefiting oneself,” the commerce ministry said in a statement.

China is the EU’s second-largest goods trading partner after the U.S., according to European Commission data. Chinese exports to the EU rose 15.3% in the first eight months of this year, according to China’s customs agency, while its imports from the EU rose 6.2%.

“The EU does not have the capacity to wage a trade war against China,” read an editorial last month in China’s state-run Global Times newspaper. “If it is truly determined to do so, then let it try.”

China’s exports to Europe, as well as Southeast Asia, Latin America and Africa, expanded after U.S. tariffs went into effect last year, but it still booked [a $1.2 trillion trade surplus](https://apnews.com/article/china-economy-trade-surplus-record-59f6fcc80ee3afc204a024f57766d319) globally in 2025. So far, China’s export machine has remained remarkably resilient despite U.S. tariffs and other trade restrictions, said Max Zenglein, Asia Pacific senior economist at The Conference Board.

This past weekend, ahead of the meeting between Šefčovič and Wang, China [launched an anti-dumping probe](https://apnews.com/article/china-antidumping-eu-trade-87ebcb909b577a5d8111e770c115169a) on EU exports of p-nitrotoluene, which is used in dyes and pharmaceuticals. The probe was initiated after Beijing warned last month that it would take retaliatory actions if the EU instituted tougher protectionist trade measures.

“China has been battle-tested by successive rounds of external pressure and, so far, has largely stared down attempts to force a change in course,” said Zenglein.

China’s economy has been largely driven by exports as [domestic demand remains sluggish](https://apnews.com/article/china-economy-trade-exports-ai-95136222f87d5a1e62918f41efab00be). The EU imports sizable amounts of Chinese lithium-ion batteries and hybrid electric vehicles, and Chinese carmakers are also expanding production capacity in Europe.

While China’s trade surplus has intensified concerns among its major trading partners, trade ties between the U.S. and China appear relatively stable following a summit between Chinese President [Xi Jinping](https://apnews.com/article/trump-xi-visit-china-trade-ai-takeaways-f7b4922c12abca2bab7262019566c08c) and President Donald Trump in Washington, wrote Bank of America economists, turning the attention to China-EU relations.

When it comes to negotiations with the EU, Chinese investment in Europe is likely to be among Beijing’s bargaining chips, Zenglein added, particularly as EU member states compete to attract capital, jobs, and new manufacturing projects.

___

Chan reported from Hong Kong.

[![Image 9: Sam Cooper's avatar](https://i0.wp.com/substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!sx_W!,w_48,h_48,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Facbe5801-cc74-4669-a030-5084dc495fb5_1136x520.png?resize=67%2C67&ssl=1)](https://www.thebureau.news/)**[Sam Cooper](https://substack.com/@samthebureau)**

[In pivotal testimony Wednesday, the senior HSBC banker who dealt directly with Huawei chief financial officer Meng Wanzhou told jurors that her assurances led him to believe the company’s business in Iran was aboveboard.](https://www.thebureau.news/p/mengs-banker-tells-huawei-jury-she?utm_source=post-email-title&publication_id=1444443&post_id=218330614&utm_campaign=email-post-title&isFreemail=true&r=lqs9o&triedRedirect=true&utm_medium=email)

Prosecutors say Meng lied to the bank, and that Huawei ran a criminal enterprise that stole technology from foreign competitors and sold equipment into sanctioned markets, Iran among them.

Huawei says some employees broke rules, that no one in management drew up a blueprint for crime, and that the racketeering case remains unproven.

Meng described Skycom—the Hong Kong company conducting Huawei’s Iranian business—as a third-party partner and said Huawei had sold its Skycom shares. Her agreed statement of facts says Huawei actually transferred Skycom to another entity it controlled, continued directing Skycom’s operations and caused approximately $100 million in U.S.-dollar transactions to pass through HSBC and clear through the United States.

Alan Thomas, HSBC’s former deputy head of global banking for Asia-Pacific, testified that he accepted Meng’s representations “at face value,” considered Huawei’s Iran exposure small and was not overly concerned by reports about the company’s dealings there. HSBC subsequently continued its lucrative relationship with Huawei.

Huawei’s lawyers used their cross-examination to argue that HSBC already possessed information connecting Huawei, Skycom and Skycom’s new owner, Canicula. They also established that Thomas asked Meng no questions, took no notes, prepared no report of their meeting and remained involved in securing major Huawei business for the bank.

Meng herself is not in the Brooklyn courtroom.

As _The Bureau_ has exclusively reported, a classified June 2019 Canadian Security Intelligence Service assessment said China’s Ministry of State Security was directed “from high levels” to prevent her extradition from Canada.

“CSIS assesses that the PRC prioritizes avoiding Ms. Meng’s extradition partly due to concern that she may cooperate with U.S. authorities during a criminal trial and reveal privileged information in the process,” the assessment says.

The document—titled _PRC Strategy and Tactics to Influence the Meng Proceedings_—said competing MSS bureaus were tasked with making the “largest possible impact,” while President Xi Jinping received reporting on the crisis directly from the intelligence service.

The MSS campaign, according to CSIS, combined trade retaliation, pressure on politically connected Canadian business leaders, clandestine interference surrounding Canada’s 2019 election and the detention of Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor.

Meng never entered American custody. She signed a deferred prosecution agreement on September 24, 2021, and the Justice Department withdrew its extradition request. Canada terminated the proceeding, Meng returned to China, and Beijing released Kovrig and Spavor within hours.

The Brooklyn jury will not hear Meng explain the HSBC meeting or see her cross-examined about it.

But U.S. District Judge Ann M. Donnelly ruled in June that prosecutors may present Meng’s agreed statement of facts as evidence against Huawei. Meng was—and remains—the company’s chief financial officer.

That makes Thomas’s testimony the closest jurors have come to hearing the other side of the meeting at the heart of the government’s bank-fraud case.

### The Hong Kong meeting

Thomas, who spent approximately 40 years at HSBC, met Meng at the Agnes B restaurant in Hong Kong on August 22, 2013. The meeting followed Reuters reports linking Huawei to Skycom and disclosing that Skycom had offered to sell embargoed American computer equipment in Iran.

[![Image 10](https://i2.wp.com/www.todayville.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tvrd-ab-referendum_general_728x90_todayville-2026-09-09.jpg?fit=728%2C90&ssl=1)](https://albertareferendum2026.ca/?utm_source=todayville&utm_medium=display&utm_campaign=alberta-referendum&utm_content=static)

Thomas testified that Meng spoke Chinese for approximately 95 percent of the meeting and delivered a Chinese-language PowerPoint through an interpreter. Meng said she was using an interpreter to ensure precision.

According to her agreed statement of facts, Meng described Huawei’s relationship with Skycom as “normal business cooperation” and called Skycom a “partner,” a “business partner of Huawei” and a “third party Huawei works with” in Iran.

She also said Huawei had once owned Skycom but had “sold all its shares.”

The statement of facts says those representations were untrue. Huawei had transferred Skycom from one Huawei-controlled entity to another, Canicula Holdings. Huawei continued controlling Skycom’s business, its country manager was a Huawei employee and people nominally employed by Skycom believed they worked for Huawei.

Meng also told Thomas that Huawei operated in Iran “in strict compliance with applicable laws, regulations and sanctions” and that neither Huawei nor its partners had violated export-control regulations.

Her agreed statement says those representations were also untrue because Huawei’s control of Skycom caused banks to provide otherwise prohibited services for its Iranian business while Huawei concealed the relationship.

Thomas testified Wednesday that he did not question Meng during the meeting. HSBC requested an English version of the PowerPoint but did not receive it until approximately two weeks later.

He said he was “not overly concerned” by the reports about Huawei because the Iranian business appeared limited compared with a company then generating approximately $40 billion in annual revenue.

According to the live courtroom account from Inner City Press, Thomas described an HSBC policy permitting relationships with companies whose overall sanctioned-country business remained below five percent, provided exposure to any individual sanctioned country did not exceed one percent.

“I was satisfied they were in compliance,” Thomas testified, according to that account.

Huawei’s lawyers confronted Thomas with internal bank records identifying Skycom and Canicula, seeking to establish that HSBC personnel understood more about the corporate relationships than prosecutors suggest.

One exhibit reportedly showed Skycom Europe sending €1.5 million to Skycom Iran. Huawei Technologies appeared as the applicant and shared a telephone number associated with the transaction.

The defence also explored HSBC’s financial interest in retaining Huawei.

Thomas acknowledged that the bank participated in a syndicated loan of approximately $1.5 billion to the telecommunications giant, earning about $15 million in fees. He agreed that nurturing the Huawei relationship was part of his job and that HSBC continued providing financing after concerns about Iran arose.

Prosecutors returned on redirect to what Huawei’s evidence did not disclose.

Asked whether one document shown during cross-examination contained anything indicating that Huawei was continuing to conduct Iranian business, Thomas answered: “No.”

The government’s theory is that general knowledge of Huawei’s Iranian operations was not the same as knowing Huawei secretly controlled Skycom—or that Iran-related payments were passing through the American financial system.

title: An Important Neighbor, Yet Conflict Persists: The Inside Story of Takaichi's Remarks and China-Japan Geopolitical Sparring
summary: ## Executive Summary Although Prime Minister Takaichi made a conciliatory gesture by referring to China as an "important neighbor," she did not retract her previous remarks regarding a "survival-threatening situation" over Taiwan, while rai
content:
## Executive Summary

Although Prime Minister Takaichi made a conciliatory gesture by referring to China as an "important neighbor," she did not retract her previous remarks regarding a "survival-threatening situation" over Taiwan, while raising issues in the East and South China Seas and demanding "responsible action" in the same speech. China is maintaining leverage on both economic and security fronts through rare earth export controls and the implementation of its revised National Defense Mobilization Law, while simultaneously pursuing a selective opening strategy by allowing a meeting with Vice Premier He Lifeng. Both countries are bound by an asymmetric calculus where retracting statements or responding flexibly would entail higher domestic political costs; thus, the structural conflict itself is unlikely to be resolved in the short term, regardless of whether a bilateral summit takes place on the sidelines of next month's APEC meeting. Japan finds itself in a position where it must simultaneously manage three fronts: maintaining a tough stance on China, responding to trade and currency pressures from the United States, and securing its presence in multilateral diplomacy. This issue extends beyond a simple bilateral conflict between China and Japan, affecting the critical mineral supply chain and the overall competitive dynamics of the Northeast Asian regional order, thereby demanding supply chain risk management and strategic responses from regional countries.

## I. Analysis of the Issue

## Conciliation and Pressure Coexisting in a Single Speech

On the afternoon of Monday, October 5, in the House of Representatives plenary chamber, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi delivered her first policy speech to the ordinary session of the Diet since taking office. She referred to China as an "important neighbor" and added that both countries would continue to promote a mutually beneficial relationship based on common strategic interests [[1]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-1). However, in the very same speech and in the same breath, she followed with a different message. She declared that Japan would firmly assert its position regarding the East and South China Seas, as well as China's so-called "regional military activities" and "coercive measures" [[1]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-1). She also did not fail to demand "responsible action" from China [[1]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-1). In effect, a conciliatory label and a pressuring warning were placed side-by-side within a single speech.

To understand this scene, one must go back 11 months. In November last year, during a parliamentary Q&A session, Prime Minister Takaichi stated that a blockade or armed seizure of Taiwan in a contingency could constitute a "survival-threatening situation" for Japan [[3]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-3)[[5]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-5). This remark touched a nerve in Beijing because it directly linked the conditions for exercising the right to collective self-defense to the Taiwan issue. For China, the Taiwan issue is non-negotiable [[3]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-3)[[5]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-5). Immediately after the remarks, China wielded its rare earth and magnet export control card [[3]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-3)[[5]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-5). Later, a parliamentary delegation led by Representative Shinichi Isa visited Beijing to explore restoring relations, but Luo Gang, Deputy Minister of the International Liaison Department of the Communist Party of China (CPC), made Japan's revision of its stance on Taiwan a prerequisite for any shift in China's policy toward Japan [[3]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-3). As both party and government channels simultaneously deployed the frame of "neo-militarism," the conflict transitioned into a structural phase that could not be resolved simply by retracting the remarks [[3]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-3)[[5]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-5).

## Holding onto Rare Earths, Keeping Economic Channels Open

Beijing's current response goes beyond simple protest. Foreign Minister Wang Yi repeatedly demands a "correction" of the remarks, while simultaneously employing a selective opening strategy by permitting a meeting with Vice Premier He Lifeng [[2]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-2). This is a dual-track structure that makes absolutely no concessions on political red lines while keeping economic and private-sector channels open depending on the situation. The Global Times analyzes this situation even more sharply. Some Chinese experts interpreted Prime Minister Takaichi's "important neighbor" remarks as a ritualistic response pressured by domestic and international circumstances. Given that China-Japan supply chains are deeply intertwined and the Japanese business community is demanding a return to normal economic and trade relations, the conciliatory rhetoric is evaluated as a gesture aimed at placating such demands [[1]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-1). Another article from the same outlet is even more direct. Regarding the cause of deteriorating China-Japan relations, it pointed out that the United States is condoning Japan's provocative moves against China, while conveying criticism that the Takaichi administration is repeatedly highlighting the Taiwan issue [[8]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-8).

Tokyo's moves are also complex. Nikkei Asia reported that it remains uncertain whether a China-Japan summit will take place on the sidelines of next month's APEC summit. Due to the cooling trend that has persisted since last year, it is difficult to apply the conventional formula of summit diplomacy [[3]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-3). Although the Japanese side explored the possibility of a thaw through a former foreign minister's visit to China, the messages were mixed [[3]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-3). On the security policy front, conversely, a clear stance of countering China is evident. Following Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi's remarks regarding nuclear weapons in late September, moves to increase defense spending and expand independent regional engagement have continued [[2]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-2). Diplomatic conciliatory gestures and a defense buildup trajectory appear to be proceeding in tandem.

## Who is Staking What?

The Japanese government's position is split into two tracks. The Prime Minister's Official Residence (Kantei) is conscious of the pressure to normalize economic and trade relations with China, particularly the anxiety within the business sector stemming from its dependence on rare earths. At the same time, it cannot ignore pressure from security hawks within the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and its coalition partner, Nippon Ishin no Kai (Japan Innovation Party). Retracting the "survival-threatening situation" remarks could provoke this hardline sentiment, making it a card that Prime Minister Takaichi cannot easily back down on. Nikkei Asia noted that while Prime Minister Takaichi maintains strong approval ratings, she is in a position where she must simultaneously manage inflation issues and the demands of her coalition partner [[5]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-5).

The actor landscape on the Chinese side is also not monolithic. Foreign Minister Wang Yi of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs is tasked with demanding a correction of the remarks through official channels, while the CPC's International Liaison Department sets harder prerequisites through party-to-party channels [[3]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-3). State-run media, represented by the Global Times, support the public opinion campaign by defining Prime Minister Takaichi's conciliatory remarks as "rhetoric masking continued provocation" [[1]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-1). The line under Vice Premier He Lifeng, who oversees economic affairs, maintains a relatively practical, working-level channel [[2]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-2). This division of labor demonstrates that China is operating by separating political pressure from economic pragmatism.

## The Dispute Ultimately Converges on a Single 'Taiwan Phrase'

The core issue is clear: whether Prime Minister Takaichi will retract her "survival-threatening situation" remarks. China has made this very statement a prerequisite for any shift in its policy toward Japan [[3]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-3). While Japan expresses its willingness to manage relations through the rhetoric of an "important neighbor," it shows no intention of retracting these remarks, which have become a cornerstone of its security policy. Rare earth export controls serve as leverage to maintain this deadlock. It is a structure where economic pressure will not be lifted without political concessions. The APEC summit scheduled for November could be the next turning point in this phase. Even if a meeting between the leaders takes place, the likelihood of resolving the fundamental difference in stance over the Taiwan phrasing appears low at present [[3]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-3).

## II. In-Depth Analysis of the Issue

## Not Unable to Retract, But Unwilling to Retract

Prime Prime Minister Takaichi's "survival-threatening situation" remarks were not a slip of the tongue. Given her political career and support base, they represent a calculated stance. Prime Minister Takaichi carried out her first cabinet reshuffle before the reconvening of the House of Representatives and still maintains solid approval ratings [[5]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-5). Her coalition partner, Nippon Ishin no Kai, has demanded a hardline stance on both fiscal and security fronts [[5]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-5). In this context, retracting the Taiwan-related remarks carries a high risk of being read as "capitulation" by both her conservative base and her coalition partner. With her approval ratings holding up, maintaining the remarks rather than folding them is a domestically cheaper option politically.

The calculus on the Chinese side is similar. In his speech on the eve of National Day, President Xi Jinping repeatedly emphasized promoting "reunification" with Taiwan and stated his rejection of "external interference" [[13]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-13). This speech came just days after he requested President Trump to oppose Taiwan's independence [[13]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-13). At a time when the CPC leadership has elevated the reunification narrative to this extent domestically, showing flexibility toward Japan's Taiwan-related remarks could be interpreted internally as a sign of weakness. This is why Foreign Minister Wang Yi repeatedly demands a "correction" without offering any compromise. Both sides stand on an asymmetric calculation where the domestic political cost of walking back a single statement is greater than the cost of dragging out the conflict.

## Tokyo Must Hold the Line on Three Fronts Simultaneously

The structural pressure facing the Takaichi administration does not end with relations with China. Washington has expanded its pressure beyond trade issues to fiscal and monetary policies. US Treasury Secretary Bessent and President Trump continue to exert pressure on yen policy, and the Takaichi administration appears to be stepping back from its reflationary stance [[9]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-9). At the same time, it must signal to the market that it will maintain an expansionary fiscal stance [[7]](https://global.eai.or.kr/en/reports/990814#ref-7). Oppo

# Important Update: Postponement of the IIUSA EB-5 Passport Series in China

10.07.26 | [Events](https://iiusa.org/category/events/)

*   [Follow](https://www.linkedin.com/company/association-to-invest-in-the-usa-iiusa-/ "Follow on LinkedIn")

[![Image 18](https://iiusa.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/POSTPONED.png)](https://iiusa.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/POSTPONED.png)

Invest in the USA (IIUSA) is postponing the upcoming EB-5 Passport Series events originally scheduled for this coming January in China.

This decision follows a strategic recommendation from our local Exit-Entry Association partners in response to recent regulations issued by the Chinese government regarding migration agencies. We are still working to determine the full extent of the regulations, but they may impact the operations of migration agencies. Key aspects of these regulations include

*   **Mandatory Registration:** All local migration agents are required to register officially with the Chinese government.
*   **Event Restrictions:** Limitations have been placed on the types of promotions, marketing, and physical events that agencies can host.

While this delay is disappointing, the EB-5 market simply needs time to adapt to and digest these operational changes. We are fully confident that the series will move forward successfully. Taking this necessary pause ensures that our return to the region is fully compliant, secure, and productive for all attendees.

We are actively collaborating with our Chinese exit-entry partners to lock in new dates for the second half of the year. Our team is dedicated to building an event framework that aligns perfectly with the updated regulatory landscape while maintaining the high standards of global networking and EB-5 education you expect from IIUSA.

## **Get Involved with IIUSA in Another Market!**

While our timeline for China has shifted, IIUSA still has a packed schedule of industry-leading events planned. We continue to move forward with a dynamic lineup of international and domestic platforms designed to maximize your market reach and connection to global investors.

Explore our other upcoming global engagements and domestic conferences in our [Event Calendar](https://www.eventbrite.com/o/invest-in-the-usa-iiusa-23380917723).

title: China’s Build Up of Nuclear Forces
summary: ### _China’s Build Up of Nuclear Forces with Warfighting Capabilities Threatens U.S. Defense Strategy in the Pacific_ China is currently embarked on a massive build-up of nuclear weapons and delivery vehicles. From a low-level force structu
content:
### _China’s Build Up of Nuclear Forces with Warfighting Capabilities Threatens U.S. Defense Strategy in the Pacific_

China is currently embarked on a massive build-up of nuclear weapons and delivery vehicles. From a low-level force structure designed to support its strategy of minimum deterrence, China is now striving to establish a nuclear warfighting capability that would enable it to bolster its massive conventional forces with a substantial theater nuclear force, backed up by expanded nuclear intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs). China’s objective, in the event of war, is to win a quick victory with its conventional forces, and to deter the use of U.S. nuclear weapons by threatening the employment of its large theater nuclear forces.

### **Chinese Geopolitical Offensive**

Chinese President Xi Jinping is leading his country into a new era of geopolitical dominance. China’s goal is to establish maritime spheres of influence initially out to the First Island Chain (from the Kuril Islands through Japan, Taiwan, and the Philippines), then to the Second Island Chain (from Japan through Guam to New Guinea), and eventually to the third Island Chain (Hawaii).[[1]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn1),[[2]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn2)

China is seeking to be the preponderant power in the western Pacific and to displace the United States as the region’s leading power, undermining U.S. security guarantees, and weakening America’s ties to its Asia-Pacific allies. To achieve this geopolitical dominance in the Western Pacific, China is altering its nuclear doctrine and undertaking a major buildup of its nuclear forces.

### **Chinese Nuclear Strategy – Moving from Minimum Deterrence to Limited Nuclear Deterrence**

China’s longtime official nuclear strategy had been based on minimum nuclear deterrence. In its 2003 Defense White Paper—and repeated at the Second Preparatory Committee for 2005 NPT Review Conference—it said, “China has always exercised utmost restraint towards developing nuclear weapons, kept its nuclear arsenal at the minimum level only for self-defense.”[[3]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn3),[[4]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn4)

However, numerous Chinese military officials have advocated that China transition to limited nuclear deterrence.[[5]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn5),[[6]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn6),[[7]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn7),[[8]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn8),[[9]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn9) The contrast between “limited” and “minimal” deterrence is that minimum nuclear deterrence refers to “threatening the lowest level of damage necessary to prevent attack, with the fewest number of nuclear weapons possible,” while limited nuclear deterrence“ requires a limited war-fighting capability to inflict costly damage on the adversary at every rung on the escalation ladder, thus denying the adversary victory in a nuclear war.”[[10]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn10)

China’s adoption of limited nuclear deterrence, according to these advocates, would allow it to:

*   Control and suppress escalation during a nuclear war;[[11]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn11)
*   Create a nuclear ladder; and [[12]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn12),[[13]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn13)
*   Prevent low-intensity nuclear war from further escalating.[[14]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn14),[[15]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn15)

By adopting limited nuclear deterrence and fielding forces to support it, China would move beyond threatening retaliation after U.S. nuclear use. It could instead be able to tailor nuclear responses, strike U.S. regional bases with limited attacks, attrit key U.S. military assets, win early battles, and deter further U.S. nuclear escalation. This approach could help China achieve regional political-military objectives while avoiding the large-scale damage that broader escalation could bring.

### **Chinese Deployment of Accurate, Warfighting Theater Nuclear Forces threatens Taiwan**

Giving credence to the premise that China has changed its nuclear strategy from minimum to limited nuclear deterrence is by its development and deployment of the very accurate, low-yield, nuclear capable DF-26.

According to the 2024 DOD report _Military and Security Developments Involving the People’s Republic of China_, the DF-26 can conduct precision strikes against operational- and tactical-level targets in the Western Pacific while limiting collateral damage. This capability improves China’s ability to send deliberate nuclear signals and strengthens its coercive leverage across multiple domains.[[16]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn16)

The fear is that China, by establishing escalation dominance in the Western Pacific, specifically around a potential conflict over a Chinese conventional invasion of Taiwan, could erode/revoke an American extended nuclear deterrence guarantee to Taiwan, and make a conventional invasion attempt more likely.

### **Chinese Expansion of Nuclear Forces reduces the credibility of US nuclear commitment to its Pacific Allies**

As of 2022, China has deployed 214 DF-21, DF-17, and DF-26 nuclear capable theater range missiles,[[17]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn17) while the United States has zero theater range missiles, having removed its nuclear Tomahawk Sea-Launched Cruise Missiles (SLCM) from the Pacific (and world-wide) in 1991. By 2036, China is projected to have deployed 350 nuclear capable DF-17 and DF-26 nuclear-capable theater range missiles. [[18]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn18)

Overall, China currently possesses over 600 nuclear warheads on theater and intercontinental land-based and sea-based missiles, and on bombers. By 2030, China is expected to field over 1000 warheads,[[19]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn19) 1500 in 2035,[[20]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn20) and is projected to reach strategic nuclear parity with the United States in that same year.[[21]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn21)

The Chinese nuclear buildup will degrade the credibility of U.S. extended security guarantees in Asia. It was the Soviet achievement of nuclear parity with the United States by the time the SALT Agreement in 1972 that caused European allies to worry that the United Stares would not risk Detroit to save Dusseldorf. Soon, American Asian allies may doubt that the United States may be willing to risk Tampa for Tokyo.

### **Remedy**

With the increasing Chinese nuclear threat reaching a critical point about 2035, it appears the United States has a just-in-time remedy to meet this existential danger. As part of FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act, the U.S. Congress directed the Department of Defense to produce the W80-4 nuclear warhead for the Tomahawk SLCM, and to ensure that the system achieves IOC no later than 30 September 2034.[[22]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn22) Though planned as a conventional only weapon to be deployed in Japan, the Philippines, and Australia, the U.S. Army Typhon Laucher would be technically capable of firing a Tomahawk Ground-Launched Cruise Missiles (GLCM), with the same nuclear warhead as the sea-based version as well.

This projected U.S. deployment of nuclear missiles in response to the Chinese threat very much parallels an American success story in reaction to a nuclear threat 50 years previously from the Soviet Union.

In the 1980s, the Soviet Union

*   had achieved overall nuclear parity with the United States;
*   was unilaterally deploying SS-20 intermediate range nuclear missiles;
*   was developing offensive nuclear war fighting plans to defeat NATO.[[23]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn23),[[24]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn24),[[25]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn25)

In the 2030s, China

*   is projected to achieve strategic nuclear parity with the United States;
*   will continue to unilaterally deploy DF-17, and DF-26 intermediate range nuclear missiles;
*   will develop a nuclear war-fighting theater strategy in the Pacific.

The U.S. deployment of Pershing II and GLCM INF missiles in the 1980s eliminated the Soviet unilateral advantage in theater nuclear missiles. Subsequently, the Soviets agreed to sign the INF Treaty, which removed the nuclear war fighting capability danger posed by the SS-20 missiles.

The current Under Secretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby characterized the U.S. defense buildup in the 1980s, with the INF missile deployments, as a “most successful period”, and that the INF treaty effectively marked the end of the Cold War.[[26]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn26)

Regarding today’s situation, Under Secretary Colby specifically said in that the United States was “not seeking to accentuate or increase the focus on theater-range nuclear weapons” but added that “It’s not an exclusion of theater-range systems,” [[27]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn27) and that the United States should have rational “employable, limited options that advantage us and stand the chance of favorably managing escalation.”[[28]](https://www.realcleardefense.com/articles/2026/10/07/chinas_build_up_of_nuclear_forces_1210263.html#_edn28)

The deployment of nuclear-armed SLCMs and possibly GLCMs to the Pacific region would be an outstanding counter to this aggressive Chinese nuclear expansion and adoption of offensive nuclear war-fighting plans. Perhaps lighting could strike twice, and the great success of the U.S. INF nuclear missile deployments in Europe against the Soviet Union could be replicated 50 years later with Tomahawk nuclear missile deployments against China.

* * *

**_MAJ Dennis S. Nelson_**_(U.S. Army, ret.)_

content:
中国计划在世界卫生组织(WHO)总干事改选提名截止前的最后一刻推举一位中国资深公共卫生官员角逐这一职位。分析人士警告说：“当中国籍人士担任联合国机构负责人时，他们往往优先推动北京方面的利益。”

**中国在截至日期即将结束前提名候选人**

路透社援引四名外交官和一位知情人士的消息报道说，中方准备提名的候选人是宋莉。

世卫组织官网资料显示，宋莉长期从事妇幼卫生工作，拥有超过20年的妇幼健康政策和国际合作经验。她曾任中国国家卫生健康委员会妇幼健康司副司长，并参与世卫组织妇幼卫生领域的多个专家机制。她还曾担任中国国家卫健委妇幼健康司司长，目前任中国全国妇联书记处书记、党组成员。

现任世卫总干事谭德塞(Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus)在2017年5月举行的第七十届世界卫生大会上被会员国选举为总干事，任期五年后又于2022年8月连任，他的第二任期将于2027年8月15日届满。根据世卫组织的规则，总干事只能连任一次，因此谭德塞在第二任期结束后，将无法再次连任。

下一任总干事选举程序已于今年4月启动，报名截止日期很快将至。新一任总干事预计将在2027年5月第八十届世界卫生大会上正式获得任命。

目前已有六位候选人宣布参选，他们分别来自和代表沙特阿拉伯、比利时、卡塔尔、博茨瓦纳、印度尼西亚和西班牙。

**利用美国退出世卫组织，乘机扩大影响力？**

路透社在报道中指出，北京长期以来一直寻求在联合国机构及其他多边组织中扩大影响力和承担更多责任，并表示，北京出人角逐世卫组织总干事，似乎有利用美国退出世卫组织遗留的空间，趁机扩大其影响力之嫌。

白宫2026年1月22日正式宣布退出世界卫生组织，理由是该机构“应对新冠疫情不力，且持续缺乏改革、问责和透明度”。

美国国务卿马尔科·卢比奥(Marco Rubio)当天与卫生与公众服务部长罗伯特·肯尼迪(Robert Kennedy)发表联合声明说，通过终止担任世卫组织成员职务，美国“摆脱了其种种限制”。

“这一举措是对世卫组织在新冠疫情期间失职的回应，旨在纠正这些失职对美国人民造成的伤害。承诺已做出，承诺已兑现，”声明说，“世卫组织背弃了其核心使命，并屡次采取损害美国利益的行动。”

该声明还说，尽管美国是世卫组织的创始成员国和最大资金提供者，该组织却推行“由敌视美国利益的国家驱使的政治化、官僚化议程”。“在此过程中，世卫组织阻碍了关键信息的及时、准确共享，而这些信息本可以挽救美国人的生命，世卫组织随后又以‘维护公共卫生利益’为借口掩盖了这些失职。”声明继续说道。

在此之前，特朗普政府多次指责世界卫生组织在疫情初期应对不力、缺乏独立性，并倾向于中国。不过，世界卫生组织否认了这些指控。

不过，路透社又指出，由于Covid-19疫情期间世卫组织与中国的关系引发过持续的紧张，宋莉参选有可能会面临严格的审视。

**专家警告：他们往往优先推动北京方面的利益**

宋莉如果当选，她将是世卫历史上第三位女性总干事，同时也是第二位中国籍的总干事。挪威前总理格罗·哈莱姆·布伦特兰(Gro Harlem Brundtland)曾于1998年至2003年担任世卫历史上第一位女性总干事；来自香港的陈冯富珍(Margaret Chan)曾于2007年至2017年出任世卫组织第二位女性总干事。

中国还没有正式宣布宋莉的参选。美国之音曾联络美国国务院，寻求对此事的评论，但是截止发稿，也未收到回应。

美国智库德国马歇尔基金会印太计划执行主任葛来仪(Bonnie Glaser)在接受美国之音采访时表示，不应忘记，正是在陈冯富珍于2010年担任世界卫生组织总干事期间，一份世卫组织内部备忘录遭泄露，其中显示工作人员被指示在所有组织名录中将台湾正式称为“中国的一个省”，此举引发了台湾方面的正式抗议。

“当中国籍人士担任联合国机构负责人时，他们往往优先推动北京方面的利益。这违背了联合国对其人员的要求，即必须保持公正，并将国家利益置于联合国使命之下。”葛来仪说。

每年五月，台湾都寻求参与世界卫生大会，探讨卫生与健康等非政治议题，但是北京往往全力阻挠被其视为奉行“台独“路线的台湾政府官员出席大会，即使美国及其欧亚盟友力挺台湾似乎也无济于事。

对于中国在联合国和国际组织中安插自己人的做法，美国常驻联合国代表迈克·华尔兹(Mike Waltz)今年4月在参议院的一场听证会上曾回应说，美国正努力扭转这种局面。

“我们希望今后能将重点放在中国极其活跃的领域上。中国实际上是在向这些组织输送实习生和初级官员，然后从内部培养他们。当然，随之而来的就是要求这些组织使用Deepseek或华为的产品。我们已经看到了这种模式，无论是非洲的机场，还是在全球经济中管理我们日常生活的各类组织。”华尔兹说。

美国作为最大的出资国退出世卫组织之后，作为联合国附属卫生机构的世卫组织被迫进行大规模改革和重组，包括缩减活动规模、削减高层管理职位以及裁减数千个工作岗位。

中国已宣布向世卫组织提供额外资金，但远不足以填补美国退出留下的资金缺口。世卫组织预计将在11月初各区域委员会会议结束后，公布全部的总干事候选人名单。

title: Decoding Japan PM Takaichi’s ‘important neighbour’ message to China - what it means for ties
summary: Read a summary of this article on FAST. SINGAPORE: In a [major policy speech](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/east-asia/japan-pm-takaichi-china-policy-address-6432256) on Monday (Oct 5), Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi laid out her g
content:
Read a summary of this article on FAST.

SINGAPORE: In a [major policy speech](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/east-asia/japan-pm-takaichi-china-policy-address-6432256) on Monday (Oct 5), Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi laid out her government’s priorities for a 69-day parliamentary session.

But it was her choice of words on China that drew observers’ attention.

Describing the country as an [“important neighbour”](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/east-asia/japan-pm-takaichi-china-policy-address-6432256), Takaichi also pledged to build a stable relationship between the two nations.

“We will work to ensure communication on shared challenges, promote dialogue to safeguard our national interests, and build a constructive and stable relationship,” she said in her address.

At the same time, she drew a firm line - listing a series of concerns including disputes in the East and South China Sea, along with “Chinese military activity around Japan”.

Another subject conspicuously absent from Takaichi’s speech was Taiwan, though analysts said the omission was unsurprising and does not suggest any change in her position on the island.

“It is rare for a Japanese prime minister to mention Taiwan, with which Japan has no diplomatic relations, in an inaugural address or a policy address,” said Shin Kawashima, a professor of international relations at the University of Tokyo.

“Rather, it appears to be intended to convey that her remarks last November do not signify a change in policy toward China,” he said, adding that her administration has also “explicitly stated that there has been no change in Japan’s policy toward Taiwan”.

Those remarks last November had [triggered a major diplomatic rupture](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/east-asia/china-japan-tensions-sanae-takaichi-travel-taiwan-5471656), after Takaichi suggested that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could constitute a threat to Japan’s survival and potentially warrant a military response from Tokyo.

Beijing reacted angrily, demanding that she retract the comments - something Takaichi has refused to do - as tensions spilled over into trade, tourism and other areas of the bilateral relationship.

Against that backdrop, CNA looks at what Takaichi said, what she left unsaid, and whether her latest remarks signal a shift in her approach to Beijing - or an attempt to stabilise a relationship that has been under severe strain without changing Japan’s underlying positions.

## WHAT DID TAKAICHI SAY ABOUT CHINA?

Only a relatively small portion of Takaichi’s wide-ranging speech focused on relations with China - with much of her address instead [devoted to the economy](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/watch/japanese-pm-takaichi-pledges-fiscal-discipline-outlines-policy-plans-in-diet-speech-6433366).

But the language was still carefully balanced, observers said.

“China is an important neighbour, and despite difficulties, we have built up a long-standing relationship over the years,” Takaichi told parliament.

At the same time, she also made clear that Japan would “firmly assert our country's positions”.

“We will continue to assert Japan’s position on various issues in the East and South China Sea, Chinese military activities around Japan, coercive measures, safety of Japanese citizens in China and human rights concerns, and we will strongly demand responsible action,” she said.

 This handout picture, taken and released by the Japan Coast Guard, shows a Chinese Coast Guard ship near disputed islets in the East China Sea. (File photo: AFP/Japan Coast Guard)

“She was largely reiterating Japan’s longstanding policy stance towards China,” said Sarah Soh, an associate research fellow with the Regional Security Architecture Programme at the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS).

“It might reflect some effort to temper tensions, but this diplomatic language is par-for-the-course given that it forms part of her broader policy speech.”

Inhwan Oh, senior research fellow and executive director at the East Asia Institute in Seoul, described Takaichi’s remarks as “a form of de-escalation within certain limits” - reflecting competing domestic and diplomatic considerations.

“(While) the Japanese government’s current position on Taiwan is politically popular, Japanese businesses may hope that bilateral relations will be managed differently from political ones,” Oh said.

Japanese academic Kawashima noted that Takaichi had also previously described China as an “important neighbour” after taking office last October - before her meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

The phrase has since appeared in various official Japanese foreign policy documents, Kawashima said, suggesting that its use in this week’s speech did not represent a new approach towards Beijing.

Takaichi’s tone “reciprocates” that of Chinese foreign affairs minister Wang Yi, who last week said that ties with Tokyo were “waiting to be normalised again”, noted political scientist Chong Ja Ian from the National University of Singapore (NUS).

Wang and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng had met with former Japanese foreign minister Takeshi Iwaya in Beijing in late September - the highest-level reception by Chinese officials for a visiting Japanese politician in nearly a year.

Iwaya led a 50-member business delegation of corporate executives, in a trip aimed at restoring stability.

“Even though it was non-governmental, the fact that there was a high-level Chinese reception of a Japanese delegation is some indication that Beijing wants to smooth relations even if it does not want to change its position,” said Chong.

 Takeshi Iwaya (pictured left) and Wang Yi attend the Japan-China high-level economic dialogue in Tokyo. (Philip Fong/Pool Photo via AP)

Taiwan was not mentioned during Takaichi’s Oct 5 speech.

Beijing claims the island as part of its territory and has not ruled out using force to take it.

To date, Takaichi has not retracted her controversial remarks suggesting that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could prompt a military response from Tokyo.

“It is unsurprising that Taiwan was not mentioned in her speech,” said Soh from RSIS, adding that “the fundamental source of tension remains unresolved”.

“China wants Takaichi to retract her statement on Taiwan and she cannot do so without risking political reputational damage, so a retraction is thus unlikely,” Soh said.

Chong from NUS said: “She did not disavow her previous statement, which at any rate was in response to a question rather than volunteered through prepared remarks.”

## WHAT’S NEXT FOR CHINA-JAPAN RELATIONS?

For now, signals remain mixed, experts said.

“A genuine thaw is less likely because Japan's position on Taiwan is unlikely to change,” said Oh from the East Asia Institute.

Ren Xiao, a professor of international relations at Fudan University, similarly said Beijing was unlikely to see Takaichi’s latest remarks as signalling a fundamental shift “as long as she does not adjust her position drastically”.

The differences had “placed a ceiling” on how far relations could improve, he added.

Chong from NUS said that “both sides are testing the water right now after a period of friction, while maintaining their original positions”.

“I expect both Tokyo and Beijing to take things slowly,” he added.

During his meeting with Iwaya, Wang urged Japan to “correct (Takaichi’s) erroneous words and deeds” over Taiwan, China’s foreign ministry said in a statement.

Chinese state media have also struck a sceptical tone following Takaichi’s Oct 5 speech.

In a commentary piece published on Oct 5, Chinese state broadcaster CGTN accused Takaichi of “diplomatic hypocrisy”, arguing that her conciliatory language towards Beijing was at odds with Tokyo’s actions on security and Taiwan.

“The fundamental problem is not a lack of diplomatic vocabulary. It is the widening contradiction between what Takaichi's administration says about China and what it does toward China,” wrote CGTN columnist Xu Ying.

Her “perfunctory remarks” were a “response to pressure both at home and abroad”, Lu Chao from the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences told the state-owned Global Times newspaper.

“Takaichi is attempting to ease domestic pressure by making verbal gestures of easing tensions and providing an explanation to Japan's business community,” Lu said.

Beijing, in turn, has sharply criticised Tokyo’s changing security posture as well as its positions on Taiwan and wartime history.

It has also taken a series of steps to curb economic ties with Japan - from warning citizens against travel to tightening export curbs on dual-use goods, with restrictions affecting rare earths.

“In terms of what else to watch, I would also see if Beijing quietly removes the trade and tourism restrictions on Japan and slowly changes its rhetoric,” said Chong from NUS.

So far, there has been little indication that Beijing is ready to unwind those measures, experts add.

“At present, there are no signs of change in China’s economic sanctions against Japan, restrictions on people-to-people exchange, or pressure on Japan through both words and actions,” said Kawashima from the University of Tokyo.

 Chinese President Xi Jinping shakes hands with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi ahead of their meeting in Gyeongju, South Korea, Oct 31, 2025. (File photo: Kyodo News via AP)

Still, he pointed to recent visits to China by Japanese lawmakers and other groups as attempts to improve relations, with attention now likely to turn to the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, which Takaichi is expected to attend.

“We might want to see what sort of reception she receives although there is currently no indication that either Beijing or Tokyo is pushing hard for some sort of big breakthrough,” said Chong.

Other analysts similarly cautioned that recent developments have yet to translate into a broader diplomatic thaw.

“There have been some attempts at re-engagement, but this has been conducted largely through parliamentary and business channels,” said Sarah Soh from RSIS.

High-level engagement, whether between the countries’ leaders or ministers, would be “a clearer indicator of a thaw in relations”, she added.

“The APEC meeting in November could serve as a barometer,” Soh said, pointing to whether a meeting between Xi and Takaichi takes place, as well as any ministerial meetings on the sidelines.

# 針對遇襲案偵結 矢板明夫：繼續為台灣發聲

[![Image 7: 針對遇襲案偵結 矢板明夫：繼續為台灣發聲](https://www.epochtimes.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fi.epochtimes.com%2Fassets%2Fuploads%2F2026%2F09%2Fid14858880-875985.jpg&w=1200&q=75)](https://i.epochtimes.com/assets/uploads/2026/09/id14858880-875985.jpg)

【大紀元2026年10月07日訊】（大紀元記者鍾元台灣報導）印太戰略智庫執行長矢板明夫7月6日在台中遭毆打，台中地檢署6日起訴中國籍男子、香港幫派成員廖港發，另對4名共犯發布通緝。矢板明夫指出，偵查結果顯示這是跨境暴力行動，並非單純治安事件。暴力目的是要人閉嘴，但他不因這拳而沉默，而是繼續為台灣、為自由發聲。

台中地方檢察署6日發布新聞稿表示，該署偵辦今年7月間，被告廖港發等香港地區「和勝和」幫派成員組成跨境施暴集團，對矢板明夫毆打案件，檢察官偵查終結，對廖港發依組織犯罪等罪起訴，具體求處法定刑最重的5年有期徒刑，並建請法院接續羈押。另針對潛逃出境的4名共犯發布通緝，持續追查幕後主嫌及有無在台共犯。

矢板明夫在臉書發文表示，他感謝檢警在短時間內釐清真相。偵查結果顯示事件不是「認錯人」，也不是中國國台辦所稱「單純治安事件」，而是一場「有組織、有計劃、有報酬」的跨境暴力行動。檢方更明確指出，其目的之一，就是製造寒蟬效應，達到「殺一儆百」的效果。

他說，最近幾個月，類似事件正在不同民主國家接連發生。在美國，有人被控涉嫌替中國政府監視賴清德總統在美國的家人；在韓國，一家取名「習近平」的中餐館遭4名中國籍男子闖入破壞；在台灣，卡米地喜劇俱樂部因為有表演者曾公開嘲諷習近平，場地遭人投擲混有白漆與糞便的物品。

矢板明夫表示，「這些事件讓我們看到一個值得高度警惕的現象。中（共）國式的跨境鎮壓，正在從網路恐嚇走向破壞財物、僱人施暴；從針對個人延伸到其家人；也從台灣、香港擴展到美國、韓國等民主社會。它真正想製造的，不只是一次傷害，而是一種恐懼。」「當人們開始因為恐懼而自我審查，跨境鎮壓的目的就已經達成了。」

「這一次拳頭雖然是打在我的臉上，但它真正想打掉的，是所有人說話的勇氣。所以這不只是我個人的事情，也不能只被當成一起普通的治安案件。面對跨境暴力，民主國家有必要聯合起來，台灣、美國、日本、韓國以及所有民主陣營的夥伴，應該建立起共同防線，防止中（共）國的威權政府繼續把暴力和恐懼輸出到民主社會。」矢板明夫說。

矢板明夫說，他不會因為這一拳而沉默，而是會繼續做自己認為正確的事情，繼續為台灣、為自由發聲，也繼續推動台灣與民主國家的交流合作。暴力的目的是想讓他們閉嘴，那麼最好的回答，就是繼續說自己想說的話、繼續做自己想做的事。～

# 美国8月贸易逆差扩大到1056亿美元 对台湾逆差超过中国排第三

茉莉花综合报道 2026年10月7日 08:18

美国商务部10月6日公布，8月美国的贸易逆差为1056亿美元，比7月的928亿美元增加13.7%，高于经济学家预期的1021亿美元，是一年多来最大的单月逆差。这直接影响美国的经济增长：贸易已经连续三个季度拉低美国国内生产总值（GDP），经济学家估计，第三季度可能拉低多达2.5个百分点。

按国家和地区分，8月美国商品贸易逆差最大的是墨西哥（277亿美元）、越南（240亿美元）、台湾（183亿美元）、中国（164亿美元）和欧盟（110亿美元）。台湾排在中国前面，是美国第三大逆差来源；美国对台湾的逆差一年前是122亿美元，今年8月比一年前多了61亿美元，增幅50%。对台湾的逆差扩大，和美国建设人工智能（AI）有关：进口增加集中在AI基础设施等资本品上，而芯片仍要从台湾进口。

8月美国商品贸易逆差最大的五个国家和地区（亿美元）

数据：美国商务部10月6日公布的数据

8月美国进口4208亿美元，比前一个月增加4.3%；出口3152亿美元，增加1.4%。进口增加最多的是工业用品和资本品：工业用品增加91亿美元，其中原油增加33亿美元、非货币黄金增加31亿美元；资本品增加62亿美元，主要是半导体和其他机床。第二季度美国国内需求的增长是三年半多来最快的，主要来自消费支出和企业的设备支出，设备大多与AI有关；企业要靠进口来满足需求。特朗普说，他的关税是为了缩小贸易逆差。从全年看，今年前八个月的逆差比2025年同期减少19.9%。

## 茉莉花观察

这一节是茉莉花的看法，依据是上文的事实。

我们的分析 美国对台湾的逆差一年里增加一半、超过对中国的逆差，主要是AI带来的。美国企业建设AI基础设施，要进口大量芯片和设备，而芯片仍要从台湾来；8月资本品进口增加的62亿美元里，半导体占了二十四亿美元。关税意在缩小逆差，但这类进口跟着国内需求走：需求旺盛时，企业就要靠进口来满足。

不同看法 从全年看，逆差在缩小，今年前八个月比去年同期少了19.9%；8月的扩大可能只是AI设备集中进口的一个月，不说明关税没有作用。我们同意全年的逆差在缩小；但对台湾的逆差反映的是AI投资，只要美国企业还在大量建设AI，从台湾进口的芯片就还会增加。

前瞻 美国商务部11月4日公布的9月贸易数据。我们判断，9月美国对台湾的商品贸易逆差仍会大于对中国的逆差。8月对台湾的逆差已经比一年前多了一半，进口增加集中在AI需要的资本品上；8月非国防资本品（不含飞机）的订单和出货也很强，企业的设备投资在第三季度还在继续。

title: Hu Haifeng Draws Attention Ahead of CCP Fifth Plenum as Xi Renews Security Push - Vision Times
summary: The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) will hold the Fifth Plenary Session of its 20th Central Committee from Oct. 26 to 29, according to a [Sept. 21 announcement from Xinhua](https://app.xinhuanet.com/news/article.html?articleId=202609215f91ba7
content:
The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) will hold the Fifth Plenary Session of its 20th Central Committee from Oct. 26 to 29, according to a [Sept. 21 announcement from Xinhua](https://app.xinhuanet.com/news/article.html?articleId=202609215f91ba7df196487ab25232ca078d3ed0&utm_source=chatgpt.com). With the party also moving toward its 21st National Congress in 2027, personnel changes and the future composition of the leadership are drawing growing attention.

Among the officials back in the spotlight is Hu Haifeng, the 53-year-old son of former CCP leader Hu Jintao. Hu appeared at a State Council Information Office briefing on Sept. 23, shortly before Hong Kong media raised fresh questions about whether he could advance further in the party hierarchy.

At the same time, CCP leader Xi Jinping has renewed his emphasis on domestic security, ordering officials to advance the “Peaceful China Initiative” and strengthen the party-state’s capacity to identify and contain risks.

## **Hu Haifeng returns to the spotlight**

Hu has served as vice minister of Civil Affairs since January 2024, when the [State Council announced his appointment](https://english.www.gov.cn/news/202401/16/content_WS65a66409c6d0868f4e8e323b.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) after he had spent more than five years as party secretary of Lishui in Zhejiang Province.

On Sept. 23, Hu appeared alongside Civil Affairs Minister Li Changguan and other vice ministers at a government briefing on civil affairs policy under China’s 15th Five-Year Plan. [Xinhua’s account of the briefing](https://www1.xinhuanet.com/politics/20260923/f85fc42f02af4fe887ba39ba45134576/c.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) quoted Hu extensively on children’s welfare, social organizations and charitable organizations.

Hu said authorities plan to expand services for disadvantaged children, including programs covering psychological health, safety and guardianship. He also outlined tighter supervision of social organizations and charities.

The appearance revived interest in Hu’s political future. An [Oct. 1 article in the Hong Kong Economic Journal](https://www.hkej.com/dailynews/cntw/article/4528330/%E8%83%A1%E6%B5%B7%E5%B3%B0%E8%BD%89%E4%BB%9513%E5%B9%B4%2B%E6%9C%89%E6%9C%9B%E6%99%89%E8%BA%AB%E3%80%8C%E5%85%A9%E5%A7%94%E3%80%8D?utm_source=chatgpt.com) noted that speculation over Hu’s career has followed him since he entered politics more than a decade ago and said his prospects are again attracting attention as the CCP approaches another period of leadership reshuffling.

Hu entered government work in Zhejiang in 2013 after holding positions at Tsinghua University-affiliated organizations and security-equipment maker Nuctech. He later served as mayor of Jiaxing and party secretary of Lishui before moving to Beijing as vice minister.

Despite repeated outside speculation about possible promotions, Hu remained a vice minister at the Sept. 23 briefing. There has been no official announcement of a new position.

## **Promotion questions return ahead of 21st Party Congress**

The renewed attention surrounding Hu comes as the CCP begins looking toward its 21st National Congress, expected in 2027.

The Hong Kong Economic Journal said Hu’s potential advancement should be viewed against the wider personnel maneuvering that traditionally precedes a party congress. His family background guarantees unusual scrutiny: Hu Jintao led the CCP from 2002 to 2012, making his son’s career closely watched by China observers.

However, Hu’s recent public appearance by itself does not establish that a promotion is imminent. The Sept. 23 event was an official policy briefing involving the ministry’s senior leadership, and Hu spoke on policy areas falling within his portfolio.

That distinction was largely missing from the original speculation surrounding his appearance. While media coverage may provide clues about an official’s standing, the CCP rarely discloses senior personnel decisions before they are formally approved.

## **Xi puts renewed emphasis on domestic security**

Separately, Xi has issued a fresh directive calling for China’s security apparatus to strengthen what Beijing officially calls the “Peaceful China Initiative.”

According to the [Chinese government’s account of the Sept. 28 directive](https://english.www.gov.cn/news/202609/28/content_WS6aba4404c6d00ca5f9a0d7fe.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com), Xi ordered officials to pursue a “holistic approach to national security,” strengthen the party’s leadership over security work and “prevent and mitigate all kinds of risks.” He called for efforts to make the country safer, society more orderly and governance more effective.

The initiative dates to the early years of Xi’s leadership and combines public security, social governance, legal controls and increasingly technology-based risk monitoring.

The timing has attracted attention because the directive comes as the CCP approaches another major leadership transition. The [South China Morning Post](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/politics/article/3369101/xi-jinping-demands-safer-china-communist-party-prepares-leadership-reshuffle?utm_source=chatgpt.com) described the order as a renewed focus on domestic stability ahead of the 21st Party Congress and noted that it followed Xi’s recent visit to the United States.

That context makes the coming Fifth Plenum particularly significant. Rather than proving the existence of a specific internal crisis, the simultaneous focus on personnel positioning and domestic security shows that Beijing is already preparing for a politically consequential period leading into the CCP’s next national congress.

content:
## Authors:

**Marta Oliynyk-D’omochko, Yurii Oliinyk, Anatolii Maksymov**

Experts of the Center for African Studies

[Audio 3](https://www.kas.de/documents/270026/47150255/%D0%A6%D0%B5%D0%BD%D1%82%D1%80+%D0%B4%D0%BE%D1%81%D0%BB%D1%96%D0%B4%D0%B6%D0%B5%D0%BD%D0%BD%D1%8F+%D0%90%D1%84%D1%80%D0%B8%D0%BA%D0%B8_ENG.mp3/5bcdce7c-7b59-f990-b17c-a7aeedcae9ca?version=1.0&t=1791195066878)

Audio:African Vector of Global Politics: Interests of Key Actors and Opportunities for Ukraine

_The full analytics is available for download as a PDF on the right panel of the page._

## Summary

In 2026, Africa became the main arena of competition between global centers of influence. The countries of the continent are adapting to this struggle, balancing among the interests of external players for the sake of their own development. This brief analyzes the strategies of the United States (US), the European Union (EU), the United Kingdom, China, and Russia, and identifies opportunities for strengthening Ukraine’s presence in the region.

### Transformation of American Strategy in Africa

As of 2026, US policy in Africa has transformed into a “transactional model” based on pragmatic exchange: support for investment and security in return for access to critical resources and loyalty in the global confrontation. This shift is reinforced by a change in the institutional architecture, notably the restructuring of the United States Agency for International Development and the abandonment of “non-reciprocal preferences” in the trade regime of the African Growth and Opportunity Act. At the same time, the toolkit is oriented toward direct returns for the American economy.

In the extractive sector, the implementation of this strategy proceeds through a “dealmaking approach” aimed at deconstructing the monopoly of the People’s Republic of China (PRC). Washington acts as a diplomatic mediator in conflicts in order to unlock access to strategic assets for American companies. A similar strategy of flexible pragmatism is also applied to South Africa, where Washington is purposefully consolidating control over extractive chains, minimizing the space for Beijing’s expansion.

With the same aim, Washington pragmatically weaves national interests into the global architecture of the Group of Seven (G7), notably the Partnership for Global Infrastructure and Investment (PGII) initiative, while securing control over key nodes for American corporations. The flagship project in this context is the Lobito Corridor – the modernization of 1,300 km of railways and port infrastructure in Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Zambia for the export of minerals. In addition, the US is implementing its strategy of influence in Africa through a number of other programs in the areas of the “green” energy transition (South Africa, Kenya) and institutional facilitation (through support for the Africa Virtual Investment Platform).

Washington’s systematic activity is underpinned by the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, whose portfolio focuses on hub countries: Morocco, Nigeria, South Africa, and Kenya. Beyond these countries, by investing in energy (Sierra Leone, Gabon) and logistics, the corporation integrates American capital into key network assets, turning them into a platform for the dominance of American standards. Strategic investments in regional digital platforms allow the US to introduce its own technological standards and control key data transmission nodes, limiting the influence of competitors.

At the same time, three factors constrain the US strategy. The first is high political dependence on the situation in Washington: changes of administration or shifting priorities often lead to the freezing of projects, which reduces the trust of African partners. The aggressive rhetoric of certain political leaders is an additional destabilizing factor. The second is strict compliance requirements and regulatory restrictions, which narrow access to tenders for external players and slow project implementation compared with the PRC’s directive methods. The third is that the US role in Africa has been reduced to attempts to seize the initiative from competitors. This puts Washington in a weaker position: instead of setting the rules of the game, it is forced to “embed itself” in systems where China has already established its logistical and technological standards.

The changing political situation in the Sahel and the arrival of the Trump administration have driven a number of key changes in the US military sphere in Africa. The first concerns the scaling up of counterterrorism operations under the United States Africa Command, particularly in Somalia and Nigeria. The second change concerns the relocation of infrastructure and part of the activity to Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, and Nigeria after the loss of access to bases in the Sahel. In addition, the completion in January 2026 of the expansion of the Manda Bay base (Kenya) has substantially strengthened US capabilities for air monitoring and power projection in East Africa. The third change is that the US actively uses military diplomacy – from joint exercises with representatives of the opposing sides in Libya to non-public contacts of the Africa Command in the Sahel – in order to seize the initiative from competitors and restore influence over the region’s security architecture.

Given strict US protectionism, Ukraine’s direct integration into African projects through official tenders is rather unlikely due to regulatory restrictions on the origin of services. A realistic strategy for Ukraine lies in positioning itself as an engineering subcontractor for American prime contractors, particularly at the stage of calculating and designing complex mining and beneficiation processes. Another possible option is engaging Ukrainian specialists with experience in operating critical infrastructure under conditions of security instability. Their unique experience of working in a high-risk environment gives projects high operational resilience, making it possible to maintain critical infrastructure amid acute instability of logistics and communications.

### Infrastructure and Security Architecture of EU Policy in Africa

For the EU, the African vector is critical for ensuring security and social stability on its own southern flank. Brussels’ toolkit is aimed at eliminating the root causes of migration – the absence of legal economic opportunities and constant security threats – notably through Global Gateway investments and financial support under the European Peace Facility. These measures also serve the function of geopolitical deterrence and the strengthening of the EU’s own positions.

The Global Gateway initiative is positioned as a high-quality alternative to Chinese expansion. Thanks to its financial architecture and the Team Europe approach, Brussels is mobilizing up to €150 billion, using risk-guarantee mechanisms. The strategic focus is concentrated on four key modules: digitalization, climate and energy, transport, and healthcare and education, which strengthen the EU’s humanitarian influence.

The EU’s orientation toward energy, logistics, and critical resources is a strategic response to the monopolization of these areas by the PRC, which threatens Europe’s industrial future and the success of the “Green Deal”. For example, in the energy sphere, the Africa–EU Green Energy initiative is being implemented with the aim of reaching 50 gigawatts of renewable energy sources by 2030. Through the creation of transregional energy systems, the EU seeks to integrate Africa’s energy potential into its own grid, turning the continent into a stable supplier for European industry. This is a way to offset dependence on external energy sources and to entrench the region’s technological attachment to EU standards.

However, the EU seeks to implement an approach distinct from the simple export of raw materials. The EU offers countries (for example, Namibia, the DRC, Zambia, and Rwanda, with which relevant memoranda have been concluded) an alternative, focusing on building up local processing industries. This allows African countries to retain a share of added value within their economies, which corresponds to the goals of the continent’s countries.

In the infrastructure sphere, the EU’s cooperation with the African Union on 12 strategic corridors is a key instrument for entrenching European capital in the continent’s logistics. The development of such facilities as the Lobito Corridor and the Abidjan–Lagos corridor is a priority direction of this expansion.

Despite the EU’s technological advantage, the strategy’s implementation is being slowed by two critical factors. The first is procedural slowness. Bureaucratic donor coordination and the dragging out of the feasibility-study stage reduce the speed of implementation, making the EU less competitive compared with actors that act directively. The second lies in the realm of security challenges. High risks make investment projects too expensive and risky for private capital. Accordingly, the key task becomes creating conditions under which European corporations can implement capital-intensive projects without waiting for the full stabilization of the region, relying instead on the systemic support of state financial institutions.

However, financial guarantees are insufficient where security stability is absent, which makes EU–Africa military cooperation necessary. Since 2022, the EU’s key security instrument has been the European Peace Facility (EPF), through which Brussels implements a “stabilization donor” model, focusing mainly on the supply of non-lethal equipment and the professional training of local security forces. The differentiated geography of assistance covers countering jihadism in West Africa, ensuring freedom of navigation in East Africa, and localizing conflicts in the center and south of the continent. The prioritization of partners’ requests and the shift to bilateral agreements allow the EU to respond promptly to challenges, avoiding the bureaucratic delays of collective cooperation formats.

At the same time, EU security policy faces a funding deficit due to the prioritization of Global Gateway economic projects. On the other hand, in Africa, Brussels is increasingly becoming hostage to a conflict between political principles and economic interests. A vivid example is the financing of the Rwandan contingent in Mozambique to protect the assets of TotalEnergies. By choosing Kigali as the executor, the EU finds itself in a trap: on the one hand, Rwandan forces effectively secure energy facilities, while on the other, support for Rwanda, which is destabilizing the neighboring DRC, substantially complicates pan-European efforts to settle regional conflicts and undermines trust in the European peacekeeping strategy.

Ukraine’s integration into EU projects in Africa requires a shift to a subcontracting model within consortia with European engineering, procurement, and construction contractors, which would allow Ukrainian business to bypass regulatory barriers and insurance restrictions. The key niches for cooperation are engineering and technical audit, the implementation of government technology solutions, and equipment service support, where experience of working under high-risk conditions becomes a competitive advantage. To this end, the state needs to shift its focus from political lobbying to institutional support, establishing systematic communication with European business and financial institutions in order to integrate Ukrainian companies into tender consortia.

### United Kingdom’s New Approach to African Continent
