title: Asian/American Women: Resistance against Invisibility | Blog of the APA
summary: [![Image 1: APA_HanruiChen_Header](https://blog.apaonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/APA_HanruiChen_Header.jpg)](https://i0.wp.com/blog.apaonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/APA_HanruiChen_Header.jpg?fit=5200%2C3467&ssl=1) Image prov
content:
[![Image 1: APA_HanruiChen_Header](https://blog.apaonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/APA_HanruiChen_Header.jpg)](https://i0.wp.com/blog.apaonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/APA_HanruiChen_Header.jpg?fit=5200%2C3467&ssl=1)

Image provided by Chen.

In the collection [_Making More Waves_](https://www.asianwomenunited.org/making-more-waves-new-writings-by-asian-american-women/) (1997), Asian/American activist Helen Zia raises a question: “Where are the Asian women?” By reviewing violent crimes against Asian/American women between 1984 and 1992, Helen Zia demonstrates that despite being frequent targets of racist violence, including brutal sexual assaults and lynchings, [Asian/American women](https://www.sup.org/books/literary-studies-and-literature/asianamerican) (following David Palumbo-Liu’s resistant deconstruction of the obscured term “Asian American” with a “/”) remained largely invisible within dominant social discourse. Twenty-four years after 1997, the COVID-19 pandemic witnessed another surge in anti-Asian violence. According to [NBC news](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/asian-america/there-were-3-800-anti-asian-racist-incidents-mostly-against-n1261257), the research released by Stop AAPI Hate’s report shows that 68% anti-Asian hate incidents over roughly a pandemic year were reported by Asian/American women, including heinous incidents resulting in the victim’s death.

**Invisibility as History**

This disproportionate violence toward Asian women demonstrates the never-fading aftershocks of the Exclusion Acts in the last two centuries. While the [Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882](https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/chinese-exclusion-act) restricted the entry of Chinese laborers and their spouses into the United States due to the rise of local protectionism, the earlier [Page Act of 1875](https://immigrationhistory.org/item/page-act) legitimized the dehumanization of Asian female immigrants from “China, Japan, or any Oriental country” by stigmatizing them as prostitutes emigrating for “lewd and immoral purposes.” The Page Act not only set huge obstacles for the formation of Asian immigrant families and generations, but also exacerbated the exclusion circumstances of Asian immigrants before implementing a more extensive policy of racial exclusion that lasted for more than 60 years. By juridically reifying Asian women as sexualized objects, the state reproduced and reinforced the mutually constitutive mechanisms of patriarchy and racism at the national level. According to [Erika Lee](https://uncpress.org/9780807854488/at-americas-gates/)’s historical research, John H. Wise, the collector of customs and chief of the Chinese Bureau in San Francisco, stated unequivocally in 1895 that all Chinese women would be considered prostitutes until they can sufficiently prove that they were not. Such an institutionalized discourse of stigmatization expressed in an essentialist way provided the justification for the incarceration of Asian immigrants at Angel Island, the immigration detention headquarters, as well as the invasive medical examinations imposed upon them.

The collusion between racialized gender violence and juridical-political discourse not only constructs Asian women as sexualized objects unworthy of historical recognition, but also deprives them of the opportunity to construct their history in the public sphere. According to the oral history edited by [Judy Yung and Him Mark Lai](https://history.stanford.edu/publications/chinese-american-voices-gold-rush-present), numerous first-generation Chinese immigrants remained reluctant to speak about their experiences on Angel Island, often suppressing these memories in order to protect their families from renewed state scrutiny and to safeguard the precarious legality of their residency status. It was not until the 1970s, [the period that Asian/American women begin to broadly engage in community and mainstream politics](https://www.ucpress.edu/books/unbound-feet/paper), that the history of female victims on Angel Island began to be documented as a part of history. On the level of material resources, the poems written by the imprisoned people of Angel Island on wooden planks during their darkest days were only found in the men’s barracks. In 1940 there was a fire that burnt the women’s barracks to ashes, destroying all the women’s writing during this painful historical period. We can only glean fragments of this history of pain and resistance behind the bars of women’s barracks from the memory of a very limited number of survivors recorded in [_Island_](https://uwapress.uw.edu/book/9780295994079/island/): “It was like songs people would sing […] I didn’t write on the walls, but I did compose some poems, crying at the same time.” Oral histories also record a range of practices undertaken by Asian women from tactical acts in response to inspection to more explicit forms of resistance, like the circulation of coaching notes, legal appeal, and even suicide as the most desperate refusal.

Although oral histories testify to the existence of poetic writing by Asian women during their detention on Angel Island, the loss of these poems, a century of forced reticence in the hidden history of incarnation, has resulted in an unfillable void in the history of Asian women immigrants. As mentioned in Michel-Rolph Trouillot’s [_Silencing the Past_](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/246609/silencing-the-past-by-michel-rolph-trouillot/) (1995), the entry of silence in the production of the historical narrative emerges at four moments: “the moment of fact creation; the moment of fact assembly; the moment of fact retrieval; and the moment of retrospective significance.” The dispersal of first-hand physical materials related to the place-based resistance of first-generation Asian immigrant women exemplifies the silences produced at the first two moments of historical production through the convergence of accidental catastrophes and deliberate racialized gendered violence. These silences lead to Asian/American women being largely portrayed as passive, submissive, and hypersexual objects devoid of autonomy in mainstream and exclusive historical narratives, [an image that is repeatedly reinforced by the institutionalized power](https://books.google.com/books/about/The_Administrative_Control_of_Aliens.html?id=O6kFAAAAMAAJ). [The U.S. military prostitution system in the Asian-Pacific region after World War II](https://apjjf.org/katharine-hs-moon/3019/article), [the Atlanta massacre during the pandemic](https://abcnews.com/US/atlanta-shooting-legacy-misogyny-racism-asian-women/story?id=76533776), as well as the [stereotypical depiction of Asian/American figures](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/5js0w7d3)[in the mass media](https://doi.org/10.1080/00043125.2023.2167902), all exemplify the afterlife of exclusion and objectification, through which Asian/American women continue to be constituted as targets of corporeal and psychic violence.

**Resistance Against Invisibility as Presence**

Within professional fields, this structural violence manifests itself in the consequent tendency to dismiss Asian American studies as immature and as lacking systematic framework. In [_Immigrant Acts_](https://read.dukeupress.edu/books/book/400/Immigrant-ActsOn-Asian-American-Cultural-Politics) (1996), Lisa Lowe stresses that higher education system’s promotion of a “prior” Western civilization not only imposes a kind of voiceless invisibility on students of color in the classroom, but institutionally alienates interdisciplinary fields such as Ethnic Studies and Gender Studies as merely empirical and underdeveloped.

This constructed absence also permeates more traditional academic disciplines. The essay [_Rendered Invisible: Are Asian Americans a Model or a Marginalized Minority_](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34410735/) (2021) reveals Asian women’s invisibility in psychology despite their working as trailblazers in this field since the 1970s. The similar problem also stands in the field of philosophy, where Asian/American feminism lies at the margin of its marginated fields. This absence stands in great contrast to Asian/American women’s active engagement in the construction of Third World feminism since the 1970s. [In an APA newsletter in 2014](https://cdn.ymaws.com/www.apaonline.org/resource/collection/2EAF6689-4B0D-4CCB-9DC6-FB926D8FF530/AsianV14n1.pdf), David Haekwon Kim stresses the strikingly low representation of Asian/Americans in the American Philosophical Association (APA). By tracing the historical Exclusion Acts and the identity construction of Asian/Americans, Kim argues that this absence is rooted in complicated structures of derogation, which simultaneously perpetuate the Anti-Asian process in American history and allow white people to maintain their ignorance of Anti-Asian racialization.

While “[white ignorance](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12023814/)” continues to sustain the epistemic neglect of Asian/Americans, Asian/American Philosophy as a new subfield dedicated to theorizing Asian/American oppression and diaspora from a philosophical perspective challenges such neglect by producing a new visibility. [Helen Ngo’s](https://philpapers.org/rec/NGOTHO) (2017) and [Boram Jeong’s](https://philpapers.org/versions/JEOAPO-2) (2021) discussion of racism as an embodied process that is constantly being produced and experienced in daily life reads racism as the resemblance of phenomenological events. While Ngo emphasizes racism as the violence of intersubjectivity on the ontological plane mediated by gestural expressions and cultivated habits that are constantly shrouding the bodies of racial and ethnic minorities in existential stress and uncanniness, Jeong discusses racism from the perspective of epistemological violence. Jeong stresses that the dominated, white-centered perception deprives people of color of shared time and space by altering its ontological mapping of the world, a kind of deprivation manifest as denial and invisibility upon Yellow bodies. In fact, when writing this post, I was constantly attacked by the existential stress mentioned by Ngo, as my position as an Asian subject both excluded from and complicit within structures of white supremacy and anti-Blackness urges me to re-examine my words to ensure my appeal for Asian visibility does not fuel hatred of other races. In [Shireen Roshanravan’s](https://uwapress.uw.edu/book/9780295744353/asian-american-feminisms-and-women-of-color-politics/) (2018) interpretation, it is this self-consciousness of being an inside-outsider to the Black/White racial binary that promotes the formation of a cross-racial coalition, a new terrain for resistance. [Youjin Kong](https://journals.publishing.umich.edu/ergo/article/id/2622/) (2023), on the other hand, reveals this inner struggle and its manifestation in social practice as a fluid and non-stop multifaceted process by which Asian/American women construct their own identity under identity symbols such as “yellow peril,” “model minority,” and “critical race feminist.” Kong also demonstrates intersectionality theory as a non-ideal theory that helps women from different racial background to mobilize and transform their identities in ways deconstructing the dominated social power that shapes different ethnic groups into isolated, antagonistic relationships. Only through this process can cross-racial coalitions come into existence.

The history of Asian/American women cultivating cross-racial solidarities and resisting insularity and animosity toward other racial groups—especially with Black people—produced by the “Model Minority” myth through social movements echoes the theoretical claims of Asian/American feminism. From the [Third World Women’s Alliance](https://www.dwherstories.com/timeline/radical-women-of-color-feminisms) in second-wave feminism to the [#Asians4BlackLives campaign](https://doi.org/10.1080/00447471.2019.16

title: Nancy Pelosi Championed a Hong Kong Dissident. She May Have Doomed Him. (opinion)
summary: In one of the [final speeches](http://pelosi.house.gov/news/press-releases/pelosi-calls-joshua-wongs-freedom-house-floor-we-want-be-sure-they-know-we) of her congressional career, Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D–Calif.) rose last month "to call attent
content:
In one of the [final speeches](http://pelosi.house.gov/news/press-releases/pelosi-calls-joshua-wongs-freedom-house-floor-we-want-be-sure-they-know-we) of her congressional career, Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D–Calif.) rose last month "to call attention to what is happening in Hong Kong." She was condemning the Chinese government for its prosecution of protester Joshua Wong. Yet it was exactly that attention from Congress that had helped doom Wong in the first place. Like Hmong militias and Kurdish resistance fighters in years past, leaders in the Hong Kong protest movement had a one-sided partnership with U.S. politicians that would not (and could not) be reciprocated, and that ultimately put a target on their backs.

At the center of this history, culminating with Wong's prosecution, is Pelosi herself. Pelosi has planted herself at the center of every major China debate since the end of the Cold War and, early on in her career, took risks to defend her hawkish positions toward Beijing. But brazenness does not necessarily mean bravery. Pelosi squandered political capital over the decades on inconsequential adventures, achieving no serious victories, while the price paid by people caught between Beijing and Washington may prove far more exorbitant than anything Pelosi risked.

This crusade began in 1991, when Pelosi traveled to Beijing as part of an official congressional [trade](https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/98-603.html) delegation. Three days into her trip, Pelosi quietly [snuck out](https://www.sfgate.com/news/article/Pelosi-on-China-A-voice-in-the-global-wilderness-3082494.php) of her hotel, without Chinese approval, trailed by a small posse. She was headed to Tiananmen Square, the site of the infamous 1989 crackdown that occurred two years earlier.

When Pelosi arrived in the square with two of her House colleagues, they unfurled a banner that read, "To those who died for democracy in China." The banner was written in English and Chinese, indicating that its intended audience was both their American constituents and their Chinese hosts. Upon discovering the ceremony, local police began to [chase](https://www.politico.com/news/2022/07/28/pelosi-china-taiwan-00048352) Pelosi and her fellow representatives out of the square, as onlookers and journalists were shoved, corralled, and forcefully detained for filming.

Her colleague John Miller (R–Wash.) revealed that this P.R. stunt was planned from the beginning—on a bipartisan basis. "We had one major purpose in going to Beijing," Miller [told](https://www.upi.com/Archives/1991/09/05/US-lawmakers-warn-China-on-human-rights/8682684043200/) reporters, "That was to deliver the strongest possible message to the Chinese government leaders that Americans and the American Congress have not forgotten Tiananmen Square."

Pelosi herself would admit that nothing else was achieved. The trip [failed](https://www.deseret.com/1991/9/5/18939474/human-rights-team-serves-notice-to-china/) "to see or gain the release of prominent imprisoned dissidents or get promises of human rights improvements from the officials," she said. Relations between the two countries took a sharp downward turn. But Pelosi and Miller's third colleague, Rep. Ben Jones (D–Ga.), [said](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eXNnqsfU9GI&t=109s) at Tiananmen that the event was a "special moment for us." Indeed it was a special moment—for _them_. Pay no attention to the bystanders who were roughed up by police in the process.

## **A Progressive Hawk Flies to Taiwan**

In mid-2022, Pelosi, now Speaker of the House but still a _persona non grata_ in mainland China, would perform a stunt with more grievous potential consequences. She decided to become the first high-ranking American official in [over 25 years](https://www.upi.com/Archives/1997/04/02/Gingrich-meets-with-Taiwans-president/5806859957200/) to visit leaders in Taiwan, a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory.

Word of this trip generated major backlash among the American establishment. _The New York Times_' Thomas Friedman, hardly a pro-China commentator, [called](https://www.nytimes.com/2022/08/01/opinion/nancy-pelosi-taiwan-china.html) Pelosi's planned trip "utterly reckless, dangerous and irresponsible." Members of the intelligence community [warned](https://www.politico.com/news/2022/07/22/white-house-pelosi-taiwan-trip-00047304) that a purely symbolic visit "looks like a military operation" to the Chinese government, no matter how well-intentioned or void of substance.

The late Deng Xiaoping had [once said](https://www.marxists.org/reference/archive/deng-xiaoping/1984/44.htm#:~:text=The%20question%20of%20Taiwan%20is%20the%20main%20obstacle%20to%20better%20relations%20between%20China%20and%20the%20United%20States) that "the main obstacle to better relations between China and the United States" was the treatment of Taiwan "as a U.S. aircraft carrier." Indeed, after Pelosi's visit, the Chinese military began a [live-fire exercise](https://www.npr.org/2022/08/04/1115550972/china-taiwan-missile-exercises), lobbing missiles into the Taiwan Strait.

President Joe Biden publicly [admonished](https://www.axios.com/2022/07/21/biden-pelosi-trip-taiwan) Pelosi. Yet none of this seemed to matter to Pelosi, whom _Politico_ dubbed a ["progressive hawk."](https://www.politico.com/news/2022/07/28/pelosi-china-taiwan-00048352) During one press conference, Pelosi nonchalantly [mentioned](https://www.cnn.com/2022/07/25/china/china-us-pelosi-visit-concerns-intl-hnk-mic) that American military officials warned that she could be "shot down, or something like that."

But as in her Tiananmen Square stunt, she enjoyed strong support from the Republican Party. House Minority Leader Kevin McCarthy (R–Calif.) [offered his support](https://www.foxnews.com/video/6310379716112) to Pelosi, saying, "America should always speak with one voice." From the Senate floor, Minority Leader Mitch McConnell (R–Ky.) [said](https://www.dailymail.com/news/article-11075371/Mitch-McConnell-sides-Pelosi-Senate-speech-says-right-visit-Taiwan.html) that Pelosi, independent of the White House's concerns, has "every right" to visit Taiwan. Former Defense Secretary Mark Esper and former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo enthusiastically [supported](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2022/jul/26/trump-allies-nancy-pelosi-taiwan-china-biden) Pelosi's decision as well. "Nancy, I'll go with you," Pompeo wrote on Twitter, "I'm banned in China, but not freedom-loving Taiwan."

And as in Tiananmen Square, Pelosi's Taiwan ["cheerleading"](https://www.newyorker.com/news/q-and-a/the-provocative-politics-of-nancy-pelosis-trip-to-taiwan) accomplished nothing substantive. No deals were reached, no agreements were signed. As the Taiwan scholar Shelley Rigger [told](https://www.newyorker.com/news/q-and-a/the-provocative-politics-of-nancy-pelosis-trip-to-taiwan)_The New Yorker_ during Pelosi's visit, the trip "does not benefit Taiwan, probably does harm to Taiwan's security, and it has ensured that U.S.-China relations, which were already pretty bad, are worse than they were before."

One month after Pelosi's departure, Pompeo, who was then in Taiwan on a separate visit, [complained](https://ocacnews.net/article/321250) to reporters that he'd seen local reports calling the speaker's visit "provocative" and "threatening." Pompeo dismissed this out of hand: "We should never forget who's threatening. It is not the great people of Taiwan. It is not the United States of America. The only threat to this region, the people who desire to upend what we know is right, and decent and moral, is in fact the Chinese Communist Party."

## **The nuclear option**

Refusing to take responsibility for the ripple effects of American policy in East Asia is, of course, [not new](https://www.nytimes.com/2000/11/18/opinion/the-forgotten-debt-to-vietnam.html#:~:text=In%201972%2C%20pressing%20the%20North%20to%20sign%20a%20peace%20agreement%2C%20Henry%20Kissinger%20agreed%20in%20Paris%20to%20reparations%20for%20the%20war%20damage%20to%20Vietnam.). But in Joshua Wong's case, the result of American hubris is distinctly bitter. American politicians put Wong in danger while raising his hopes in a rescue that would not come.

Wong first gained [international recognition](https://time.com/3482556/hong-kong-protest-teenagers/) in 2014 for his leading role in Hong Kong's [Umbrella Movement](https://www.bbc.co.uk/newsround/49862757), a series of anti-government protests that comprised both student organizations, including Wong's Scholarism, and major civil society groups. As part of the 1997 handover agreement between the United Kingdom and China, Hong Kong was [guaranteed](https://treaties.fcdo.gov.uk/awweb/pdfopener?md=1&did=68291) 50 years of legislative, legal, and economic autonomy under China's "one country, two systems" framework. Over time, however, this autonomy would be challenged and degraded. But on August 31, 2014, the Standing Committee of China's National People's Congress [declared](https://www.elegislation.gov.hk/hk/A212) that politicians running for office in Hong Kong's upcoming elections must "love the country," meaning China, "and love Hong Kong." Candidates would have to be screened by Beijing and, if approved, only then could run in the region's popular elections.

This was a nonstarter for many in Hong Kong, including Wong, who had already gained the attention of his classmates and local authorities for his resistance to mainland interference. Wong had, in fact, led a successful student campaign against a 2012 curriculum change [pushed](https://www.nytimes.com/2012/07/30/world/asia/thousands-protest-chinas-curriculum-plans-for-hong-kong-schools.html) by the Chinese government.

Although the 2014 protests were unsuccessful at stopping the new election law, Wong gained the attention of American supporters. He made it on the [cover](https://time.com/3482556/hong-kong-protest-teenagers/) of _TIME_ magazine as "The Face of Protest" and one of its [25 Most Influential Teens](https://www.youngpostclub.com/yp/discover/news/global/article/3058294/joshua-wong-named-one-times-25-most-influential-teens-2014?isbot=1). Other outlets called Wong the "next tank man," a reference to an iconic [Associated Press photo](https://edition.cnn.com/interactive/2019/05/world/tiananmen-square-tank-man-cnnphotos/) from the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests. When the U.S. government announced its lukewarm support for the 2014 protests, _The Wall Street Journal_[report](https://www.wsj.com/video/joshua-wong-wants-action-not-words-from-obama/41E32D3F-879B-43F5-A2EC-D32254DED609) used Wong to slam then-President Obama. "Hong Kong," Wong explained, "needs more than a few words from Obama."

Like Wong, many U.S. legislators wanted more than words from the White House. Rep. Christopher Smith (R–N.J.), co-chair of the Congressional-Executive Commission on China, [drafted](https://www.congress.gov/bill/113th-congress/house-bill/5696) the Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act. It would impose economic sanctions that Steve Tsang, director of the University of London's SOAS China Institute, dubbed "[the nuclear option](https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/what-hong-kong-losing-its-special-status-would-mean/2020/07/01/a6586164-bbfc-11ea-97c1-6cf116ffe26c_story.html)," because they would destroy China's main link to the global financial system.

Meanwhile, Pelosi would meet with the now-famous Wong for the first time in [2015](https://x.com/SpeakerPelosi/status/666795258747953152), and again in [2016](https://x.com/SpeakerPelosi/status/799655824784326656) and [2019](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pvJLgwBi5ds). That final meeting caught particular attention from the Chinese government, culminating in Wong's most recent, and most serious, trial.

That year, the Chinese government put forward another piece of legislation that many in Hong Kong viewed as destructive to the "one country, two systems" framework

# U.S.-China Trade Truce Extended Two Months: BIS Affiliates Rule Suspension Follows

By [Scott Wise](https://www.crowell.com/en/professionals/scott-wise), [Chandler Leonard](https://www.crowell.com/Professionals/Chandler-Leonard)&[Nate Young](https://www.crowell.com/en/professionals/nate-young) on September 30, 2026

Posted in [Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS)](https://www.cmtradelaw.com/category/bureau-of-industry-and-security-bis/), [China](https://www.cmtradelaw.com/category/china/), [Department of Commerce](https://www.cmtradelaw.com/category/department-of-commerce/)

*   **Key takeaway #1:** The U.S.-China trade truce has been extended through January 10, 2027, and the Bureau of Industry and Security’s (BIS’s) suspension of the Affiliates Rule will be [extended](https://exportcompliancedaily.com/article/view?search_id=90451&id=2872385) accordingly.
*   **Key takeaway #2:** The Affiliates Rule, [issued](https://www.crowell.com/en/insights/client-alerts/bis-issues-affiliates-rule-to-dramatically-expand-applicability-of-entity-and-military-end-user-lists) as an Interim Final Rule on September 29, 2025, expanded U.S. export restrictions by subjecting any non-U.S. entity owned 50% or more, directly or indirectly, by one or more parties on the Entity List, Military End-User (MEU) List, or certain Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN List) to the same license requirements as the listed parent.
*   **Key takeaway #3:** While the suspension delays immediate compliance obligations, the rule has not been repealed. Companies that have not yet used the past year to build out Affiliates Rule-ready compliance programs should consider doing so before the suspension potentially expires.

**What Happened?**

On September 24, 2026, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that the United States and China agreed to extend their trade truce through January 10, 2027, two months beyond the original timeline established last November. The extension correspondingly pushes back the effective date of the BIS Affiliates Rule, which had been [scheduled](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/11/12/2025-19846/one-year-suspension-of-expansion-of-end-user-controls-for-affiliates-of-certain-listed-entities) to go back into effect on November 9, 2026. As of the date of this writing, BIS has not yet published a Federal Register notice formally extending the suspension by two months.

The original truce was reached at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Busan, South Korea on October 30, 2025, with BIS formally publishing a one-year suspension of the Affiliates Rule on November 10, 2025. Under the deal, the U.S. suspended the Affiliates Rule in exchange for Beijing suspending its export restrictions on rare earth minerals.

A quick refresher on the Affiliates Rule:

**What Is the Scope of the Affiliates Rule?**

*   **Summary:** The Affiliates Rule expanded U.S. export restrictions under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to cover foreign affiliates owned 50% or more (directly or indirectly) by one or more entities on the Entity List, MEU List, or certain SDN designees (collectively, “covered-list parties”).

Key features include:

*   **Rule of Most Restrictiveness:** Where multiple listed entities together own 50% or more of an affiliate, the most restrictive license requirements of any owner apply, even if that owner holds the smaller stake. If any owner is subject to a Foreign Direct Product Rule (FDPR), the FDPR applies to the affiliate as well.
*   **SDN Coverage:** The Affiliates Rule applies to SDNs identified under §744.8 of the EAR, including those designated pursuant to Belarus, Russia, WMD, terrorism, narcotic, and criminal network sanctions programs, to better prevent diversion and align EAR restrictions with corresponding Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) restrictions.
*   **Affirmative Duty/Red Flag 29:** BIS added Red Flag 29, requiring that if an exporter has “knowledge” that a foreign entity is partially owned by a covered-list party but the ownership percentage is unknown, the exporter must resolve the red flag through additional due diligence or apply for a BIS license.
*   For background on the Affiliates Rule, see our prior client alert [here](https://www.crowell.com/en/insights/client-alerts/bis-issues-affiliates-rule-to-dramatically-expand-applicability-of-entity-and-military-end-user-lists).

**What Is the Rationale for the Rule?**

BIS explained that the Affiliates Rule was intended to close loopholes allowing restricted parties to operate through “legally distinct” foreign affiliates and subsidiaries. The rule more closely aligns the BIS ownership standard with the traditional OFAC standard for SDN-equivalent restrictions and is consistent with recent BIS enforcement actions holding parties accountable for inadequate due diligence where diversion risks were realized.

**What Are the Implications for Exporters?**

While the suspension is not a repeal, companies should not treat the extension as a reason to delay compliance preparations further. The Affiliates Rule has been suspended for nearly a year, and companies that have not already begun updating their due diligence procedures, ownership verification protocols, end-user certificates, and contractual provisions should do so now. The Affiliates Rule’s regulatory text and reimposition mechanism remain in place, and the additional two months of runway should not be mistaken for a signal that the rule is going away. A formal BIS Federal Register notice is still required to extend the regulatory effective date, and practitioners should watch for that notice in the coming weeks.

Crowell & Moring will continue to monitor the Affiliates Rule and related U.S.-China trade developments.

Scott Wise is a partner in Crowell’s Denver office and a member of the firm’s International Trade Group. His practice focuses on export controls, economic sanctions, and outbound investment issues across industries, with an emphasis on emerging technologies and the technology industry.

Working with established and start-up tech companies, Scott helps clients to develop unique compliance programs that are responsive to the full range of regulations governing the exports of goods and services. He also trains and counsels clients on compliance with relevant export control regulations such as the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) and the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). In addition to technology companies, Scott advises companies in the aerospace and aviation, automotive, chemical, defense, electronics, energy, engineering, financial and insurance, manufacturing, professional services, security, and transportation industries, among others.

Prior to joining Crowell, Scott was the Assistant General Counsel for Global Trade at a multinational technology company where he led a consolidated team focusing on export controls, economic sanctions, and outbound investment. He was the lead export controls and economic sanctions attorney for key business groups ranging from emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence and quantum computing, to aerospace and defense contracts, and to commercial software and gaming. In that role, Scott developed the company’s compliance approach to new regulations governing the export of various new technologies, including AI, integrated circuits and chips, and quantum computing, which involved coordination between senior government officials and business leaders. Scott also has prior law firm experience in the international trade practice area.

# Justice For All’s Save Uyghur Campaign Commemorates 77 Years of CCP Illegal Occupation of East Turkistan

*   September 30, 2026
*   [Press Releases](https://www.justiceforall.org/category/resources/press-releases/), [Save Uyghur](https://www.justiceforall.org/category/campaigns/save-uighur/)

**FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE**

WASHINGTON, D.C. (September 30, 2026)********On October 1, 2026, marking 77 years since Mao Zedong proclaimed the establishment of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) in Beijing, Justice For All’s [Save Uyghur](http://saveuyghur.org/) Campaign commemorates the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) illegal military occupation and colonization of East Turkistan that occurred later that month. With Soviet backing, Chinese communist forces launched a belligerent armed invasion of East Turkistan in October 1949. By December 22, 1949, the independent East Turkistan Republic was overthrown and illegally annexed into the PRC. During the initial years of military occupation between 1949 and 1954, People’s Liberation Army forces killed hundreds of thousands of East Turkistanis who resisted Chinese rule.

East Turkistan possesses a documented history of statehood, including the first and second East Turkistan Republics established in 1933 and 1944. The Chinese colonial term “Xinjiang,” which translates to “New Territory” or “New Frontier,” was forcibly imposed following the Manchu Qing invasion in 1884, a designation rejected by the native Turkic population. Prior to the 1949 invasion, Soviet intelligence operatives assassinated core leaders of the East Turkistan Republic in late August and September 1949, undermining local governance ahead of Chinese military entry. Under international law, East Turkistan remains an illegally occupied country, and its forced incorporation into the PRC constitutes an international conflict rather than an internal Chinese matter.

“For 77 years, the Chinese Communist Party has attempted to erase the sovereignty, culture and identity of East Turkistan through military occupation, state-directed colonization and mass atrocity,” stated Arslan Hidayat, Save Uyghur Team Lead at Justice For All. “Today, as Beijing celebrates its national day, millions of Uyghurs, Kazakhs and Kyrgyz remain interned in concentration camps, subjected to forced sterilizations, forced labor and systematic destruction. Silence and diplomatic hesitation only embolden Beijing’s ambition to turn East Turkistan into an eternal colony. The international community must move beyond symbolic gestures, recognize East Turkistan as an occupied nation and pursue legal accountability against CCP officials at the International Criminal Court.”

Justice For All’s Save Uyghur Campaign presents five key policy demands to international governments and international institutions:

1.   Formally recognize East Turkistan as an illegally occupied country under international law.
2.   Reject Chinese colonial terminology (“Xinjiang”) in official diplomacy and media, adopting the proper name, East Turkistan.
3.   Initiate and support legal proceedings against Chinese state officials at the International Criminal Court (ICC) and International Court of Justice (ICJ).
4.   Enforce comprehensive import bans on goods produced through forced labor and impose sanctions on the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps (XPCC) and affiliated corporate entities.
5.   Investigate and dismantle Chinese transnational repression and covert intelligence operations targeting East Turkistani diaspora activists abroad.

NEW DELHI: India's consul general in Shanghai Pratik Mathur on Wednesday met Shanghai Mayor Zhu Zhongming and conveyed New Delhi's greetings ahead of the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China.The consulate general of India in Shanghai shared images of celebrations marking Guo Qing Jie, or National Day, in Shanghai in a post on X."Consul General Shri Pratik Mathur conveyed our best wishes to Shanghai Mayor HE Zhu Zhongming on Guo Qing Jie, the 77th anniversary of the founding of the PRC," the consulate said.

Zhu is among the first leaders born in the 1970s to serve as Shanghai mayor, a position held by several Chinese leaders who later rose to the Politburo. Previous Shanghai mayors include Jiang Zemin, Zhu Rongji and current Chinese Vice President Han Zheng.Both Chinese President Xi Jinping and Premier Li Qiang have also previously served as Shanghai Party secretaries.October 1 marks the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China, proclaimed by Mao Zedong in 1949.The outreach comes as India and China seek to advance bilateral ties following Prime Minister Narendra Modi's meeting with Xi on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi earlier this month.

title: ICT brings Tibetan children’s rights, enforced disappearances and political prisoners into focus at UN Human Rights Council
summary: The International Campaign for Tibet, in partnership with the Central Tibetan Administration, Tibet Action Institute, and other Tibetan and rights groups, raised the rights of Tibetan children, enforced disappearances, arbitrary detention a
content:
The International Campaign for Tibet, in partnership with the Central Tibetan Administration, Tibet Action Institute, and other Tibetan and rights groups, raised the rights of Tibetan children, enforced disappearances, arbitrary detention and the implications of China’s new “Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress,” among other human rights concerns, during the ongoing 63rd session of the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva this month.

The panel of the side event on children’s rights in Tibet, organized by the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights on Sep. 24, 2026. (Source: FIDH)

Opening the session with his [oral update to the Council](https://www.ohchr.org/en/statements-and-speeches/2026/09/high-commissioner-turk-updates-human-rights-council-human-rights), UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk renewed his criticism of Beijing’s policies in Tibet. “In China, tightening restrictions on the rights of the Tibetan people, including their freedom of religion, are deeply troubling,” he said, while calling for an “urgent U-turn” on these policies.

_High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk’s intervention on China and his call to repeal Beijing’s repressive policies in Tibet._

During the session, a number of states and the [European Union](https://www.eeas.europa.eu/delegations/un-geneva/hrc63-eu-statement-hrc63-item-4-human-rights-situations-require-councils-attention_en) echoed concerns about the human rights situation in Tibet, with several also raising the potential impact of China’s repressive new so-called “ethnic unity law.” States that specifically addressed Tibet included Australia, Denmark, [Finland](https://finlandabroad.fi/web/geneve/current-affairs/-/asset_publisher/h5w4iTUJhNne/content/hrc63-general-debate-on-human-rights-situations-that-require-the-council-s-attention/384951), Germany, Ireland, [Japan](https://www.geneve-mission.emb-japan.go.jp/itprtop_en/statements_rights_20260922_2.html), Sweden, Switzerland and the [United Kingdom](https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/un-human-rights-council-63-uk-statement-for-the-item-2-general-debate) (see below for more details).

### Side-event highlights systematic violations of Tibetan children’s rights

Ahead of the upcoming review of China by the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child, scheduled for 2027, ICT participated in a side event focused on the worsening human rights situation faced by Tibetan children and organized by the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights (HFHR) on Sept. 24. Speakers at the side event included Thinlay Chukki, Representative of His Holiness the Dalai Lama in Geneva; Lhadon Tethong and Dr. Gyal Lo of the Tibet Action Institute (TAI); and Kai Müller of ICT. ICT’s Vincent Metten moderated the discussion on behalf of the HFHR.

In his presentation, Müller, who serves as Executive Director of ICT Germany, highlighted how China’s recently adopted “Ethnic Unity and Progress Law” further entrenches policies and practices that violate the rights of Tibetan children by Chinese authorities in Tibet, [as documented by ICT](https://savetibet.org/new-prc-ethnic-unity-and-progress-law/). Müller also pointed to the increasing [indoctrination and militarisation](https://savetibet.org/baptism-of-youth-china-continues-to-subject-tibetan-children-to-military-style-training-and-political-indoctrination/) of Tibetan children, alongside systematic restrictions on their freedom to practice their religion.

The side event was attended by representatives of states, observer delegations, and a number of civil society groups.

### Oral statements address enforced disappearances and arbitrary detention

ICT representatives also delivered three oral statements by video on behalf of the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights during the Council session, drawing attention to enforced disappearances, arbitrary detentions and the serious implications of China’s repressive new “ethnic unity law.

“When Tibetans disappear into custody, many do not come back alive,” Kai Müller warned in his [statement](https://youtu.be/X8FZ_yLJI4Y) on Sep. 15 during the Interactive Dialogue with the UN Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances. Müller highlighted the case of Tibetan Buddhist teacher [Choktrul Dorje Ten Rinpoche, who was detained by Chinese authorities on Dec. 4, 2025 and whose whereabouts remain unknown](https://savetibet.org/nine-months-after-his-detention-prominent-tibetan-buddhist-leader-choktrul-dorje-tens-whereabouts-well-being-remain-unknown/). He also cited an [ICT report](https://savetibet.org/justice-denied-the-pattern-of-deaths-in-and-after-custody-in-tibet/) documenting the cases of 16 Tibetans who died in custody or shortly after their release between 2014 and 2026.

_ICT’s Vincent Metten’s intervention on China’s systematic use of arbitrary detention in Tibet._

The following day, Vincent Metten highlighted the “systematic use of arbitrary and incommunicado detention in Tibet” in his [statement](https://youtu.be/Kgyk964KYFE) during the Interactive Dialogue with the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention. He drew attention to the arbitrary detentions of Tibetans for peacefully defending their language, culture, religion and environment. Metten called on China to release all those arbitrarily detained, disclose the fate and whereabouts of disappeared Tibetans, guarantee detainees access to lawyers and their families, and investigate allegations of torture and ill-treatment.

On Sep. 22, during the General Debate under Item 4 — Human rights situations that require the Council’s attention — ICT President Tencho Gyatso delivered a [video statement](https://youtu.be/IczJEpjdOsA) in which she highlighted concerns over China’s new “Ethnic Unity Law,” which entered into force on July 1, 2026 and codifies China’s forced assimilation and Sinicization of Tibetans and other non-Chinese people. Gyatso welcomed Türk’s call for the law to be abolished, saying that his appeal reflected the absence of fundamental rights to which the Tibetan people are entitled.

_ICT President Tencho Gyatso giving a video statement on behalf of the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights during the General Debate on Item 4 on Sep. 22, 2026. (Source: UN Web TV)_

In another oral [statement](https://tibet.net/lobga-rangzens-sacrifice-renews-attention-on-the-tibet-cause-at-unhrc-63-as-ctas-un-advocacy-officer-challenges-chinas-policies/), Phuntsok Topgyal of the Tibet Bureau in Geneva, speaking on behalf of the Society for Threatened Peoples, raised the case of [Lobga Rangzen, who died on July 2, 2026 after self-immolating outside the UN Headquarters in New York](https://savetibet.org/ict-mourns-passing-of-tibet-activist-lobga-rangzen-following-first-tibetan-self-immolation-on-us-soil-calls-for-action-on-tibet/), one day after China’s new ethnic unity law entered into force.

### Governments and EU raise Tibet at Human Rights Council

The following states and observers specifically mentioned Tibet in their statements during the Sep. 22 General Debate on human rights situations requiring the Council’s attention:

**Australia:**_“We remain gravely concerned by ongoing human rights violations against Uyghurs and Tibetans. Consistent with international law and norms, governments should not interfere in the selection of religious leaders including the Dalai Lama.”_

**Denmark:**_“We reiterate our serious concerns over the human rights situation in China, in particular in Xinjiang, Tibet and Hong Kong”_

**Finland:**_“Finland remains concerned about the erosion of civil and political rights in Xinjiang and Tibet as well as restrictions in Hong Kong.”_

**Germany:**_“In China the space for freedom of speech and peaceful assembly is as restricted as ever. With great concern we note that the law on promoting ethnic unity and progress further reinforces existing restrictions on cultural and religious freedoms, particularly in the Tibet Autonomous Region and the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous region.”_

**Ireland:**_“On China we remain concerned over restrictions on civic spaces in Hong Kong, the treatment of Tibetans, repression of Uyghur people in Xinjiang, and the potential impact of the new law on promoting ethnic unity and progress.”_

**Japan:**_“On China, Japan is concerned about the recent trend of tightening restrictions on human rights defenders, intellectuals and other individuals. Freedom, respect for fundamental human rights and the rule of law must be ensured in China, including Hong Kong, Xinjiang and Tibet. We strongly urge China to take further constructive and concrete action including enhancing transparency.”_

**Sweden:**_“We also remain seriously concerned about the situation in China, not least in Hong Kong, Tibet and Xinjiang. We urge China to implement the recommendations from the UPR, the OHCHR report on Xinjiang and Special Procedures.”_

**Switzerland:**_“Switzerland expresses its concerns about the consequences of the new law on ethnic and progress in China. Implemented in its current form, it will seriously undermine linguistic, cultural and religious autonomy of ethnic minorities especially Tibetans Uyghurs and Mongols.”_

**European Union (with Albania, Montenegro and Liechtenstein aligning):**_“We reiterate concerns about the situation in China including in Tibet, Xinjiang and Inner Mongolia and about the ethnic unity law.”_

In addition, the UK delivered the following statement during the Item 2 General debate on the oral update of the High Commissioner on Sept. 8:

**United Kingdom:**_“Evidence of violations in Xinjiang and Tibet persists, freedom of religion or belief is being further restricted, and the Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress risks undermining the rights of individuals belonging to minorities. We welcome the High Commissioner’s continued engagement on these issues.”_

title: Israel to ramp up pilot checks after flydubai scare
summary: * Summary * Israel to check identities of all pilots flying into country, PM office says * Saudi authorities arrest and interrogate co-pilot after flight diverts safely to Saudi Arabia * Flydubai warns against premature speculation and says
content:
*   Summary

*   Israel to check identities of all pilots flying into country, PM office says
*   Saudi authorities arrest and interrogate co-pilot after flight diverts safely to Saudi Arabia
*   Flydubai warns against premature speculation and says much remains unclear

JERUSALEM, Sept 30 (Reuters) - Israel is ​set to ramp up security checks on pilots flying into the country, a spokesperson for the prime minister's office said, after it said a co-pilot ‌on a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv had stabbed the pilot and attempted to crash the plane.

The dramatic incident was only defused after passengers helped subdue the [co-pilot](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/diverted-flydubai-flight-israel-was-not-hijacking-incident-israeli-prime-2026-09-30/) before other on-duty pilots employed by the airline on the plane landed the aircraft safely in Saudi Arabia. The Dubai state-owned airline warned against "premature speculation" and said much remained unclear.

The Reuters Iran Briefing newsletter keeps you informed with the latest developments and analysis of the Iran war. Sign up [here.](https://www.reuters.com/newsletters/reuters-iran-briefing/?location=article-paragraph&redirectUrl=%2Fworld%2Fmiddle-east%2Fisrael-ramp-up-pilot-checks-after-flydubai-scare-2026-09-30%2F)

Saudi authorities have arrested and interrogated the co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073 from the United Arab ​Emirates to Israel that was carrying 174 people, almost all Israelis, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said.

The incident has sharpened questions about how pilots are vetted and what sorts ​of security protocols they face, including but not limited to the Middle East, according to government officials and aviation analysts.

Israel's government frequently urges ⁠Israelis and Jews to remain vigilant when travelling outside Israel, amid concerns that they could be targeted. This comes as antisemitism has surged globally in recent years, including violent and sometimes ​deadly attacks against Jews. So far, however, no motive has been given for the flydubai incident.

"Every pilot that is going to be flying into Israel, we are going to know the ​pilots' identities, know who they are, and do some type of security check," Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for the Israeli prime minister's office, told Reuters.

He said Netanyahu had instructed authorities to "ramp up security" on flights to Israel operated by Israeli and non-Israeli carriers.

"Anywhere that an Israeli is going to be flying into Israel. Our job right now is to do our best - even if they're not on Israeli airlines - to make ​sure that those security procedures are much higher," Spielman said.

The UAE civil aviation regulator, the GCAA, did not respond to a Reuters request for comment on how its pilots are ​vetted.

Netanyahu identified the pilot who was attacked as Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar. He said that, despite being "stabbed and seriously injured," Machchhar fought back and opened the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew ‌to overpower ⁠the attacker.

Travelers board a FlyDubai aircraft at Ben Gurion International Airport after a separate FlyDubai flight from the United Arab Emirates to Israel was diverted to Saudi Arabia following an emergency signal, in Lod, near Tel Aviv, Israel, September 30, 2026. REUTERS/Ammar Awad [Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab](https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/flydubai-flight-diversion-prompts-wait-at-ben-gurion-airport/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX1JDMlBUTkFTSE5WVg%3D%3D/?utm_medium=rcom-article-media&utm_campaign=rcom-rcp-lead)

## PILOT VETTING TOUGHER POST 9/11

Pilots have faced substantial security screenings, especially since the 9/11 attacks in New York 25 years ago, experts told Reuters.

"Every pilot goes through extensive background checks but also continuous medical and psychological assessments," said Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in Britain.

Individual countries and airlines are responsible for implementing screening and security standards as set out by the International Civil Aviation Organization, but there is flexibility in how these are interpreted, experts told Reuters.

Two pilots working in the Middle East but not for flydubai ​told Reuters that pilots have to go through ​the same security screenings as passengers, ⁠meaning they would not be able to bring weapons such as knives or guns on board.

"It's always the airline's responsibility," said Eric Schouten, the head of aviation intelligence consultancy Dyami.

"The airline has to do a proper vetting according to national guidelines on who is in the cockpit ​and every country does it differently."

The European Aviation Safety Agency told Reuters that flydubai's certification and safety oversight rest with the GCAA. "This ​includes responsibility for ensuring ⁠that the operator meets the applicable requirements concerning its flight crews and their fitness to fly," EASA said.

Reuters could not determine what weapon was used by the pilot to stab the other. Passengers on board the flight have reported that a man was holding a knife while one of the pilots lay bloodied. A pilot flying in the region but not for flydubai told Reuters pilots ⁠might have ​access to metal knives from a meal service or a crash axe available in most cockpits.

Spielman said Israel ​already had some of the toughest security checks, and these would only get tighter.

"This is an opportunity for everyone to wake up. Israel has the most thorough security checks in the world, and they're there for a reason. They're ​there so that an incident like this doesn't take place," he said.

Updates detail of number of passengers in paragraph 3, identity of pilot who was attacked in paragraph 10

Reporting by Sarah el-Safty, Alexander Cornwell, Federico Maccioni and Joanna Plucinska; Editing by Alex Richardson, Gareth Jones and David Gaffen

Our Standards: [The Thomson Reuters Trust Principles., opens new tab](https://www.thomsonreuters.com/en/about-us/trust-principles.html)

Alexander has over a decade of international reporting experience. He is currently a senior correspondent in Jerusalem covering Israel & the Palestinian Territories and was formerly in Dubai where he covered the Arabian Peninsula, including the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Yemen, often writing about foreign policy, security and economic-related issues.

Joanna reports on airlines and travel in Europe, including tourism trends, sustainability and policy. She was previously based in Warsaw, where she covered politics and general news. She wrote stories on everything from Chinese spies to migrants stranded in forests along the Belarusian border. In 2022, she spent six weeks covering the war in Ukraine, with a focus on the evacuation of children, war reparations and evidence that Russian commanders knew of sexual violence by their troops. Joanna graduated from the Columbia Journalism School in 2014. Before joining Reuters, she worked in Hong Kong for TIME and later in Brussels reporting on EU tech policy for POLITICO Europe.

title: Trump says he discussed release of political prisoners with Xi
summary: Item 1 of 2 US President Donald Trump meets Chinese President Xi Jinping in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, D.C., US, September 24, 2026. REUTERS/Evan Vucci **[1/2]**US President Donald Trump meets Chinese President Xi Jin
content:
Item 1 of 2 US President Donald Trump meets Chinese President Xi Jinping in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, D.C., US, September 24, 2026. REUTERS/Evan Vucci

**[1/2]**US President Donald Trump meets Chinese President Xi Jinping in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, D.C., US, September 24, 2026. REUTERS/Evan Vucci [Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab](https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/us-president-donald-trump-and-chinas-president-xi-jinping-meet-at-the-white-house-in-washington-dc/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX1JDMlJQTkFCWUc4QQ%3D%3D/?utm_medium=rcom-article-media&utm_campaign=rcom-rcp-lead)

WASHINGTON, Sept 30 (Reuters) - US President [Donald ​Trump](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/donald-trump/) said on Wednesday he discussed the release of ‌political prisoners with Chinese President [Xi Jinping](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/) when the [two leaders met](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/trump-plans-grand-spectacle-potentially-tense-xi-talks-2026-09-23/) last week.

Make sense of global markets with the Trading Day newsletter. Sign up [here.](https://www.reuters.com/newsletters/trading-day/?location=article-paragraph&redirectUrl=%2Fworld%2Fchina%2Ftrump-says-he-discussed-release-political-prisoners-with-xi-2026-09-30%2F)

## DETAILS AND QUOTES:

*   "I did with President Xi. I did," Trump told reporters when asked if ​he brought up the cases of political prisoners like Myanmar ​scholar and US citizen Min Zin, who was arrested in ⁠June, and Hong Kong's most vocal China critic and media ​tycoon Jimmy Lai.

*   "We talked, and I think we had some very, very ​important discussions. Hopefully, fruitful discussions," Trump added.

*   The White House had said ahead of Xi's visit that Trump was expected to bring up cases of people wrongfully ​detained in China with the Chinese leader.

*   The White House did not ​say if Trump aimed to directly raise broader rights issues related to Tibet, the ‌Uyghur ⁠Muslim minority group, and China's new "ethnic unity" law.

*   Trump has made winning freedom for Americans held overseas a priority, including in China, even as he has largely avoided talking about China's treatment of Tibetans, Uyghurs ​and voices of ​dissent.

*   Lai's case [had sparked ⁠global concerns](https://www.reuters.com/business/media-telecom/trump-says-china-may-release-detained-pastor-tycoon-lai-is-tough-one-2026-05-15/) over the national security clampdown in Hong Kong, in part reflecting his prominence as founder ​of the now-shuttered Apple Daily newspaper. He was ​sentenced to ⁠20 years in jail in February on two counts of conspiracy to collude with foreign forces and one count of publishing seditious materials.

*   Washington designated ⁠Myanmar ​scholar and US citizen Min Zin as [wrongfully ​detained](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/us-designates-american-held-by-china-wrongfully-detained-2026-08-20/) in August after his arrest by Chinese authorities in June.

Updates with question asked to Trump, his response, background of Xi visit in bullets

Reporting by Gram Slattery ​and Kanishka Singh in Washington; Editing by Caitlin Webber and Michelle Nichols

Our Standards: [The Thomson Reuters Trust Principles., opens new tab](https://www.thomsonreuters.com/en/about-us/trust-principles.html)

Gram Slattery is a White House correspondent in Washington, focusing on national security, intelligence and foreign affairs. His work covers how key U.S. foreign policy decisions are debated, shaped and executed. He was previously a national political correspondent, covering the 2024 presidential campaign. From 2015 to 2022, he held postings in Rio de Janeiro, Sao Paulo and Santiago, Chile, and he has reported extensively throughout Latin America.

Kanishka Singh is a breaking news reporter for Reuters in Washington DC, who primarily covers US politics and national affairs in his current role. His past breaking news coverage has spanned across a range of topics like the Black Lives Matter movement; the US elections; the 2021 Capitol riots and their follow up probes; the Brexit deal; US-China trade tensions; the NATO withdrawal from Afghanistan; the COVID-19 pandemic; and a 2019 Supreme Court verdict on a religious dispute site in his native India.

title: US Supreme Court sides with Tennessee to allow its first execution of a woman in 200 years
summary: * Summary * Christa Pike, 50, convicted of murder at age 18 * Failed clemency bid cited childhood sexual abuse, neglect * Pike diagnosed with bipolar, post-traumatic stress disorder Sept 30 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court ruled on Wednesda
content:
*   Summary

*   Christa Pike, 50, convicted of murder at age 18
*   Failed clemency bid cited childhood sexual abuse, neglect
*   Pike diagnosed with bipolar, post-traumatic stress disorder

Sept 30 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court ruled on Wednesday that [Tennessee](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/tennessee/) could proceed with its first execution of a woman in 200 years, clearing the way for ​Christa Pike to be put to death by lethal injection for murdering a schoolmate as an 18-year-old three decades ago.

The Tennessee Department of Correction said ‌in a statement to Reuters afterwards that it planned "to move forward with the execution today."

The Misinformation Monitor newsletter rounds up international misinformation narratives, with a "Real or Fake?" quiz in every edition. Sign up [here.](https://www.reuters.com/newsletters/misinformation-monitor/?location=article-paragraph&redirectUrl=%2Fworld%2Fus%2Ftennessee-due-execute-woman-first-time-two-centuries-2026-09-30%2F)

Pike, 50, whose clemency petition highlighting childhood trauma and sexual abuse was denied by Governor Bill Lee on Monday, would also be the only person in the modern era of US capital punishment to be executed in Tennessee for a crime committed as a teenager.

In an order decided by its 6-3 conservative majority, the Supreme ​Court lifted a stay of execution that was granted by a three-judge panel of the 6th US Circuit Court of Appeals one hour before Pike had ​been scheduled to be put to death.

The appellate panel voted 2-1 to order a "short stay" to allow time to weigh Pike's claim ⁠that evidence of her childhood sexual abuse was not adequately considered during her sentencing.

But the Tennessee attorney general's office immediately asked the US Supreme Court to vacate the stay. And ​the high court's decision siding with Tennessee marked the final word on whether the execution was permitted to go forward before her death warrant expires at midnight CDT (0500 GMT).

The state ​did not give a precise new time frame for the execution, which was set to take place at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, the state capital.

If the state were to run out of time to conduct the execution, it would need to obtain a new warrant from the Tennessee Supreme Court, according to Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center.

## GRISLY KILLING

Pike was 18 ​in January 1995 when she, a 17-year-old boyfriend and a third companion lured 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a classmate at their Knoxville Job Corps vocational center, into a wooded area ​where they tortured and killed her.

The grisly nature of the slaying, which involved the perpetrators carving the shape of a pentagram in the victim's chest and taking a chunk of her skull as ‌a souvenir ⁠of the carnage, drew intense media coverage at the time.

Trial testimony indicated that Pike viewed Slemmer as a rival for the affections of her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp.

Pike and Shipp both were convicted of first-degree murder. Pike was sentenced to death, while Shipp received a life sentence with the possibility of parole.

Their co-defendant, Shadolla Peterson, who was 18 at the time of the murder and acted as a lookout for the other two, testified for the prosecution and received probation.

Currently the only woman on Tennessee's death row, Pike was also convicted in ​August 2001 of attempted first-degree murder in an ​assault on another inmate, according to ⁠the Tennessee Department of Correction.

## TEEN WHO COMMITTED MURDER 'NO LONGER EXISTS'

In the 226-page petition asking the governor to commute her death penalty to a life sentence without the possibility of parole, Pike's lawyers documented her history as the childhood victim of violence, neglect and sexual abuse, ​including two rapes at ages 11 and 17. They also cited the diagnoses she received in prison for bipolar disorder and ​post-traumatic stress disorder.

Moreover, they ⁠pointed to evidence that Pike's mother drank heavily during pregnancy, contributing to faulty brain development that made it difficult for their client to control her impulses as a young person.

"The 18-year-old girl suffering from severe mental illness and near-debilitating trauma no longer exists," her lawyers wrote in response to Lee's denial of clemency. "Christa is a 50-year-old remorseful woman who understands her actions, receives proper ⁠treatment for ​her mental illness, and provides for and guides fellow incarcerated women."

Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, has spoken out in ​support of the execution.

Executions of female prison inmates are exceedingly rare in the US, with women accounting for just 18 of the 1,683 people put to death since the Supreme Court allowed capital punishment to resume in ​1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Before Wednesday, Tennessee had executed 17 people.

Adds background, details of the case, execution history, paragraphs 14-19

Reporting by Steve Gorman in Los Angeles; Editing by Lincoln Feast, Bill Berkrot and Neil Fullick

content:
伦敦 —

英国人权组织“西藏观察”(Tibet Watch)星期三(9月30日)发布调查报告称，中国当局正在西藏建立从警用无人机、自动机巢到反无人机设备的空中管控体系。报告也促使部分英国议员和人权人士呼吁英国政府，重新审查对中国无人机的相关采购。

这份75页的报告，题目为《高原上的眼睛》(Eyes Above the Plateau)分析查阅了2017年至2026年中国政府的采购公告、警方通报、培训记录和飞行管制文件。“西藏观察”指出，当局一方面把无人机用于巡逻、人群监测、边境管理和救援，另一方面采购无人机侦测和反制设备，并加强对民用无人机的管控。

**监控从地面延伸到空中**

报告发现，在西藏一些曾发生抗议的地区出现新的警用无人机部署。

四川德格县2024年曾发生反对岗托水电站建设的抗议。约15个月后，当地警方在川藏公路检查站升级项目中采购四套大疆自动机巢、四架无人机及调度系统，其中大疆核心设备价值约60.2万元人民币。

2013年曾发生抗议的西藏比如县，则拥有报告数据库中最大的县级警用无人机机队，共18架、涉及五种型号，用于日常巡逻。

日喀则桑珠孜区警方称，自2024年5月以来，无人机已执行5723次勤务，飞行超过2.27万公里，任务包括大型活动人流监测。

西藏观察组织发言人凯特·桑德斯(Kate Saunders)对美国之音说，中国安全部门在购买无人机、自动机巢和反无人机设备的同时，也限制其他人的飞行。西藏警方还将“维稳”列为无人机培训任务之一。

不过，桑德斯强调，采购地点与过去发生抗议的地区重合，并不能证明无人机曾被用于监控某次具体抗议。“没有任何文件显示，无人机曾飞越某一场具体抗议、节庆或某座寺院；我们的报告也没有这样声称。”她说。

报告也指出，无人机被用于搜救等正常警务工作，领导人访问的安保需要也可以解释部分临时飞行限制。

报告确认了12项涉及大疆设备的政府采购，买方包括西藏自治区公安厅反恐部门、拉萨城关警方、日喀则边境管理部门和武警西藏总队等。

报告所列12项采购的整个项目合同总额约2479万元人民币，但其中包括大量非大疆设备。报告还强调，大疆并不是这些采购合同中的直接卖方，设备均通过经销商或系统集成商提供，现有文件不能证明大疆知道最终用途或直接参与相关警务行动。

**英国采购受到质疑**

与此同时，报告援引2023年的数据称，当时37支英国警队拥有的337架无人机中，至少230架为大疆产品。

英国政府2022年要求各部门停止在敏感场所安装由中国生产的监控设备，并建议提前移除和更换已经部署的设备。英国政府2025年11月表示，最初识别出的相关敏感政府场所已经完成设备更换。

西藏观察呼吁英国政府将相关限制延伸至无人机。

英国上议院议员、议会人权联合委员会前主席戴维·奥尔顿勋爵(Lord David Alton)对美国之音说：“西藏人民如今被迫生活在乔治·奥威尔所设想的那种警察国家中。”他进一步表示,“除非英国限制警方使用中国制造的无人机，否则它将成为极权主义的合作者。”

国际人权组织“强化权利”(Fortify Rights)高级主任罗杰斯(Benedict Rogers)也对美国之音表示，这是一份“极为重要且令人担忧”的报告，揭示了他所称的中共在西藏广泛使用无人机监控，同时限制他人使用藏区空域的情况。

“这应当促使英国和其他民主国家政府质疑，采购中国制造的警用无人机是否明智、是否符合伦理和道德，”罗杰斯说。他将这类无人机称为“监控、镇压和间谍活动的工具”。

**报告证据的边界**

西藏观察强调，其数据库并非中国在藏区部署无人机的完整清单。系统性资料收集从2025年4月开始，2022年至2024年的资料仍在补充，青海和甘肃藏区也存在资料缺口。因此，报告明确没有声称无人机采购近年来出现加速。

报告也没有找到无人机针对某个具体藏人、某场抗议或某座寺院进行监控的直接记录。它所记录的是无人机和反无人机能力被部署到包括曾发生抗议、举行大型宗教活动以及边境在内的地区，而“维稳”和大型活动人流监测已成为警方公开列出的任务。

大疆此前否认参与侵犯人权活动，并表示其产品为民用及和平用途开发。

美国之音向英国政府、英国全国警察局长理事会、中国驻英国大使馆和大疆请求回应。但截至发稿前，均未收到回复。

# 韩国“习近平餐馆”遭中国人跨境喷漆袭击

图像来源，News1

图像加注文字，监控影片显示，一群蒙面男子在韩国京畿道城南市的这家餐厅内喷洒油漆。

**Article Information**
*       *   Author, 黄思琪（Kelly Ng）

*   Published 2026年9月30日早上8点23分
*   阅读时间: 2 分钟

韩国警察表示，当地一家以中国国家主席习近平命名的餐厅遭一群中国籍人士破坏，而他们在施袭后立即逃离韩国，返回中国。

位于首尔以南京畿道城南市的这家餐厅的监控录像显示，9月24日凌晨，四名蒙面男子闯入店内，砸毁傢具并喷洒清漆。

餐厅老板向当地媒体表示，他之所以取名“习近平”，是因为他“希望它成为（韩国）最好的中餐馆”。他补充说：“没有任何政治意图。”

《朝鲜日报》报导称，这家餐厅已经营八年，但直到过去一年才开始收到要求更改店名的诉求。

End of content

去年8月，当有消息传出习近平将出席在韩国举行的亚太经济合作组织（APEC）峰会时，老板表示，他接到了数十通与这些诉求有关的电话。他说，有些人甚至提出愿意付钱。

他向《朝鲜日报》表示：“一些自称在中国经营生意的人提出愿意给予大笔金额，只要我们改名。他们非常执着。”

今年4月，有人就餐厅菜单上一道名为“习近平特色炒饭”的菜式向韩国知识产权部门提出投诉，但该部门最终结案，认定不存在问题。

老板表示，上星期的袭击是他过去一年来遭遇过规模最大的一次。他告诉当地媒体，财物损失约为1,500万韩元（1.08万美元；7.2万元人民币；32.4万元新台币）。

习近平餐厅在袭击后关闭五天，并于星期二（9月29日）重新营业。老板表示，其团队现正考虑为餐厅更换新名称。

警方星期二表示，四名嫌疑人均为年龄介乎20至40岁的中国男子。据信他们在施袭后已逃往上海及山东烟台。

警方表示，计划为这四名男子申请国际刑警组织红色通报（Interpol Red Notice）。红色通报并非逮捕令，而是请求世界各地警方在引渡程序完成前拘留有关人士。

根据网上分享的截图，习近平餐厅供应种类广泛的中式菜肴，菜单中亦包括一些韩国菜式。Google用户给予该餐厅平均五星中的四星评分。

# 军情五处警告：中国资助英国研究，成果交予北京间谍机关

图像来源，Getty Images

图像加注文字，英国军情五处表示，一个曾资助英国研究项目的组织，一直在支援北京的间谍机关。

**Article Information**
*       *   Author, 多米尼克·卡夏尼（Dominic Casciani）
    *   Role, BBC英国内政及法律事务记者

*   Published 2026年9月30日下午4点31分 最近更新： 1 小时前
*   阅读时间: 2 分钟

英国军情五处警告，中国透过一家为其情报及安全部门效力的掩护机构，取得超过100名与英国院校有联系的学者协助，用于针对英国的间谍活动，这些学者对此并不知情。

这个英国的国内安全情报机关罕有地公开[发出警告](https://www.mi5.gov.uk/mi5-issues-espionage-alert-cgtri-%E4%B8%AD%E5%9B%BD%E9%80%9A%E7%94%A8%E6%8A%80%E6%9C%AF%E7%A0%94%E7%A9%B6%E9%99%A2)，提醒各大学和学者，如果继续与中国通用技术研究院（China General Technology Research Institute，简称CGTRI）保持联系，最终可能因协助外国而面临刑事检控。

英国安全事务国务大臣丹·贾维斯（Dan Jarvis）表示，军情五处的警告揭露了中国情报机构企图利用英国的学术研究，损害英国国家安全。

他表示，自己已致函所有大学校长，要求终止与该机构的关系。

今年6月，[英国军情五处与美国、加拿大、澳洲和新西兰的主要合作伙伴联合发出警告](https://bbc.com/zhongwen/articles/cj3pkgrzrd8o/trad)，指中国军事情报机关正以职业社交网站和网上求职平台为目标。

这次英国独立发出的最新警告更进一步，揭示军情五处所称正在英国学术机构内不断加剧的威胁。

军情五处表示，中国通用技术研究院——英文名称有时也译作China Academy of General Technology（简称CAGT）——与中国国家安全部有“非常密切的联系”。

警告说：“军情五处确认，中国通用技术研究院的主要目的，是资助能够直接提升中国国家安全部间谍技术能力的学术研究。”

警告又说：“超过100名与英国有联系的学者，曾参与由中国国家安全部透过中国通用技术研究院资助的项目。”军情五处补充，在部分个案中，研究人员可能并不知道这家掩护机构在其项目中所扮演的角色。

英国学者曾参与由中国通用技术研究院资助的项目，研究范畴包括人工智能、网络安全、隐蔽通讯系统和讯息隐写术。隐写术是指把秘密讯息或档案隐藏在普通讯息或物件之中。

军情五处说：“这些活动有助中国国家安全部进行间谍活动，对英国国家安全构成威胁。”

安全警告表示，许多学术机构和个人可能是“出于善意”与中国通用技术研究院合作，因为该机构与中国国家安全部的关系一直被“刻意掩饰”。

警告续称：“强烈建议英国学术机构立即检视任何正在进行或计划与中国通用技术研究院展开的合作，以确保中国国家安全部无法再从英国的大学或研究机构获益。”

这项公开警告意味，未有立即采取行动的英国学者，最终可能触犯法律。

该警告强调，英国在2023年通过、旨在打击国家间谍活动的重要法例《国家安全法》，订立了协助外国情报机关的新罪行，如果当事人按理应该知道自己的行为是在提供这类协助，便可能干犯该罪。

丹·贾维斯说：“这项警告揭露了中国情报机构企图暗中利用我国学者的专业知识和研究成果，从而损害英国及其盟友的国家安全。”

title: Exclusive: U.S. Lawmaker Warn South Korea’s Tilt Toward China Poses Risk
summary: Published 2026.09.30. 20:00 Updated 2026.09.30. 20:25 Republican John Moolenaar, chairman of the U.S. House of Representatives' U.S.-China Strategic Competition Special Committee. /Chosunilbo DB Republican Congressman John Moolenaar (John M
content:
Published 2026.09.30. 20:00 Updated 2026.09.30. 20:25

Republican John Moolenaar, chairman of the U.S. House of Representatives' U.S.-China Strategic Competition Special Committee. /Chosunilbo DB

Republican Congressman John Moolenaar (John Moolenaar), Chairman of the House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the 28th, stating, “South Korea’s shifting stance in economic, technological, and diplomatic areas toward the People’s Republic of China is posing a significant risk to U.S. interests.” Beyond the controversy over discrimination against U.S. digital companies like Coupang, the letter broadly addressed diplomatic and security issues, including President Lee Jae Myung’s position on the Taiwan issue and allegations of classified information leaks by Unification Minister Chung Dong-young. It argued that frictions between the U.S. and South Korea could lead to a “structural shift” in South Korea’s foreign policy and emphasized the need for close monitoring and joint measures.

The House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), established in January 2023, is a bipartisan body in the House of Representatives involving around 20 Republican and Democratic lawmakers, including Korean-American Young Kim and pro-Korea faction member Tom Suozzi. It analyzes economic, military, and technological threats from the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and leads legislative and policy responses. Moolenaar, a six-term congressman, is a leading hawk in Congress who has criticized China’s military and economic coercion and urged unified action by allies, including South Korea, Japan, and the U.S. In the letter sent to Rubio, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, he stated, “The ROK-U.S. alliance remains indispensable,” but added, “Differences in views between allies on critical national interests cannot be taken lightly.”

Moolenaar referenced Rubio’s remarks in Congress in June that “South Korea’s elected leaders are taking positions contrary to U.S. national interests.” He evaluated that the pace of summits between South Korean and Chinese leaders over the past nine months, including Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to South Korea in October 2025 and President Lee Jae Myung’s state visit in January 2026, was unprecedented. Amid diplomatic conflicts between Japan and the People’s Republic of China over the Taiwan issue, he criticized Xi’s mention of Japan’s “sacrifices” against militarism 80 years ago as a “blatant attempt to drive a wedge between the U.S.’s two treaty allies.” Moolenaar also expressed concern that South Korea and the People’s Republic of China expanding export control and supply chain consultation channels could create a separate structure from the U.S. He further labeled Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix’s semiconductor factories in the People’s Republic of China as “leverage” for the CCP, stating, “The South Korean government may create commercial incentives to compromise with the People’s Republic of China.”

President Lee Jae Myung, left, and U.S. President Donald Trump meet for a summit on the 22nd during the UN General Assembly in New York. /News1

While acknowledging South Korea’s “progress” in sharing the U.S.’s burden, Moolenaar pointed out that achievements like increased defense spending and wartime operational control transfers are framed not as expanded contributions to the alliance but as reduced dependence on the U.S. He cited discord between the U.S. and South Korea over the U.S. Forces Korea’s sortie into the West Sea in February this year and the U.S. restricting intelligence sharing after allegations of classified leaks by the Unification Minister. He stated, “Seoul’s attitude toward regional emergencies is concerning.” Moolenaar also invoked President Lee’s past remarks, “What happens in the Taiwan Strait has nothing to do with us,” arguing, “The South Korean government seems to have effectively ruled out supporting potential regional responses to a Taiwan crisis triggered by the People’s Republic of China’s aggression.”

Moolenaar also highlighted the expansion of Chinese companies like AliExpress and Temu in the South Korean market and issues related to personal information and consumer protection. He claimed, “This contrasts sharply with immediate and repeated law enforcement actions against U.S. companies in South Korea.” He noted, “While South Korean regulators did not conduct an on-site investigation for four months after AliExpress concealed a platform hack, they launched an aggressive, multi-agency crackdown against Coupang over a low-sensitivity personal information leak, imposing a staggering $409 million fine.” The Personal Information Protection Commission (PIPC) imposed a record penalty of 624.681 billion Korean won on Coupang in June. The Coupang issue has acted as an obstacle in bilateral relations for nearly a year. Moolenaar requested the State Department to provide a follow-up briefing to the committee by October 31 on changes in South Korea–People’s Republic of China relations and the U.S. government’s response.
