title: ‘Terrifying’: US erupts at Albo’s ‘power grab’
summary: The Albanese government will give eSafety the power to create “sock puppet” accounts to push AI-generated content, in a plan dubbed “Orwellian”. The Albanese Government has been urged to explain why it needs the power to create “sock puppet
content:
The Albanese government will give eSafety the power to create “sock puppet” accounts to push AI-generated content, in a plan dubbed “Orwellian”.

The Albanese Government has been urged to explain why it needs the power to create “sock puppet” accounts on social media to push AI-generated content, after the proposed laws were branded “terrifying” and “Orwellian” overseas.

Over the weekend, independent US journalist [Michael Shellenberger](https://x.com/shellenberger/status/2104266049830969693) took aim at Labor’s long-awaited “digital duty of care” laws, unveiled earlier this month, billed as a way to give Australian social media users more power over their algorithms and protect users from “harmful” content.

**Be the first to know when news breaks. [Download our new app](https://onelink.to/wpmth9)**

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was hit with a brutal question on the world stage, creating an awkward moment during a high-profile appearance.

Public feedback on the exposure [draft bill](https://www.infrastructure.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/exposure-draft-online-safety-amendment-digital-duty-of-care-bill-2026-september2026.pdf) closed last week, with critics — including the Trump administration and the federal opposition — accusing the Albanese Government of attempting to sneak through “censorship” powers after its failed attempt to pass “misinformation and disinformation” laws in 2024.

“Anonymous online accounts threaten democracy and must be banned, say politicians,” Shellenberger said on X.

“But now, the Australian government wants to use anonymous ‘sock puppet’ bot accounts as part of its broader push for sweeping online censorship. Terrifying, unprecedented, and Orwellian.”

This article contains features which are only available in the web version[Take me there](https://www.news.com.au/technology/online/social/orwellian-digital-duty-of-care-laws-to-allow-esafety-commissioner-to-run-sock-puppet-accounts/news-story/ab517c6d7a133904cec94b77eda45185)

Labor’s draft bill defines a sock puppet identity as “a false or fictitious identity assumed by a person in the course of using, or carrying out any activity in relation to, an online service”.

It states that the eSafety Commissioner “may assume a sock puppet identity for the purposes of performing the Commissioner’s functions or exercising the Commissioner’s powers under this Act”.

It also allows “approved researchers” to “assume a sock puppet identity for the purposes of undertaking online safety related research”.

A spokeswoman for Communications Minister Anika Wells said, “Sock puppet accounts will allow the eSafety Commissioner and accredited academics to test the systems platforms have in place to protect Australians from harms like child sexual abuse, extreme violence and terrorism.

“Sock puppet accounts will be used to audit the systems and processes of platforms to protect Australians from harmful material like child sexual abuse, extreme violence and terrorism – not individual accounts.”

Anthony Albanese says a ‘global reckoning’ is coming for big tech. Picture: Martin Lelievre/AFP

The law would authorise “without limitation” the use of sock puppet identities by the eSafety Commissioner or approved researchers to create and operate accounts, observe, download and record material, engage with the online service or provider, engage with “a user of an online service (but only to the extent necessary to prevent closure of an account with the service)”, test features, and test the platform’s response to actions taken using sock puppet accounts.

A second provision additionally authorises the eSafety Commissioner to use sock puppet identities to “generate material using an online service (including by means of artificial intelligence) to the extent that the production, dissemination or possession of that material is not an offence against a law of the Commonwealth, a State or a Territory”.

Liberal Senator Sarah Henderson, Shadow Minister for Communications and Digital Safety, told news.com.au that while “protecting Australians online is important … these powers go well beyond simply checking whether a platform is doing the right thing”.

“The exposure draft expressly allows eSafety and approved researchers to create false identities, access services, observe and record material, and test how platforms respond,” she said.

“The government needs to explain why it needs powers this broad. Online safety laws should target real harm, not create a blank cheque for government surveillance of lawful online activity. Labor’s digital duty of care is not about protecting children but giving the government unprecedented powers to impose political censorship.”

Ms Henderson added, “Whether it is sweeping ministerial powers over lawful content, dangerously vague definitions of online harm, or covert surveillance powers for the regulator, Labor must scrap these draconian laws and go back to the drawing board.”

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the UN General Assembly. Picture: Supplied

Margaret Chambers, research fellow at the IPA, a conservative think tank, said the proposed use of sock puppets was “a form of information warfare”.

“It’s a well known intelligence and information warfare technique,” she said.

“What [the proposed law] does is sanction the eSafety Commissioner to develop these bots for her own malicious ends. The interesting thing to note is the same people have been calling for internet censorship and ending anonymous accounts, warning about election interference because of bots.”

Labor, in its abandoned misinformation laws, previously attempted to give the communications regulator [the power](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/legislation/ems/r7239_ems_13b01a0b-4684-4e0e-b336-0028d4c0e3cd/upload_pdf/JC014003.pdf;fileType=application%2Fpdf) to force social media platforms to remove content and block users engaging in “inauthentic behaviour … for example, co-ordinated bots, troll farms or fake accounts”.

“It’s rules for thee but not for me,” Ms Chambers said.

“The government is moving to adopt whatever powers it can to achieve its ends. They’re waking up to the reality that AI is this hitherto-unused and unprecedented censorship tool, and that in the hands of the state this could be really [effective].”

Ms Chambers said the “most charitable” explanation for the powers “is that they need it to monitor compliance, but I don’t think that’s true at all”.

eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant “would say that they’re doing it to test that the accounts aren’t exposed to harmful content” but Ms Chambers argued “it’s highly likely” that sock puppets would be used to manipulate online conversations.

“It’s a power grab and it’s within her playbook of an aggressive and [unaccountable regulator](https://theipa.substack.com/p/a-power-unto-herself-part-one) that’s seeking to justify more power for herself,” she said.

IPA research fellow Margaret Chambers. Picture: Supplied

But Dr Aashish Srivastava, senior lecturer in business law and taxation at Monash Data Futures Institute, said the sock puppet provisions were far more benign than were being made out by critics.

“Reading from [the draft], I think it’s giving the eSafety Commissioner more power to actually have an ID to see what the platforms are doing without disclosing that [to the companies],” he said.

Dr Srivastava said the second provision, which references the use of artificial intelligence, was likely intended to test how platforms identified and dealt with AI-generated content.

“I think what they’re trying to do is … create some sort of AI stuff that is of course not illegal but at the same time helps them find if the platforms are fulfilling their obligations under the Online Safety Act,” he said.

“For example creating a fictional image, a non-illegal, synthetic piece of content that engages with the platform’s systems to then test how the platform is performing.”

Dr Srivastava supported giving more approved researchers the ability to create sock puppet accounts.

“There is so much power that has been given to these online platforms,” he said. “They have always resisted checks and balances.”

Zoe Jay Hawkins, deputy executive director of the Tech Policy Design Institute (TPDi), also hosed down fears that the provisions would be used by the government to push propaganda.

“It’s predictable that headlines like this cause unease for Australians, but there is a limitation in how it’s drafted,” she said.

“This is for the purposes of the Commissioner’s powers as already existing under the act, it’s not granting additional influence responsibilities.”

A teenage boy uses his phone in Sydney. Picture: Rick Rycroft/AP

Ms Hawkins said sock puppets were “a really important mechanism to make sure that the laws we have in place can actually be enforced”. “It’s easy for them to be misunderstood,” she said.

“Their purpose is about not letting tech companies mark their own homework.”

She stressed that there were already “bad actors using that tech [AI]” to run bot accounts to influence the public and “at the moment we have no tangible way for authorised regulators or researchers to confirm that the platforms are doing something to prevent that”.

The US Government, in [its response](https://au.usembassy.gov/u-s-government-response-to-the-australian-consultation-on-the-online-safety-amendment-digital-duty-of-care-bill-2026/) last week, raised a number of concerns related to freedom of speech and the impact on US-based companies.

“A framework that empowers governments to enforce vague definitions of ‘harm’ risks becoming a mechanism for viewpoint-based censorship, as platforms will be incentivised to over-moderate speech that should be protected to avoid regulatory penalties,” it said.

The draft laws list various types of material defined as “seriously harmful”, including illegal content such as child sexual abuse, promotion of terrorism, crime or drug use, as well as threats and harassment.

Content deemed “harmful to children” includes “material or conduct that encourages or promotes hostile attitudes towards women or gender equality”.

The IPA, in a [research note](https://ipa.org.au/wp-content/uploads/IPA-Research-Note-September-2026-Digital-Duty-of-Care.pdf) earlier this month, noted that the laws would allow the Minister and the eSafety Commissioner to expand the categories of harms at will.

eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant. Picture: Martin Ollman/NewsWire

“The eSafety Commissioner has … taken a broad view of the office’s public advocacy role, becoming a prominent commentator on issues outside the office’s remit, including the proposed misinformation/disinformation laws,” Dr Andrew Bushnell wrote.

“The eSafety website also provides information that goes well beyond protecting people from unlawful behaviour, like, for example, propaganda aimed at ‘young men and boys’ about ‘toxic’ masculinity.”

The Trump administration posed a number of questions to the Albanese Government.

“What role will third-party organisations or the eSafety Commissioner play in the enforcement of the duty of care regime?” it said.

“What safeguards will ensure that any biases and preferences of Australian government officials and regulators do not influence platform design in ways that disadvantage independent or minority-viewpoint speech?”

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson blasted the proposed laws, saying a “government that cannot be trusted to tell Australians the truth should not be given more power over what Australians can see and say online”.

“How are Australians supposed to call out Labor’s lies if the government can pressure platforms to silence its critics and restrict free speech?” she said in a statement earlier this month. “All this talk from Albanese about a digital duty of care and controlling algorithms is just cover for what it really is — a Chinese Communist Party-style internet censorship bill.”

title: Japan Is Giving the United States a Chance in Asia: But Washington Risks Missing It
summary: Japan, a country constitutionally bound to pacifism since World War II, is investing in its defense and contributing to regional security in ways that were previously unthinkable. Tokyo has nearly doubled its defense budget, purchased long-
content:
Japan, a country constitutionally bound to pacifism since World War II, is investing in its defense and contributing to regional security in ways that were previously unthinkable. Tokyo has nearly doubled its defense budget, purchased long-range missiles capable of striking military targets in China and North Korea, signed agreements that allow it to deploy its military overseas, stepped into combat roles in multilateral military exercises, and even lifted its prohibition on exporting weapons.

Japan’s current strategy benefits the United States. Tokyo is not moving away from its alliance with Washington or seeking strategic autonomy; instead, it is increasing the durability of U.S. power in the Indo-Pacific. The United States should be helping accelerate these reforms because a stronger Japan that is closely linked with other U.S. allies and partners in the region is essential to deterring a highly capable and assertive China. Japan is offering the United States a way to protect its vital interests in the Indo-Pacific at a much lower cost and with less risk than Washington would otherwise have to bear.

The United States, however, risks squandering this opportunity by not prioritizing its relationship with Japan. In November 2025, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made comments about defending Taiwan that led Beijing to launch a massive coercion campaign against Tokyo, including throttling its supply of heavy rare-earth minerals and suspending Japanese seafood imports. Despite Takaichi’s statements being in line with U.S. policy preferences, Washington chose not to forcefully stand up for her in public. Then, in May 2026, Washington informed Tokyo that because of the war in Iran, it was delaying the delivery of Tomahawk missiles that Japan had purchased more than two years earlier, and in August, Washington temporarily moved the only aircraft carrier permanently deployed outside the United States from East Asia to the Middle East.

For now, Japan has looked past these developments and is still investing in its partnership with the United States. It does not have any better alternatives to Washington. But the U.S.-Japanese alliance will not automatically endure forever, and the current U.S. approach could soon drive Japan to lower its ambitions for the alliance. The U.S.-Japanese relationship is nearing an inflection point, where complacency in Washington about the alliance and dismissiveness toward Tokyo could leave the United States with less power and influence across the Indo-Pacific. The United States needs to visibly demonstrate its desire for a more ambitious U.S.-Japanese alliance and expand economic and military collaboration with Japan before it’s too late.

### PATROLLING ALONE

For decades, the U.S.-Japanese alliance rested on a division of labor: the United States guaranteed Japan’s security and Japan channeled its national energy into economic reconstruction. This bargain, although asymmetric, satisfied both parties. The United States got a secure regional presence to contain Soviet power in Asia during the Cold War while also preventing a revival of Japanese militarism, and Japan obtained the security it needed to rebuild its shattered economy.

But a cascade of external shocks in the past two decades forced Japanese leaders to revisit this postwar bargain. In 2010, when tensions flared over the disputed Senkaku Islands (known in China as the Diaoyu Islands), Beijing imposed an informal embargo on rare-earth mineral exports to Tokyo, showing its willingness to weaponize supply chains and highlighting Japan's vulnerability to coercion.After U.S. President Barack Obama declared Syria’s use of chemical weapons to be a “redline” but did not enforce it, and as Washington did little to halt China’s militarization of islands and shoals in the South China Sea, Japan started to question the credibility of U.S. commitments. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, in 2022, further demonstrated that great powers were willing to use force to redraw territorial borders. And in the wake of U.S. Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s visit to Taiwan that same year, China’s aggressive live-fire military exercises made clear to Japan that a cross-strait conflict was no longer only a theoretical concern. Tokyo gradually concluded that it needed to invest in its own power and take more responsibility for protecting its interests.

Since 2016, Japan has pursued a strategy known as the “free and open Indo-Pacific,” which seeks to connect countries along the Indian and Pacific Oceans with a shared commitment to the rule of law, freedom of navigation, and free trade. As part of this strategy, Japan worked with the United States to revive the Quad—a partnership among Australia, India, Japan, and the United States—which has worked to improve the detection of illegal maritime activities and protect undersea cables. Since 2022, Japan has signed reciprocal access agreements with Australia, the Philippines, and the United Kingdom, allowing military personnel to train and operate in one another’s territory. These agreements laid the groundwork for further military cooperation. Earlier this year, Japan sent 1,400 troops to participate in combat roles for the first time in the annual U.S.-Philippine joint military exercises, where they fired a surface-to-ship missile from Philippine soil—another first in the postwar era. The possibility of revising Article 9 of Japan’s constitution, which renounces war and prohibits a traditional standing army, is no longer taboo in Tokyo.

> The U.S.-Japanese alliance will not automatically endure forever.

Japan is also increasingly translating its industrial power into security partnerships. It is developing a sixth-generation fighter jet with Italy and the United Kingdom. In 2023, Japan launched an official security assistance program to provide military equipment and infrastructure to its partners, including giving coastal radar systems and patrol boats to the Philippines to help it track Chinese activity in the South China Sea. In 2026, Tokyo lifted its decades-long ban on exporting lethal arms and agreed to build three frigates for Australia and to jointly produce eight more.

Most significant, Japan has indicated that it is willing to play a more active role in U.S.-led efforts to deter a conflict over Taiwan. In November, Takaichi stated that a Chinese blockade of Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan—a designation that would give Tokyo the legal authority to exercise collective self-defense and respond militarily. A solid majority of Japanese citizens supported Takaichi’s comments: they know that Japan cannot avoid such a conflict because Yonaguni, Japan’s westernmost island, is only 70 miles from Taiwan. That reality was brought home when Chinese missiles landed in Japan’s exclusive economic zone as part of the intimidation campaign Beijing launched after Pelosi’s 2022 visit to Taiwan.

To back up its rhetoric, Japan has upgraded its military infrastructure in the Ryukyu Islands, the territory closest to Taiwan. In 2024, Japan’s navy also transited the Taiwan Strait for the first time, and Tokyo procured 400 Tomahawk cruise missiles from the United States. In 2025, Japan established a permanent Joint Operations Command to unify its land, sea, air, and cyberspace domains under a single operational commander and to enable direct, real-time coordination with U.S. forces.By increasing its military might and complementing U.S. capabilities, Japan is aiming to preserve U.S. power in the region while deterring Chinese aggression.

### ATROPHY IS NOT A TROPHY

The United States, however, has done little to publicly embrace Japan’s policy shift. It also has not taken steps that would calm a nervous region. In addition to delaying missile shipments to Tokyo and withdrawing its aircraft carrier from the region, the United States has scaled back or canceled joint military exercises with South Korea. It put a major arms sale to Taiwan on hold, and the war in Iran is likely to further delay the delivery of weapons that Taiwan has already purchased. At the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore, in May, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth omitted Taiwan from his remarks—the first time it had not appeared in such a speech in a decade—casting further doubt on the strength of U.S. commitments to Taipei. Some administration officials argue that Washington is merely trying to avoid unnecessarily infuriating Beijing. But rhetoric matters, especially since China wants to exploit signs of supposed American decline to make its rise to regional dominance appear inevitable.

Japan remains committed to its alliance with the United States and is still trying to strengthen it. But this should not breed complacency in Washington. Without sustained support from Washington, the U.S.-Japanese relationship will weaken, depriving the United States of its best partner in the world’s most consequential region. If U.S. President Donald Trump were to make major concessions to Beijing on Taiwan’s status, withdraw troops from South Korea, or refuse to defend the Philippines during a clash in the South China Sea, Japan would have no choice but to consider reorienting its foreign policy away from the United States.

> The United States has not taken steps that would calm a nervous region.

An uncertain Tokyo would need to reassess many of its relationships, and it may seek closer ties with U.S. adversaries in ways that go against Washington’s interests.To reduce pressure on its northern flank and gain access to much-needed energy supplies, Japan would likely accommodate Russia by reducing support for Ukraine. Japan could also seek to improve its ties with the military junta in Myanmar to secure access to critical minerals and might even explore purchasing discounted Iranian oil. Most consequentially, absent U.S. leadership, Japan could pull back its support for Taiwan, leaving the island vulnerable to Chinese aggression.

If Japan felt it could no longer rely on U.S. extended deterrence, it would likely seek to develop nuclear weapons of its own. China, North Korea, and Russia, after all, each have large nuclear arsenals. Japan would feel compelled to make itself invulnerable to nuclear coercion. If Japan were to pursue nuclear arms, which it could do relatively quickly, South Korea would not be far behind, turning the region into a nuclear powder keg.

Japan would almost certainly embark on a massive conventional military build-up. China, assessing that Japan was exposed without U.S. protection but that its window to act might close as Japan increased its military power, would likely press its claims in the East China Sea, sharply increasing the risk of conflict. Without the United States acting as mediator, Japan’s cooperation with South Korea could also erode, leading Tokyo and Seoul to revert to their more traditionally antagonistic relationship.

If Japan also decided that it did not want to host as many U.S. forces, Washington would lose its best foothold in the region, diminishing its ability to project power in the Indo-Pacific and to ensure that vital markets remain open. Although the United States could base more forces on Guam or seek greater access in Australia, these are farther from places where conflict is likely to emerge—namely, Taiwan and the South China Sea—and would limit U.S. options for how to respond.

### WHAT’S GOOD FOR TOKYO IS GOOD FOR WASHINGTON

The United States should reward Japan’s faith in the alliance rather than ignore it. Washington can take steps to encourage Japan to continue in a strategic direction that benefits the United States, bolster deterrence at a time when doubts about U.S. commitments are growing, and send a powerful signal to China that its coercion of Japan will not succeed, in turn deterring Beijing from attempting to coerce other U.S. allies and partners. title: Launch on warning: How China is rewriting its nuclear doctrine
summary: * WIADOMOŚCI * ANALIZA Oliwier Gorgoń Just now 8 min. Photo. Pxhere, CC0 The sensors and the command chain say more about the shift in Chinese doctrine than the rising warhead count. The consequences for strategic stability are graver than
content:
*    WIADOMOŚCI
*    ANALIZA

Oliwier Gorgoń

Just now

8 min.

 Photo. Pxhere, CC0

The sensors and the command chain say more about the shift in Chinese doctrine than the rising warhead count. The consequences for strategic stability are graver than the arsenal statistics alone would suggest.

## What did minimum deterrence mean?

For half a century, Chinese nuclear doctrine rested on an assumption that set it apart from the American and Soviet approaches. Beijing held that deterrence required no more than the ability to deliver a handful of warheads to an adversary’s territory, and that this made high readiness unnecessary. Warheads were stored separately from missiles, the arsenal numbered around two hundred devices, and no first use was declared without qualification. Early warning had no place in this arrangement: if the response were to come after an enemy strike rather than after its detection, a few extra minutes could change nothing.

That model is now ending, and the clearest evidence lies not in warhead numbers but in the warning and command infrastructure. The Pentagon’s 2019 report conceded that People’s Liberation Army writings saw interest in launching missiles upon warning; however, the Pentagon called this an aspiration. Four years later, the same document describes the implementation of an arrangement that Chinese terminology calls early warning counterstrike (预警反击). David Logan of the Fletcher School and Phillip Saunders of the National Defence University, in a July 2025 study for the Defence Threat Reduction Agency, stated plainly that China has assembled all three elements that such a concept requires: sensors able to detect and track incoming missiles, forces held at a readiness allowing launch within minutes, and a command chain capable of reaching a decision in time.

## Sensors in space and on the ground

An intercontinental missile launch is detected in the infrared, by the exhaust plume standing out against the cold Earth. The pace of Chinese progress can be read from the Pentagon’s own reports: in 2019, China had at least one early warning satellite, three years later, at least three. They are attributed to a programme codenamed Huoyan (火眼), “fire eyes,” hidden behind the civilian designation of communication technology test satellites, with estimates running from three to five. They are positioned over the Indian Ocean, the South China Sea, and the Pacific. The ground segment rests on large, phased-array radar stations, erected since 2009. Logan and Saunders count at least seven such stations across six sites, among them Huanan, Yiyuan, Hangzhou and Korla. Chinese reporting puts their detection range at around 4,000 km, and their parameters approach those of the American PAVE PAWS stations.

However, these numbers indicate that the system is still limited. Three satellites can support only a rudimentary network of early detection, and with so few of them the loss of a single satellite could leave the whole system blind. Chinese analysts acknowledge this themselves, arguing that more sensors are required to confirm incoming missiles with confidence. The weakness is still there, and that is making the whole network prone to failure in a crisis and, at the same time, an attractive target for an adversary. Without redundancy, the system is at once fragile and tempting as a target.

*    See also  ![Image 3: Xi Jinping siedzi - zdjęcie poglądowe](https://cdn.defence24.pl/2026/09/17/1920xpx/gBzdod7KaY1qF2Rsw8uXMzHtkvV1Zh2OyBLfXfoz.fxho.webp)

## Command and readiness

Sensors are useless without a command chain able to turn their readings into an order, and here the changes are equally marked. The Rocket Force now keeps part of the arsenal on continuous alert and has adapted crew training and certification accordingly. The shift comes through in the language: after the 20th Party Congress, in October and November 2022, the Rocket Force newspaper began equating ordinary peacetime duty with a wartime posture, using the formulations “missiles on the rack, on high alert” (弹在架上，高度戒备) and “duty is battle” (值班就是战斗). In one reported case, a brigade received warning of an incoming strike just as it finished preparations and managed to fire its missile and disperse its equipment a minute before the enemy warheads arrived. Yang Chengjun, a retired Rocket Force strategist, claimed unit reaction times had been cut “from days and hours to minutes.” A graduated alert system probably exists as well; John Lewis and Xue Litai described a four-stage alert scale as early as 2012.

## What the Chinese doctrinal texts say

Officially, Beijing does not confirm any departure from its established doctrine, but the doctrinal texts have their own say. The Academy of Military Science’s Science of Military Strategy of 2013 states that once it has been established with certainty that the enemy has launched nuclear missiles, and before his warheads have reached their targets and detonated, a counterstrike may be launched rapidly.

One contradiction remains unresolved, and it touches the core of China’s declared policy. The 2013 edition assumes that launching before an enemy warhead detonates does not breach no first use, since an enemy strike remains the precondition. Yet Fu Cong, then director-general of the arms control department at the Chinese foreign ministry, declared in 2019 that the concept does violate the principle, and called on all nuclear powers to abandon it.

The Defence Intelligence Agency stated in 2024 that the newer silos are being folded into precisely this arrangement.

*    See also  ![Image 4: Flaga Wysp Cooka powiewa nad turkusową wodą przy małej wyspie z rajską plażą porośniętą lasem](https://cdn.defence24.pl/2025/12/04/1920xpx/DqRAJ7g7ha7IF0SWLrCad0vgsXkAIN9Snuyq8u6C.o4fv.webp)

## Consequences: a compressed decision window

The first consequence concerns time. Launch on warning was calculated for intercontinental missiles, which leave roughly half an hour between launch and impact; submarine-launched, hypersonic and depressed-trajectory missiles shorten that window drastically. Stationing shorter-range American nuclear missiles in the Indo-Pacific would therefore strain the Chinese system further and raise the odds of a decision taken on a misreading of intent.

The second is the use of the same sensors for nuclear and conventional roles. The same radars and other systems serve missile defence and non-nuclear operations; an attack on them during a conventional conflict would be regarded as a strike against the capability of nuclear retaliation. This results in a classic escalation mechanism created by entanglement.

## Consequences: the gap in the safeguards

The third axis is the gravest and the least examined. The Americans and the Soviets both required a warning to be confirmed by two independent kinds of sensor, precisely to limit the risk of a false alarm. Chinese writing runs the other way: a 2018 review of hundreds of Chinese academic papers found that analysts fear missing an attack far more than an unfounded alarm, and in CNKI, China’s principal academic repository, the equivalent term does not appear at all. A 2017 report on Rocket Force work praises the finding that an excess of checkpoints slows command down. The paradox is that a system without redundancy is the one that most needs procedures guarding against false alarms, and those are exactly what the Chinese literature lacks.

## Consequences: who can halt the order

The fourth axis is a concern about the peak of the mountain of nuclear forces that is China’s high command and political decision-making chain. An order for a nuclear strike reportedly must come from both the Central Military Commission and the Politburo Standing Committee, and summoning both within less than half an hour would be practically impossible. The most important observation lies in the usual reasoning of delegated authority; Xi Jinping matters not because he alone can order launch, but because he alone can forbid one, should the attack prove accidental or limited. The greater danger is not that an order arrives too late, but that a pre-planned response is set in motion and no one manages to stop it.

## A complication: the decision predates the buildup

Work on the concept began earlier than assumed. As early as 2010, the Second Artillery Force ordered research on early warning counterstrike to be strengthened, and a year later its service newspaper revealed the creation of a research group at the Second Artillery Academy in which the subject was named, alongside deterrence, as a pillar of operational theory. The decision therefore came before the arsenal expansion of 2015–2016. A conclusion relevant to arms control follows. Beijing reached for the concept when its arsenal was small and vulnerable to destruction in a single disarming strike, and when rapid response compensated for weakness. Today the arsenal has grown and would survive a strike better than ever, which largely voids the original justification.

*    See also  ![Image 5: J-10CE](https://cdn.defence24.pl/2026/09/02/1920xpx/kbeiSpcHW0YfG82rWJpCDbPQQ7Bc781OXEXc0aM2.tzw8.webp)

## What we do not know

The limits of this analysis should be stated clearly. China’s lack of transparency obscures where its arsenal is heading, and this has pushed some American officials towards assuming the worst. A study by the Centre for Global Security Research, however, concludes that Beijing has not abandoned no first use and is most likely not seeking parity with the United States. Logan and Saunders themselves concede that the exact rules governing nuclear use cannot be reconstructed from open sources. Since the 2013 Science of Military Strategy recommends measured ambiguity towards an adversary, some of the Chinese material may also have been written with Western readers in mind. The direction of travel is nonetheless clear. The satellites, radars, continuous alert duty and doctrinal language described above make sense only if China intends to respond within minutes, a break with the minimum deterrence that set it apart from the other nuclear powers for half a century. The effect on strategic stability will therefore depend less on the number of Chinese warheads than on three things that open sources cannot reveal:

**1. How much of the force is kept on high alert.**

**2. How much certainty Beijing will demand before ordering a counterstrike.**

**3. Who will be able to stop that order once it has been given.**

title: New logic of modern data center
summary: BUSINESS growth in Asia-Pacific is entering a new phase. The sustained increase in data, process automation, and the advancement of artificial intelligence are redefining the way enterprises compete and operate. In this scenario, computing
content:
BUSINESS growth in Asia-Pacific is entering a new phase. The sustained increase in data, process automation, and the advancement of artificial intelligence are redefining the way enterprises compete and operate.

In this scenario, computing has ceased to be a technical support function and has become a strategic factor, directly linked to productivity and growth capacity.

The growing adoption of artificial intelligence, advanced analytics, and automation is increasing the demands placed on enterprise technology infrastructure. As models and workloads become more complex, organizations require platforms that can scale efficiently while maintaining performance and optimizing energy consumption. In this context, modern computing architectures are evolving toward models that enable greater processing capacity to be consolidated within a smaller physical infrastructure footprint. The typical result is a more efficient operation, with reduced space, power, and management requirements. In fact, comparing a solution powered by 5th Gen AMD EPYC processors to a legacy solution to deliver the same workload showed that the EPYC solution could reduce the number of servers required by up to 86 percent, lower energy consumption by as much as 69 percent, and decrease total cost of ownership (TCO) by up to 41 percent over a three-year period.

*   [Accentuate professional development better at Accenture](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/09/business/accentuate-professional-development-better-at-accenture/2442156)

[![Image 1: TRANSFORMATIONAL SHIFT Growing adoption of artificial intelligence, advanced analytics, and automation is increasing the demands placed on enterprise technology infrastructure. AI-GENERATED GRAPHICS](https://manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/10/1254162.jpg)](https://manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/10/1254162.jpg)
TRANSFORMATIONAL SHIFT Growing adoption of artificial intelligence, advanced analytics, and automation is increasing the demands placed on enterprise technology infrastructure. AI-GENERATED GRAPHICS

This shift is driving a transformation in data center architecture. The model based on physical expansion — more servers, more space, more consumption — is being replaced by schemes that prioritize efficiency, compute density and load consolidation. In practice, this means doing more with less: running more applications on fewer servers, reducing costs and operational complexity.

 delivered to your inbox

Sign up for The Manila Times newsletters

By signing up with an email address, I acknowledge that I have read and agree to the [Terms of Service](https://manilatimes.net/terms-of-service "Terms of Service") and [Privacy Policy](https://manilatimes.net/privacy-policy "Privacy Policy").

The approach can have a direct impact on total cost of ownership (TCO). By optimizing the use of existing infrastructure, companies can reduce energy consumption, reduce space requirements and simplify technology management. This approach is especially relevant in markets such as the Philippines, where operational efficiency has become a key factor in sustaining competitiveness.

At the same time, energy efficiency has become a priority. Electricity consumption represents one of the main costs in data centers, so improving performance per unit of energy not only has a financial impact but also affects the sustainability commitments that more and more companies are assuming.

*   ![Image 2: 10 special non-working days declared for Oct](https://miopia.newsroom.bi/statics/i/ps/manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/09/1252382.jpg?width=113&crop=113:85)
[10 special non-working days declared for Oct](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/09/regions/10-special-non-working-days-declared-for-oct/2442158)

Another central element is scalability. Organizations require infrastructure capable of adapting to variations in demand, especially in environments where artificial intelligence demands real-time processing. Frictionless scaling allows you to accelerate service deployment and respond more quickly to market needs.

In the Philippines’ case, this change in focus offers potential benefits: greater processing capacity without the need for physical expansion, reduced operating costs and an infrastructure prepared to sustain future growth. In an environment where digital transformation is progressing unevenly, the adoption of more efficient models can make a significant difference in terms of competitiveness.

In this sense, recent technological evolution points toward more compact, efficient platforms designed for modern workloads. The focus is no longer on the volume of infrastructure but on its capacity for performance and optimization.

The breaking point is clear: the future of the data center is not necessarily about growing in size but about improving efficiency. Consolidating loads and optimizing resources has become a strategic decision to help reduce costs and sustain growth in the digital economy.

*   ![Image 3: Cayetano’s words, Cayetano’s shame](https://miopia.newsroom.bi/statics/i/ps/manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/09/1253567.jpg?width=113&crop=113:85)
[Cayetano’s words, Cayetano’s shame](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/10/opinion/columns/cayetanos-words-cayetanos-shame/2442752)

As a final reflection, the opportunity for companies in the Philippines is not only to adopt new technologies but to do so with a strategic approach. Organizations that understand that computing is the core of their growth, and not just a support function, will be better positioned to capture the value of artificial intelligence. Today, efficiency is not optional; it is the basis on which tomorrow’s competitiveness is built.

title: When persuasion begins to erode trust
summary: AT A RECENT marketing community event, I shared with a peer why I have become more selective about where I spend my time online. Facebook and LinkedIn increasingly feel like crowded marketplaces of expertise, with professionals competing fo
content:
AT A RECENT marketing community event, I shared with a peer why I have become more selective about where I spend my time online. Facebook and LinkedIn increasingly feel like crowded marketplaces of expertise, with professionals competing for attention through articles, commentary, advice and carefully produced content. Artificial intelligence (AI) has made it easier to participate in this competition. Still, I have begun questioning whether producing more content in already crowded feeds is necessarily the best way to build meaningful connections.

During our conversation, my peer raised another concern: the amount of manipulative content circulating on social media. Even the way some posts are scripted can make readers feel that their emotions or decisions are being deliberately influenced. The observation stayed with me because it pointed to a problem beyond content saturation. When people become suspicious of what they encounter online, even useful information may struggle to earn their confidence.

Marketing has always involved persuasion. Businesses communicate value, appeal to customer needs and encourage people to act. Storytelling is part of this process because decisions are influenced not only by facts but also by experiences, aspirations and emotions. The concern is not that businesses want to influence decisions. It is whether they do so in ways that respect the audience’s ability to make informed choices.

*   [When security creates friction, employees find workarounds](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/11/business/sunday-business-it/when-security-creates-friction-employees-find-workarounds/2443042)

**When polished content raises questions**

While preparing a digital storytelling session for tourism stakeholders in two provinces lately, I explored how a destination could be communicated through information, promotion and storytelling. Information helps travelers understand what is available. Promotion gives them reasons to consider a destination. Storytelling helps them imagine what an experience might mean to them.

Get the latest news
 delivered to your inbox

Sign up for The Manila Times newsletters

By signing up with an email address, I acknowledge that I have read and agree to the [Terms of Service](https://manilatimes.net/terms-of-service "Terms of Service") and [Privacy Policy](https://manilatimes.net/privacy-policy "Privacy Policy").

AI can now help transform a narrative into realistic images, videos and social media materials. This creates opportunities for smaller businesses that previously lacked the resources for professional content production. However, it also introduces questions about authenticity. An imagined visitor experience can look convincing even when no such visit occurred.

Fictional illustrations have legitimate uses in marketing and education, provided audiences are not misled about their nature. Problems arise when invented experiences resemble actual customer testimonials or when edited visuals create expectations that the business cannot fulfill.

There is also a less obvious consequence. As people become more familiar with AI-generated content, they may question genuine photographs and stories simply because they appear unusually polished. Businesses therefore face a communication challenge that cannot be solved by improving production quality alone.

*   ![Image 1: Senate impeachment court to rule on dropped bribery charge next week](https://miopia.newsroom.bi/statics/i/ps/manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/10/1253968.jpg?width=113&crop=113:85)
[Senate impeachment court to rule on dropped bribery charge next week](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/10/news/senate-impeachment-court-to-rule-on-dropped-bribery-charge-next-week/2442987)

**Difference between persuasion, manipulation**

Manipulation does not require AI. Misleading claims, selective information, manufactured urgency and exaggerated emotional appeals existed long before generative tools became widely available. AI can make producing and adapting such messages faster, but the responsibility remains with those deciding what to communicate.

A story can be emotional without being manipulative. A customer sharing a meaningful experience may help others appreciate a product or service. But when a business invents that experience, omits important limitations or creates pressure that prevents thoughtful evaluation, it risks crossing a different line.

This distinction matters because successful communication does not end when someone clicks, inquires or makes a purchase. The customer eventually encounters the actual product, service or experience. If reality falls short of the impression created, the attention gained through marketing may come at the expense of confidence in the business.

*   ![Image 2: 10 special non-working days declared for Oct](https://miopia.newsroom.bi/statics/i/ps/manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/09/1252382.jpg?width=113&crop=113:85)
[10 special non-working days declared for Oct](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/09/regions/10-special-non-working-days-declared-for-oct/2442158)

**Why relationships matter again**

My growing preference for Viber communities and participation in professional associations reflects a different approach to communication. I still value Facebook and LinkedIn, but I increasingly prefer spaces where conversations can continue beyond a single post and where people have opportunities to get to know one another through shared activities and discussions.

These environments are not automatically more trustworthy. Misleading content and self-promotion can appear anywhere. What makes them useful to me is the additional context that relationships provide. When people have interacted with someone, asked questions and observed how that person responds, they have more information on which to form their judgments.

This also changes how I think about visibility. Reaching a large audience is useful, but it is not the only measure of meaningful communication. A smaller group of people who read, question, respond and remember may contribute more to a lasting professional relationship than a much larger audience that encounters a post briefly before moving on.

*   ![Image 3: Cayetano’s words, Cayetano’s shame](https://miopia.newsroom.bi/statics/i/ps/manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/09/1253567.jpg?width=113&crop=113:85)
[Cayetano’s words, Cayetano’s shame](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/10/opinion/columns/cayetanos-words-cayetanos-shame/2442752)

For businesses, the implication is not to abandon social media or stop using AI. Both remain valuable for communication, discovery and customer engagement. The opportunity is to connect digital visibility with experiences and relationships that support the claims being made.

As creating persuasive content becomes easier, the challenge may increasingly shift from attracting attention to sustaining confidence. Businesses will still need compelling messages, but those messages must be supported by accurate information, credible behavior and experiences that justify customer expectations.

Perhaps the more useful question is no longer how to become more convincing online, but how to give people genuine reasons to believe us.

title: No first-round bye for Eala at Wuhan
summary: DUE to a smaller draw, projected No.13 seed Alexandra “Alex” Eala won’t receive a first-round bye at the WTA 1000 Wuhan Open in China. [![Image 1: Alexandra ‘Alex’ Eala POC PHOTO](https://manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/1
content:
DUE to a smaller draw, projected No.13 seed Alexandra “Alex” Eala won’t receive a first-round bye at the WTA 1000 Wuhan Open in China.

[![Image 1: Alexandra ‘Alex’ Eala POC PHOTO](https://manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/10/1254216.jpg)](https://manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/10/1254216.jpg)
Alexandra ‘Alex’ Eala POC PHOTO

The Filipino tennis ace will compete in the tournament — her first Tour event after a bronze medal finish at the 20th Asian Games in Japan — slated from Oct. 12 to 18.

Unlike most 1000 events where 96 players make up the field and the top 32 players receive first-round byes, Wuhan is limited to a 56-player draw.

In this case, only the top eight get to skip the first round and start their campaign in the second.

The same rule applies to the only two other 1000 events with a 56-player draw in Doha and Dubai.

 delivered to your inbox

Sign up for The Manila Times newsletters

By signing up with an email address, I acknowledge that I have read and agree to the [Terms of Service](https://manilatimes.net/terms-of-service "Terms of Service") and [Privacy Policy](https://manilatimes.net/privacy-policy "Privacy Policy").

Thus, world No.18 Eala won’t have the bye she used to have in previous 1000 events.

The 56-player draw — comprising 43 direct entrants, eight qualifiers, four wildcards and one special exemption — is also the reason why Eala had to go through the qualifiers last year.

*   ![Image 2: Senate impeachment court to rule on dropped bribery charge next week](https://miopia.newsroom.bi/statics/i/ps/manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/10/1253968.jpg?width=113&crop=113:85)
[Senate impeachment court to rule on dropped bribery charge next week](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/10/news/senate-impeachment-court-to-rule-on-dropped-bribery-charge-next-week/2442987)

Eala was No.58 at the time and therefore could not get a direct entry.

She lost to Moyuka Uchijima in the first round of the qualifiers last year, 4-6, 6-3, 2-6.

This year, Eala is projected to be seeded five places higher than her actual ranking due to the withdrawals of five higher-ranked players.

World No.1 Elena Rybakina (foot),No.4 and last year’s champ Coco Gauff (fatigue),No.11 Amanda Anisimova (wrist),No.15 Victoria Mboko (knee) and No.17 Naomi Osaka (change of schedule) pulled out of the competition.

*   ![Image 3: 10 special non-working days declared for Oct](https://miopia.newsroom.bi/statics/i/ps/manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/09/1252382.jpg?width=113&crop=113:85)
[10 special non-working days declared for Oct](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/09/regions/10-special-non-working-days-declared-for-oct/2442158)

World No.2 Aryna Sabalenka,No.3 Jessica Pegula,No.5 Mirra Andreeva,No.6 Linda Noskova,No.7 Elina Svitolina,No.8 Karolina Muchova,No.9 Iga Swiatek and No.10 Marta Kostyuk made the top eight, in that order, and will be the ones to get first-round byes.

The singles draw ceremony was scheduled for Saturday at 4 p.m.

After the Asian Games, Eala went to France for Paris Fashion Week on Oct. 5.

The 21-year-old also appeared in tennis great Maria Sharapova’s podcast “Pretty Tough.”

*   ![Image 4: Alex Eala faces a qualifier to start singles campaign, reunites with Sönmez in doubles at Wuhan](https://miopia.newsroom.bi/statics/i/ps/manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/10/1254261.png?width=113&crop=113:85)

Last Thursday, the Wuhan Open shared photos of Eala training already.

**JERUSALEM —** The axe-wielding co-pilot who attacked the captain of a FlyDubai flight to Tel Aviv last month intended to seize control of the airplane and fly it into the passenger terminal at Israel’s main international airport, authorities in the United Arab Emirates said Friday.

The suspect, an Omani national, did so “with the intention of causing the greatest possible number of human casualties,” the UAE’s top prosecutor said in a statement carried by the state news agency WAM. Most of the 174 passengers on the flight were from Israel.

The statement said the co-pilot “drew inspiration” from the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks in the United States and used two previous flights from Dubai to Tel Aviv to “familiarize himself with the flight route and the airport.”

It said none of FlyDubai's security or professional checks had indicated that the pilot, who was identitifed by The Associated Press as 29-year-old Hamam al-Hammami, harbored extremist views or plans to carry out an attack.

Hammami “admitted that he had acted alone, without the involvement of others,” the statement said, adding that he “provided a detailed confession outlining his motives and the stages of planning and execution” in the presence of his lawyer. It also suggested he was radicalized at a mosque in Australia while attending the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology in 2017.

title: Haze prompts school closures in Malaysia
summary: **KUALA LUMPUR** — Malaysia closed schools in Kuala Lumpur and other parts of the country on Friday as haze from fires in neighboring Indonesia again plunged local air quality to among the world’s worst. Toxic smoke from peatland and forest
content:
**KUALA LUMPUR** — Malaysia closed schools in Kuala Lumpur and other parts of the country on Friday as haze from fires in neighboring Indonesia again plunged local air quality to among the world’s worst.

Toxic smoke from peatland and forest fires has shrouded cities in the region for more than a month, sending respiratory complaints skyrocketing.

The school closures came as Malaysia’s leader discussed the choking smoke with his Indonesian counterpart and called for an urgent regional meeting.

*   [Trump: No new Iran attack before midterms](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/10/world/americas-emea/trump-no-new-iran-attack-before-midterms/2442642)

Air quality in Kuala Lumpur has been firmly in “unhealthy levels” this week, with a Swiss-based air quality monitor ranking the Malaysian capital among the world’s most polluted cities on most days.

Malaysia’s Education Minister Fadhlina Sidek said she has instructed whole school closures in four states and two federal territories, as well as one partial closure in central Pahang state.

[10 special non-working days declared for Oct](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/09/regions/10-special-non-working-days-declared-for-oct/2442158)

Malaysia’s king, Sultan Ibrahim, weighed in on the matter on Thursday, saying schools should be closed as air quality readings reached 150 or higher on the Air Pollutant Index (API).

Under Malaysian guidelines, API readings above 100 are classified as unhealthy, above 200 as very unhealthy and above 300 as hazardous. Reading beyond 500 constitute the threshold for declaring a local emergency.

Kuala Lumpur on Friday showed a reading of around 170 API.

The city was the second-most polluted globally behind neighboring Singapore on Friday morning, Swiss-based air monitor IQAir said.

[Duterte’s tax records need audit – BIR exec](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/10/news/dutertes-tax-records-need-audit-bir-exec/2442826)

‘Worrying level’

Malaysia’s Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Thursday he discussed the fire situation with Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto.

“The haze issue is indeed at a worrying level. And I have personally contacted President Prabowo,” Anwar said.

“And he also agreed to take the necessary steps,” the premier added, without going into specific details.

*   ![Image 4: Man arrested after breaching NAIA security to reunite with OFW wife](https://miopia.newsroom.bi/statics/i/ps/manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/09/1252636.jpg?width=113&crop=113:85)
[Man arrested after breaching NAIA security to reunite with OFW wife](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/09/news/man-arrested-after-breaching-naia-security-to-reunite-with-ofw-wife/2442354)

He said Malaysia has been taking measures to combat the haze, including increasing attempts to trigger rain via cloud seeding.

Experts said the flames were being fanned by a turbo-charged El Niño weather phenomenon, causing the worst pollution conditions in years.

Anwar said he had asked Malaysia’s Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan to contact the 11-nation Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ secretariat for an urgent meeting between environmental ministers to discuss the matter.

“So these are all the steps we are taking, but we are monitoring and will try the measures that we ought to take next,” Anwar said.

Singapore’s air quality levels also dipped into the “very unhealthy” range, with a reading of 205 on the Air Quality Index (AQI), according to the IQAir website.

The AQI converts measurements of pollutants into a single figure indicating air quality and potential health risks.

Readings above 150 are classified as unhealthy, while levels above 300 are considered hazardous.

title: Xinjiang’s “Blue Miracle”
summary: A cold-water fish breeding base in Turpan, Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, August 21, 2025. _Credit: Gou Lifeng/Xinhua via [Getty Images](https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/this-photo-taken-on-aug-21-2025-shows-a-cold-water-fi
content:
A cold-water fish breeding base in Turpan, Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, August 21, 2025. _Credit: Gou Lifeng/Xinhua via [Getty Images](https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/this-photo-taken-on-aug-21-2025-shows-a-cold-water-fish-news-photo/2287190051?phrase=fish%20farm%20xinjiang&adppopup=true)_

China’s Xinjiang region, located on the country’s far northwest frontier, is a land of unforgiving extremes. At Xinjiang’s southwest border stands K2, the second-highest mountain in the world at 28,251 feet.

The Karakoram Range, where K2 is situated, is just one of four major ranges abutting, slicing through, or ringing Xinjiang. The Kunlun runs along the province’s southeastern border; the Altai is found in Xinjiang’s northern reaches, and the Tian Shan spans its center. Together, the mountains, while breathtaking to look at, work to keep much of Xinjiang starved of moisture. Barely six inches of rain fall every year across Xinjiang’s 600,000 square miles.

An aerial view of a small oil town in the Taklamakan Desert in Xinjiang, China. _Credit: Zheng via [Adobe Stock](https://stock.adobe.com/images/aerial-view-of-a-small-oil-town-in-the-heart-of-the-taklamakan-desert-in-xinjiang-china/1844330384?prev\_url=detail)_

A huge swath of Xinjiang is taken up by China’s largest desert, the Taklamakan. The Taklamakan’s ever-shifting dunes can top 600 feet, taller than the Great Pyramid of Giza in Egypt.

In total, less than 10 percent of Xinjiang has ever been fit for human habitation. Those who have eked out an existence have mostly been nomadic herdsmen, with refuge for them and their families found around a modest number of oases fed by mountaintop glaciers in the Tian Shan and Kunlun. Historically, Xinjiang’s native populations have included Turkic Uyghurs, Han Chinese, Kazakhs, Mongols, and Tajiks.

Central Chinese authorities were long content to regard Xinjiang as a remote and rugged strategic buffer against an outside threat from the west. Shortly after the 1949 revolution, though, the state began to imagine Xinjiang as more than a wild outpost, and rather as a valuable territorial holding to be tamed and exploited, its people persuaded or conscripted to join China’s emergence into the modern world, and, in time, its campaign for global economic supremacy.

Exploratory wells, Tarim oilfield, Xinjiang. _Credit: SASAC_

Beginning in the 1950s, Chinese government geologists discovered oil and gas in three of Xinjiang’s topographical basins — the Tarim, Junggar, and Tuha — and mounted some of the deepest drilling programs ever seen. Xinjiang became the western anchor of what was called the West-East Gas Pipeline, a monumental project completed in 2004 that sends natural gas over 2,400 miles to cities such as Shanghai.

At the same time, the state reengineered the Tarim River, Xinjiang’s longest, in a bid to turn the province’s hard and dry soil into farmable land. Reservoirs were built on the Tarim’s tributaries; diversion gates measured and allocated flow, and lined canals carried water to what would become newly leveled farmland. The Tarim, once an unremarkable waterway prone to seasonal flooding in an otherwise parched landscape, was suddenly a highly regulated and reliable supply system. The controlled use of the Tarim would help jumpstart the growing of a range of crops in Xinjiang, including an aggressive push to plant and harvest cotton.

[Video 13](https://www.thewirechina.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Troops-Xinjiang.mp4)

Troops from the People’s Liberation Army entered Xinjiang in 1949. Demobilized troops became part of the XPCC, Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps, established under a directive to “cultivate and guard border areas” in 1954. _Credit: VideoChinaTV, Channel 4_

Amid the discovery of natural resource riches and the marvels of technology, there was always the daunting human project of somehow creating a workforce for the state’s ambitions in Xinjiang. The Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps would handle that feat of reinvention. The XPCC is a corporate unit of the Chinese army, made up of former soldiers turned economic developers. They were sent to Xinjiang as the government agents meant to convert herdsmen into farmers. Land was seized, training programs were implemented and enforced, state-backed companies were launched, the reluctant were threatened with detention, and many were shipped out of Xinjiang to work in China’s larger eastern cities.

The company’s record of coercive tactics in Xinjiang has earned it a notorious international reputation. Over the past decade, the XPCC has seized more than half a million acres in Xinjiang to use for growing cotton, as well as for a variety of other industries, from fruit farming to solar fields. The company has also helped the government relocate more than 10 percent of Xinjiang’s population — over 2.5 million people between 2014 and 2019 — through labor transfers. If brutal, the XPCC’s work in Xinjiang has been effective. Today, Xinjiang produces roughly 20 percent of the world’s cotton supply and is a major source of export crops such as tomatoes, lavender, and wine grapes.

Left: Workers load cotton onto a truck in Alar, Xinjiang. Right: Farmers put harvested tomatoes on a sunning ground for air-drying in Yanqi Hui Autonomous County, Xinjiang. _Credit: IC Photo via Depositphotos_

Of all the successes in Xinjiang over the last 75 years none may be as remarkable as the latest: The Chinese are growing fish in Xinjiang, a place often referred to as the most landlocked spot on the planet.

> China’s desert fish farming project is actually as much a consequence of self-preservation as creative ingenuity… Aquaculture, a 2024 report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies explained, is central to Beijing’s efforts “to bolster food security.” As a result, China has been perhaps the most aggressive practitioner of fish farming.

It turns out that in China’s earliest efforts to pull oil out of Xinjiang, its government drilling teams were regularly turning up evidence of underground aquifers, including underneath the Taklamakan. Researchers knew that the Taklamakan had once been entirely underwater, connected to one of Earth’s oceans. The desert’s sand and soil were littered with ancient coral fragments, microscopic plankton, bivalves, and gastropods. The Taklamakan’s salty soil, in fact, helped explain why some of the world’s best-preserved mummies had been unearthed there.

[Video 14](https://www.thewirechina.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Sand-Dunes.mp4)

Qiemo County Shishixian Aquatic Products built a roughly eight-acre fish farm on the southeastern edge of the Taklamakan Desert in March 2024. Today, the farm raises golden pomfret, grouper, and mullet in two outdoor ponds and an indoor greenhouse with 68 tanks. _Credit: Xinhua_

The aquifers found beneath Xinjiang’s arid vastness would eventually be mapped, and tests would be done on the discovered water — to see both how pressurized and just how salty the water was. Initially, the tests suggested the waters under the Taklamakan and elsewhere across Xinjiang were too salty to be used for farming, too bitter to be consumed by humans. Chinese scientists eventually realized that the underground waters in Xinjiang could be adjusted to mimic seawater.

As a result, over 1,000 fish farms now dot Xinjiang, producing about 200,000 tons of seafood annually. Atlantic salmon, lobster, bass, carp, crab, shrimp — all of them and more raised in Xinjiang. Chinese media calls it the “Blue Miracle,” a maritime economy in a frontier home to what is known as the Eurasian Pole of Inaccessibility. [The Outlaw Ocean Project](https://theoutlawocean.com/), a news organization in Washington, DC, mapped these farms as part of a sweeping [investigation](https://foodforfeed.theoutlawocean.com/) showing how much seafood is reaching the U.S., including government facilities, in violation of the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA).

In recent years, China has pushed fish farming into its arid and high-altitude far west, particularly in Xinjiang and across the Tibetan Plateau. [This map](https://chinafishfarms.theoutlawocean.com/) highlights more than 1,000 of these farms and provides access to a national database of over 63,000 sites. _Credit: [The Outlaw Ocean Project](https://chinafishfarms.theoutlawocean.com/)_

“Raising fish in the desert?” China’s state broadcaster CCTV wrote in a 2025 article. “It sounds impossible, but in Xinjiang, it’s becoming a reality.”

###### **FARMERS OF FISH**

Aquaculture is a global phenomenon. More than half of all seafood the world consumes now comes from aquaculture rather than wild catch. India alone produces some 11 million metric tons of farmed fish products every year. The raising of clams, oysters, scallops, and mussels — distinctive aquaculture marvels because they require no feed and very little freshwater — has driven much of the explosive growth. In a 2019 report, the Nature Conservancy argued that by 2050, sustainably managed fish farms should become humanity’s primary source of seafood.

A floating fish farm in Xiapu, Fujian, China._Credit: [Yujie](https://stock.adobe.com/images/aerial-view-of-the-sea-fish-farm-cages-and-fishing-village-in-xiapu-fujian-province-china/727202819?prev\_url=detail)_

Most ambitious fish farming falls into a small handful of models. In Asia, the dominant system is the freshwater pond: excavated basins stocked with hatchery-raised juveniles, fed daily, and aerated mechanically to prevent oxygen crashes. Along coasts, floating net pens hold fish in open water, relying on currents to disperse waste. Some fish farms operate fully enclosed recirculating systems, filtering and reusing water inside warehouses.

The $313 billion industry has generated varied and extraordinary benefits. In India, it is a major source of employment, particularly for women. In Bangladesh, the expansion of fish farming has helped drive down prices, making seafood more affordable for poorer households. The industry, even accounting for transporting the farmed fish around the world, is a far smaller source of carbon emissions than beef or pork.

Recent efforts to push the nature and reach of the business have wound up pushing the boundaries of the imagination and technology. The Norwegians have built enormous, semi-submersible structures in the open ocean, capable of holding volumes of water great enough to house 1.5 million salmon. The Chinese have built “aquaculture ships,” huge vessels sent to sea with 15 breeding cabins capable of holding 90,000 cubic meters of water.

[Video 15](https://www.thewirechina.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Fish-Farms-in-Desert.mp4)

On the southern rim of the Taklamakan Desert in Xinjiang, two companies, Hotan Yujianjianglai and Qiemo Shishixian, began farming fish around 2024. Roughly 250 fish farms in and around the Taklamakan produce $100 million in desert seafood — including species like cod and grouper — every year. _Credit: Hotan Yujianjianglai Aquaculture, Xinhua News_

In Scotland, underwater robots are used to combat the threat of sea lice, a parasite that feeds on salmon. The robots identify the lice and fire laser pulses to eradicate them. The inventions have not been exclusive to major commercial farm fishing. Modest fish farms in Indonesia have been using smartphone apps to manage timed, more cost-effective feeding schedules at their ponds.

And then there is the engineering of the fish themselves. In the U.S., the seafood company AquAdvantage has won approval to raise cloned salmon. Fish farming, therefore, isn’t only about cages, pumps, and sensors anymore. It’s also about re-writing biology — treating growth rates and production timelines as variables that can be redesigned, not just managed.

But as with many feats of human ingenuity and profit-making, aquaculture is freighted with a multitude of downsides. Crowding millions of fish together produces

title: UN extends Darfur arms embargo, blocks broader Sudan sanctions proposal
source: 菲律宾在中国紧张局势中加强其最北端的防御
summary: _Russia and China block US efforts to expand the Darfur arms embargo to cover all of Sudan amid ongoing conflict._ The United Nations Security Council extended the arms embargo on Sudan’s Darfur region by two months but failed to agree on a
content:
_Russia and China block US efforts to expand the Darfur arms embargo to cover all of Sudan amid ongoing conflict._

The United Nations Security Council extended the arms embargo on Sudan’s Darfur region by two months but failed to agree on a US proposal to widen it to the whole country, after permanent members Russia and China opposed it.

The 15-member council unanimously adopted Resolution 2830 on Thursday, extending the sanctions regime until December 11 to allow more time for negotiations.

list of 3 items
*   list 1 of 3[The battle for Kordofan: The corridor linking Sudan’s east and west](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1/the-battle-for-kordofan-the-corridor-linking-sudans-east-and-west)
*   list 2 of 3[Washington’s diplomacy in Sudan has backfired](https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/10/2/washingtons-diplomacy-in-sudan-has-backfired)
*   list 3 of 3[Sudan’s army says it captured RSF stronghold in North Kordofan](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/2/sudans-army-says-it-captured-rsf-stronghold-in-north-kordofan)

end of list
It also extended the mandate of the panel of experts that monitors the measures until January 11, 2027. The UN described the text as a short-term “technical rollover”, after the regime was last renewed for one month on September 11.

The sanctions were first imposed in 2005 under Resolution 1591.

The council set up an arms embargo on [armed actors in Darfur](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1/the-battle-for-kordofan-the-corridor-linking-sudans-east-and-west), a travel ban and an asset freeze on designated individuals and entities, and a five-member panel of experts to monitor them.

Despite weeks of discussion, the United States failed to secure approval to expand the embargo. Russia and China have argued for keeping the existing regime.

## ’20 years outdated’

“The current sanctions regime is over 20 years outdated, and is insufficient to address the realities of the war today,” US Ambassador Jeff Bartos told the council last month, urging it to “expand the arms embargo across the entire territory of Sudan”.

Russia’s deputy UN ambassador, Anna Evstigneeva, said at the time: “We will not allow even a hint of broadening the restrictions by the council on Sudan.”

Sudan’s UN ambassador, Al-Harith Mohamed, argued that a total embargo goes against the UN Charter’s guarantee of the right to self-defence.

The war between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which began in April 2023, has killed at least 59,000 people, though aid groups warn [the toll could be far higher](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/7/9/un-probe-finds-mass-killings-gang-rapes-by-sudans-rsf-amount-to-genocide).

It has also displaced about 13 million people and pushed parts of the country into famine.

The army holds central and eastern Sudan, while the RSF controls Darfur in the west and parts of the south.

Darfur, a region about the size of Spain, has seen some of the worst violence, with displacement camps attacked and repeated ethnic massacres killing thousands at a time.

SEOUL, Oct. 8 (Yonhap) -- The heritage authority said Thursday it has yet to decide whether to raise admission fees for its major palaces and royal tombs, with the planned increase still under review.

The Korea Heritage Service (KHS) had planned to announce the fee hikes in November so they could take effect in January 2027, citing the relatively low fees compared with those at major heritage sites abroad.

But the service said the timing of the fee increases remains "undecided," in a document submitted to Rep. Choi Min-hee for an annual parliamentary audit.

Gyeongbok Palace in central Seoul is crowded with visitors, in this file photo taken Sept. 24, 2026, the first day of the extended Chuseok holiday. (Yonhap)

[](https://en.yna.co.kr/view/AEN20261008007900315 "Opens in new web browser window")

In the document, the service's Royal Palaces and Tombs Center said it will instead improve visitor services in January after reviewing the free admission programs for visitors wearing hanbok and the potential financial burden of the fee hike on the public.

"At present, there are not enough rest areas, information desks and facilities for people with disabilities, and the reservation systems are not sufficiently equipped," Huh Min, chief of the KHS, said. "We are currently addressing these shortcomings."

The admission fees have remained unchanged since 2005, despite growing visitor numbers and calls for better preservation of the heritage sites and improved visitor experiences.

Adult admission to Gyeongbok Palace and Changdeok Palace currently costs 3,000 won (US$2.20), while Changgyeong Palace, Deoksu Palace and Jongmyo Shrine charge 1,000 won. Fees for Joseon-era royal tombs range from 500 won to 2,000 won.

The service has considered a three-stage increase, including fees of 5,000 won for all palaces and Jongmyo, and 3,000 won for royal tombs, according to a separate document cited by Rep. Kim Jae-won of the minor opposition Rebuilding Korea Party.

About 17.81 million people visited South Korea's four major palaces, Jongmyo and the royal tombs in 2025, and some 69 percent of the visitors were admitted free of charge, according to figures from the agency.
