title: The Real Reason Xi’s Trump Meeting Was So Short - Domino Theory
summary: Xi Jinping’s (習近平) visit to Washington last month was heavy on pageantry but light on substance. Why? According to conventional wisdom, the reasons were strategic. China wanted time to shore up vulnerabilities in its economy. The U.S. was c
content:
Xi Jinping’s (習近平) visit to Washington last month was heavy on pageantry but light on substance. Why?

According to conventional wisdom, the reasons were strategic. China wanted time to shore up vulnerabilities in its economy. The U.S. was cowed by the threat of another Chinese crackdown on rare earth exports. Combine that with Trump’s emphasis on personal relationships in foreign policy, and a summit devoid of tough conversations on real issues makes sense.

But a string of recent reports suggests that something else might have been going on.

Reporting from Beijing, the South China Morning Post revealed on Tuesday that China’s repeated efforts to plan a more substantive itinerary were rebuffed by U.S. officials.

“Beijing suggested Xi could engage with the American business community and public, pushed to raise dozens of diplomatic and security issues with Trump, and proposed talks on artificial intelligence between Chinese and American executives,” the newspaper [reported](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomacy/article/3369774/beijing-wanted-more-xis-washington-state-visit), citing “people with knowledge of the matter.”

The U.S. side apparently rejected those suggestions, according to the report, arguing that the visit should be equivalent to Trump’s three-day summit in Beijing in May, where the leaders also sipped tea and toured historic sites.

But Dennis Wilder, a former senior U.S. intelligence official, was skeptical. “This SCMPNews story looks fanciful,” he [wrote](https://x.com/dennisw5/status/2107407375900590110) on social media. “I think anonymous sources in Beijing are trying to beat back the stories of Xi’s frailty by claiming he sought a robust US visit. Seems pretty transparently propaganda to me.”

The backstory is this. On Monday last week, The Wall Street Journal published a [story](https://www.wsj.com/world/china/xi-jinping-health-caf250f1) with the headline: “Unusual Rest Breaks for Xi Jinping Sucked Hours Out of Summit With Trump.” According to the article, Beijing requested a private room inside the West Wing for Xi to take rest breaks between events.

That request, along with the Chinese side rejecting a U.S. suggestion that Trump and Xi hold a working lunch, as they had in Beijing, contributed to the summit’s thin schedule. When Trump took Xi to visit the National Archives on the final day of the visit, the Chinese leader only spent about 10 minutes inside, according to the Journal’s sources.

The Journal’s report, like the South China Morning Post one that followed it, was based on unnamed sources. And presumably the information on Xi’s rest breaks came from people on the U.S. side.

But it also quoted Wilder, who said that the hold-room arrangement in the West Wing was unprecedented. Wilder also found the length of substantive discussions during the summit, which totalled only a few hours, unusually brief. “That’s amazingly short for a summit like this,” he said.

Wilder’s suspicion that Chinese officials are using anonymous tips in the South China Morning Post to shape the narrative around Xi comes in the aftermath of a summit that left many observers underwhelmed.

It also sheds light on media coverage of a related issue: Why didn’t Xi give a speech at the United Nations while he was in the U.S.?

Trump addressed the General Assembly on September 22, a day before Xi arrived in Washington. Had Xi come a day earlier, he could easily have delivered a speech of his own.

According to a [report](https://asia.nikkei.com/spotlight/trump-xi-summit/xi-skips-un-address-to-show-china-as-equal-to-rival-us) from Nikkei Asia, Xi chose to skip the U.N. to send a signal that China is the United States’ equal. “Beijing limits leader’s visit to 3 days, mirroring Trump’s trip in May,” the article’s subheadline read.

“According to the Chinese government source, Beijing prioritized sending a message to the rest of the world that China was on an equal footing with the U.S.,” the article read.

It’s not clear how Xi skipping the U.N., where Trump himself gave a speech, signals that China is on an equal footing with the U.S. And if the point is that Xi will only travel to the U.S. for bilateral summits, then it’s hard to explain Trump’s planned visit to Shenzhen for APEC next month.

Let’s review. The South China Morning Post’s Beijing sources say China wanted a much longer trip, but the U.S. side wouldn’t agree. Nikkei Asia’s Beijing sources say China limited the length of the visit to show that Xi is Trump’s equal. One of these anonymous sources isn’t telling the truth.

As for The Wall Street Journal’s reporting, one could argue the Washington sources are playing the same manipulation game they play in Beijing. But it’s hard to ignore the images of Xi walking down the ramp at Joint Base Andrews, holding on for dear life to his wife’s hand.

America is no stranger to aging leaders who stumble around, clearly in the grips of physical decline, yet surrounded by a loyal cadre of advisors who insist nothing is wrong. Look how that turned out.

title: Survey shows strong Chinese support for limited attack if Taiwan declares independence
summary: * By Hollie Younger / Staff writer * * [Add TT as Preferred Source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=taipeitimes.com) * [_![Image 1](https://www.taipeitimes.com/assets/images/x.png)_](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Survey+
content:
*   By Hollie Younger / Staff writer

*       *   [Add TT as Preferred Source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=taipeitimes.com)
    *   [_![Image 1](https://www.taipeitimes.com/assets/images/x.png)_](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Survey+shows+strong+Chinese+support+for+limited+attack+if+Taiwan+declares+independence%20https%3A%2F%2Fwww.taipeitimes.com%2FNews%2Ftaiwan%2Farchives%2F2026%2F10%2F07%2F2003865564)
    *   [_![Image 2](https://www.taipeitimes.com/assets/images/facebook.png)_](http://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.taipeitimes.com%2FNews%2Ftaiwan%2Farchives%2F2026%2F10%2F07%2F2003865564&t=Survey+shows+strong+Chinese+support+for+limited+attack+if+Taiwan+declares+independence)
    *   [_![Image 3](https://www.taipeitimes.com/assets/images/line.png)_](https://lineit.line.me/share/ui?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.taipeitimes.com%2FNews%2Ftaiwan%2Farchives%2F2026%2F10%2F07%2F2003865564?utm_medium=P&utm_campaign=SHARE&utm_source=LINE)

About 77 percent of Chinese surveyed supported military operations against Kinmen and Lienchiang (Matsu) counties if Taiwan declares independence, the latest China Pulse survey found.

About 24 percent supported a full-scale military attack on Taiwan if it were to declare independence, rising from 21 to 29 percent following the summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) in May, China Pulse said in the survey published on Friday last week.

China Pulse publishes a twice-annual survey of Chinese public opinion on international relations conducted by the Carter Center and Emory University in the US.

## Chinese People’s Liberation Army soldiers march with a national flag in an undated photograph.

Photo: Reuters

The latest survey was fielded between April 16 and June 26 — during the Trump-Xi summit in May and ahead of their second meeting of the year last month — gathering responses from 2,500 Chinese across the demographic spectrum.

The proportion of those who oppose the use of force to unify Taiwan "under any circumstances" increased from 32 percent to 40 percent following the summit, it found, although the majority disagreed with that statement.

However, were Taiwan to make an official declaration of independence, 24 percent supported using military force, 59 percent supported a military blockade on commercial shipping and maritime traffic in the Taiwan Strait and 56 percent supported imposing economic sanctions on Taiwan, it found.

A summary for the Carter Center's US-China Perception Monitor publication said that, within China, it is believed that a declaration of independence from Taiwan would amount to an act of war to which Beijing must respond.

However, a narrow majority of 51 percent of respondents believed that the use of force against Taiwan would worsen the issue of cross-strait relations, the survey found.

The most popular non-coercive approach to cross-strait relations was cultural exchange, with an 83 percent support rate, while support for reciprocal economic exchanges increased to 82 percent from 78 percent late last year.

Support for official negotiations on a peaceful agreement increased from 52 percent to 66 percent since the last survey, although support for unilateral concessions decreased from 27 to 15 percent.

The article suggested that the increase may be a reaction to Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun's (鄭麗文) highly publicized visit to China in April, during which she met with Xi in Beijing.

The survey began just four days after her visit concluded, it said.

Meanwhile, Chinese favorability toward Taiwan ranked at 61 out of 100, higher than any other country or region in the survey, including Russia and Singapore, the survey found.

Asked why Taiwan is important, 82 percent said that "both sides of the Strait share the same cultural heritage and are like one family," up from 67 percent in the last survey, while 77 percent said that unification with Taiwan would symbolize resolving a long-standing historical issue.

About 63 percent said Taiwan's strategic location is important for China to break through US strategic containment, 53 percent said the advanced semiconductor industry is important to Beijing's long-term technological development and 48 percent said Taiwan's open and inclusive society would provide China with a "useful reference" for social development, it found.

Belief in the importance of shared cultural heritage seems to have increased since Cheng's visit, while recognition of Taiwan's semiconductor industry rose "significantly" after the Trump-Xi summit for all demographics, except college-educated Chinese, the article said.

The survey "did not reveal a Chinese public eager for a preemptive attack on Taiwan to force unification," it said, although it revealed a widening gap between those who oppose the use of force and those who do not.

For the Chinese public, improvement of cross-strait relations by diplomatic means is possible, but the consequences of any sudden action could be severe due to belief in cultural and historical nationalist positions on Taiwan that are intensifying amid the US-China artificial intelligence race, it said.

Minors.](https://www.chinatradingdesk.com/post/china-strengthens-online-protection-for-minors-what-marketers-need-to-know)

China’s regulation of artificial intelligence is moving further from broad principles towards active, platform-level enforcement.

In our previous article, **“China Strengthens Online Protection for Minors: What Marketers Need to Know,”**we examined how China’s “Clear and Bright” initiatives are placing greater attention on the digital environment surrounding younger users. That campaign addressed harmful content, unsafe online interactions, inappropriate commercial practices, recommendation systems and the effectiveness of minor-protection modes. It also highlighted AI-generated material as an emerging area of concern, particularly where automated content could expose children and teenagers to misleading, disturbing or inappropriate information.

The latest regulatory development extends this broader direction of online governance into AI applications themselves. The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) has moved into the **second phase of its separate “Clean and Clear: Rectifying Disorder in AI Applications” campaign**.

### **From AI System Compliance to AI-Generated Content**

Phase One focused heavily on whether AI platforms and developers had appropriate safeguards in place.

The CAC targeted areas including failure to complete required large-model filings, inadequate safety and content-filtering systems, problematic model-training data, AI data poisoning, insufficient implementation of **AI-generated content identification requirements**, misuse of AI technologies and inadequate security management of open-source models.

By July, authorities reported action against more than **14,000 non-compliant AI products, websites, applications and intelligent agents**, alongside the removal of more than six million pieces of non-compliant information and action against over 26,000 accounts.

Phase Two goes further into the **AI-generated content ecosystem**.

According to the CAC’s September update, more than **5.61 million pieces of illegal or non-compliant information have been removed, over 49,000 accounts have been dealt with and more than 2,400 websites and applications have faced action**during the second phase.

Instead of concentrating mainly on how AI systems are developed, trained and technically governed, regulators are examining how AI is being used to produce false information, low-quality content, synthetic identities, inappropriate material and artificial online engagement.

For global brands, advertisers, agencies and digital marketers operating in China, the campaign provides a clearer picture of how **China AI regulation in 2026**is moving from technical compliance towards the everyday production and distribution of AI-generated content.

### **Seven AI Misuse Categories Targeted in Phase Two**

The CAC has specifically identified **seven forms of inappropriate or non-compliant AI use**under the second phase of the campaign.

**1. Using AI to distort classic works and create “digital swill”**

Authorities are targeting the use of generative AI to substantially alter classic literature, traditional culture, historical figures and well-known entertainment works for attention or traffic.

Examples include changing established characters, inserting vulgar or violent storylines and mass-producing low-quality content with confused logic, little meaningful value or distorted cultural representations.

**2. Creating and distributing false information with AI**

The second category concerns **AI-generated misinformation and synthetic fake content**.

Regulators have taken action against the creation of fabricated disaster scenes and rescue footage, false social news, misleading information around public events and other synthetic content presented as authentic.

The scope also covers misleading use of **AI digital humans**, including synthetic presenters used to make false promotional or commercial claims.

**3. Using AI to impersonate other people**

AI-powered **face swapping, voice cloning and digital impersonation**are another focus.

The campaign targets the unauthorised use of AI to imitate public figures or other individuals, including synthetic images, videos and audio created for misleading communication or commercial purposes.

This means brands using AI avatars, virtual spokespersons or synthetic voices should pay closer attention to authorisation, identity management and the way generated content may be interpreted by audiences.

**4. Producing violent, vulgar or inappropriate AI-generated content**

The CAC is also targeting the mass creation and distribution of AI-generated material containing **violent, frightening, grotesque, vulgar or sexually suggestive elements**.

This applies across formats including images, videos, written content and other synthetic media.

**5. Using AI-generated content in ways that harm minors**

Protection of minors remains a significant component of China’s wider approach to **AI content governance**.

The CAC identified AI-generated depictions of minors involved in situations inconsistent with their age, including pregnancy and fighting, as well as disturbing animations, abusive content and so-called “cult” videos based on characters or imagery familiar to children.

Authorities stated that such content can damage or distort the image of minors and affect their physical and mental wellbeing.

**6. Using AI-managed accounts for fake engagement and “online water army” activities**

Another focus is the use of **AI automation to imitate human social-media activity**.

This includes using AI-managed accounts to simulate real users, automatically operate social accounts, generate comments and interactions, mass-produce repetitive content or artificially influence traffic and online discussion.

**7. Non-compliant AI products, services and applications**

The final category focuses on **AI applications and services themselves**.

Authorities have identified AI agents, applications and services containing pornographic, inappropriate or otherwise harmful content, including information considered harmful to minors.

Where operators refuse to make corrections, measures can include warnings, fines, application removal or closure.

### **Beijing, Shanghai, Zhejiang and Guangdong Strengthen Local AI Governance**

The second phase is also being implemented through targeted measures by local cyberspace authorities.

**Beijing**has guided online platforms to upgrade their content-review strategies and improve their ability to identify and manage new variations of non-compliant content.

**Shanghai**has instructed platforms to strengthen internal reviews and corrective measures, increase action against illegal content and accounts, and introduce an AI application “knowledge package” to help the public identify potential risks.

**Zhejiang**has adopted a more platform-specific approach, providing tailored compliance guidance to major local platforms, encouraging improvements to internal governance systems and taking action against problematic AI applications.

**Guangdong**has held working meetings with major platforms and conducted targeted corrective supervision of applications with identified compliance issues.

These measures indicate that **AI compliance in China is increasingly being implemented through both national policy and local platform supervision**.

### **Chinese Platforms Are Strengthening AI Content Detection**

Major Chinese digital platforms are also expanding their technical controls.

Douyin, Kuaishou, Weibo, Tencent, Baidu, Bilibili, Xiaohongshu, Zhihu, Douban and Taobao have been upgrading **multimodal AI detection models**, expanding facial, voiceprint and violation-sample databases and introducing functions such as real-time facial-content governance systems.

Platforms have also published **46 AI governance notices**during the campaign.

Chinese AI platforms including **Doubao, Yuanbao, Qwen and ERNIE**have tightened reviews of source material, restricted prohibited outputs and strengthened implementation of AI-generated and synthetic content identification requirements.

At the application-distribution level, **Huawei, Xiaomi, OPPO and vivo**have introduced stricter developer admission and application-listing requirements, while conducting inspections and retesting applications already available in their app stores.

### **What China’s AI Regulation Means for Marketers**

For businesses using **generative AI in China marketing**, the latest campaign reinforces the need to consider compliance throughout the entire AI content workflow.

AI-generated images, videos, copy, digital humans and social-media content should be reviewed before publication. Brands should verify factual claims, establish appropriate controls around face and voice generation, monitor AI-generated content labelling requirements and review how automated tools are being used for social engagement.

Protection of minors should also remain part of the approval process, particularly for campaigns distributed through **Douyin, Xiaohongshu, Weibo, WeChat and other Chinese digital platforms**, where content can reach audiences beyond the advertiser’s original targeting assumptions.

The same principle applies to influencer marketing and content automation. Generative AI can improve production efficiency, but mass-generated low-quality content, synthetic engagement and automated account behaviour may create additional compliance concerns.

title: Trump’s Taiwan Arms Calculus: Bargaining with Beijing, Reassuring the Region
summary: The Trump administration's handling of Taiwan arms sales points to a broader shift in the way Washington is managing its China policy. A roughly USD 14 billion package for Taiwan, primarily air-defence systems, missiles and counter-drone ca
content:
The Trump administration's handling of Taiwan arms sales points to a broader shift in the way Washington is managing its China policy. A roughly USD 14 billion package for Taiwan, primarily air-defence systems, missiles and counter-drone capabilities, has reportedly been kept in abeyance, with Trump describing it as a “very good negotiating chip” with Beijing. The message is unmistakable: Taiwan's security assistance is no longer being treated simply as an element of US deterrence policy, but also as an instrument in the wider US-China bargain. That approach may offer Washington tactical leverage. But it also creates strategic uncertainty for Taiwan and, more importantly, for US allies and partners across the Indo-Pacific.

## Taiwan As An Instrument

Congress advanced the roughly USD 14 billion package earlier in 2026, but Trump has yet to give final approval. Following his May summit with Xi Jinping in Beijing, he said the package was being held “in abeyance” and that its fate “depends on China.” He also acknowledged that Taiwan arms sales had been discussed with Xi in considerable detail.

This is significant because it moves beyond the traditional logic of US arms transfers to Taiwan. The Six Assurances, alongside the Taiwan Relations Act, have long provided the framework within which Washington has maintained Taiwan's defensive capacity while avoiding an explicit commitment to Taiwanese independence. Consulting Beijing over the timing or substance of arms deliveries risks giving China a degree of influence over a policy that Washington has historically sought to keep within its own strategic calculus.

> The Six Assurances, alongside the Taiwan Relations Act, have long provided the framework within which Washington has maintained Taiwan's defensive capacity while avoiding an explicit commitment to Taiwanese independence.

The administration has offered more than one explanation for the delay, including the desire to retain leverage with Beijing and pressure on US munitions stocks because of military operations involving Iran. These explanations need not be mutually exclusive. But from the perspective of allies, the important issue is not merely why a particular package is delayed. It is whether future security commitments can similarly become contingent on unrelated negotiations with Beijing.

A previous package of roughly $11 billion was approved in late 2025, underscoring that the administration has not abandoned arms transfers to Taiwan. The question, therefore, is less about an immediate rupture in policy than about the emerging pattern of conditionality.

## The China Arms-Sale Episode

The reported remarks by US Ambassador to China David Perdue add another layer of uncertainty. Last week, following Xi's state visit to Washington, Perdue said on _Fox News_ that Trump had at one point asked Xi whether China would like to buy US weapons, arguing that Washington sells arms to countries around the world. The White House and State Department quickly rejected the suggestion that there was an actual offer or plan to sell weapons to China, pointing to US law prohibiting such sales. Trump himself disputed Perdue's characterisation, suggesting that the ambassador may have been referring to Taiwan and saying that China would probably prefer superior American equipment, while adding that such a sale had not been discussed.

The episode is therefore best understood as a contested account rather than evidence of an actual US plan to arm China. Yet the fact that the remark required such rapid clarification is itself revealing. Strategic signalling is not simply about what governments intend; it is also about what allies and adversaries believe Washington is prepared to contemplate.

## The Alliance Problem

For US allies, Taiwan is not an isolated issue. Japan, Australia, the Philippines and South Korea all have an interest in the credibility of American deterrence in the western Pacific. A conflict over Taiwan would have consequences for regional sea lanes, military deployments, supply chains and the broader balance of power. This makes the handling of Taiwan arms sales a test of alliance confidence.

If Washington can temporarily suspend a major Taiwanese arms package to gain leverage with Beijing, allies will inevitably consider what this means for their own security relationships with the United States. The concern is not necessarily that Washington will abandon Taiwan. Rather, it is that security commitments could become increasingly transactional, with their implementation conditioned by the demands of a larger US-China bargain.

That perception could encourage greater hedging. Japan and Australia may accelerate indigenous defence capabilities; Southeast Asian partners may diversify security relationships; and governments across the region may become more cautious about aligning themselves too closely with Washington during periods of intensified US-China competition.

> The wider US problem of competing munitions demands, from Europe and the Middle East to the Indo-Pacific, only reinforces these pressures.

The practical consequences are also important. Taiwan already faces long delivery timelines for many American systems. Additional delays thus have effects beyond the immediate political signal. They complicate defence planning and force modernisation and the sequencing of military capabilities. The wider US problem of competing munitions demands, from Europe and the Middle East to the Indo-Pacific, only reinforces these pressures.

## Beijing's Opportunity

For China, the episode offers both a diplomatic and informational advantage. Beijing has consistently opposed American arms sales to Taiwan, which it regards as part of its territory, and has sought to constrain or delay such transfers. If Chinese objections can contribute to postponing US weapons deliveries, Beijing gains something more consequential than a single policy concession: evidence that diplomatic engagement with Washington can influence the operational tempo of American support for Taiwan.

Chinese state media has already used Trump's comments to question the reliability of American backing for Taipei. Such narratives serve Beijing's broader objective of persuading Taiwan that dependence on the United States carries risks, and that accommodation with China may ultimately be unavoidable. The strategic question, therefore, is whether Beijing is being given a de facto role in determining the timing of US military assistance to Taiwan. That would represent a significant shift in the regional balance of signalling.

## The Larger Dilemma

The central tension is between transactional diplomacy and strategic consistency. Trump's approach places a premium on using every available instrument-trade, agriculture, aircraft purchases, military sales and diplomatic engagement - to shape Chinese behaviour. From that perspective, delaying Taiwan arms sales can be presented as pragmatic statecraft rather than abandonment.

But deterrence depends not only on capabilities; it depends on expectations. Allies and adversaries must have some confidence that commitments will survive changes in the diplomatic weather. If weapons deliveries to Taiwan become another variable in summit negotiations with Xi, the United States risks creating uncertainty precisely where deterrence requires clarity.

The distinction between a temporary delay and an indefinite freeze is thus crucial. A short postponement linked to logistics, stockpile management or immediate diplomatic circumstances is one thing. A prolonged delay explicitly conditioned on Beijing's satisfaction would send a very different signal.

For Washington's partners, the issue is consequently larger than the USD 14 billion package itself. They will be watching whether the package, or a modified version of it, eventually moves forward, whether the administration continues to reaffirm the Taiwan Relations Act and Six Assurances, and whether future US-China summits produce similar conditionality.

The reported discussion about possible US arms sales to China, even after being denied and disputed, adds to the uncertainty. At a time when the Indo-Pacific is already adjusting to a more contested balance of power, Washington's challenge is not simply to negotiate effectively with Beijing. It is to ensure that the pursuit of a better US-China relationship does not generate doubts among the very partners whose confidence underpins American strategy in Asia.

title: Taiwan seeks drone partnerships with partners amid China threat
summary: The Taiwan Coast Guard joined forces with the Ministry of National Defense and the Air Service Corps to carry out the Haian 12 military exercises in June 2025 Taiwan Coast Guard [![Image 1: Reuters](https://media.assettype.com/bairdmaritime
content:
The Taiwan Coast Guard joined forces with the Ministry of National Defense and the Air Service Corps to carry out the Haian 12 military exercises in June 2025 Taiwan Coast Guard

[![Image 1: Reuters](https://media.assettype.com/bairdmaritime%2F2024-12-02%2F7e0yqzaz%2Freuters_logo_icon_170782.png?w=48&auto=format%2Ccompress)](https://www.bairdmaritime.com/author/reuters)

Published on:

28 Sep 2026, 10:35 am

Taiwan must deepen cooperation with its democratic partners on developing drones which are crucial to fighting modern warfare, President Lai Ching-te said on Monday.

Taiwan's government has made defence modernisation and increased spending a core policy given stepped-up military pressure from China, which views the democratically governed island as its own territory.

Speaking in southern Taiwan's Chiayi for the groundbreaking ceremony for a new drone development centre, Lai said the site's significance has become even more prominent with changes in the international situation.

"From the Ukrainian battlefield to Indo-Pacific regional security, unmanned systems have become important combat strength in modern defence," Lai said.

"At the same time, we must deepen cooperation with democratic partners and jointly build a safer and more resilient unmanned aircraft supply chain, providing solid support for Indo-Pacific regional peace and stability," he added.

Taiwan possesses world-class semiconductor and information and communications technology capabilities, as well as a deep precision manufacturing foundation.

Taiwan's cabinet earlier this month proposed [an additional TW$145.7 billion ($4.59 billion) in defence spending](https://www.bairdmaritime.com/security/naval/unmanned-naval-systems/taiwans-46b-defence-budget-top-up-includes-suicide-drone-boats) for this year for systems including drones and anti-ballistic missiles.

Those spending plans incorporate more than 600 coastal surveillance and reconnaissance drones, over 40,000 coastal attack drones, and the first batch of over 100 small suicide drone boats.

Lai and his government reject Beijing's sovereignty claims, saying only the island's people can decide their future.

_(Reporting by Yi-Chin Lee and Ann Wang; Writing by Ben Blanchard; Editing by Lincoln Feast.)_

The FBI has arrested a “Chinese foreign agent” at Los Angeles International Airport accused of spying on the Taiwanese president’s son.

Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, was arrested on Sunday before her planned departure to China, the first assistant US attorney for the Central District of California, Bill Essayli, said in a post on X.

Authorities charged Zhang, 34, of Irvine, California, with acting as an unregistered foreign agent.

Zhang surveilled Taiwanese President William Lai Ching-te’s son, the FBI said. The agency did not directly name Zhang’s alleged target, but later shared a news article identifying him as Lai Ting-yu.

The US Justice Department said Zhang travelled to Seattle in 2025 at the behest of Chinese officials. She sent photos, video and license plate information of the Taiwanese leader’s son and his family to China.

Essayli called Zhang a “Chinese foreign agent” and said she “used tradecraft to avoid detection”.

“She never notified the Attorney General she was acting for a foreign government, a federal offense,” he added.

Essayli said Zhang will appear in a Los Angeles federal court on Monday.

William Lai Ching-te and his Democratic Progressive Party say that [Taiwan](https://www.aljazeera.com/where/taiwan/) is already an independent country separate from China. Beijing views the island as Chinese territory.

Washington does not have ⁠formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan, but the US is bound by law to provide the island with the means to ‌defend itself.

Earlier this week, the US[delivered](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/2/us-delivers-f-16v-fighter-jets-to-taiwan-as-island-eyes-threat-from-china) two F-16V ⁠Block 70 fighter jets to Taiwan as the island seeks to build its defence capabilities to deter a feared attack by [China](https://www.aljazeera.com/video/101-east/2026/8/15/is-china-seeking-to-copy-irans-strait-of-hormuz-blockade-around-taiwan).

summary: 伦敦 — 国际刑警组织(INTERPOL)第94届全体大会将于11月30日至12月3日在香港举行。中国长期以来被指利用国际刑警组织追查政治目标，分析人士担心，中国可能借主办大会的机会，为自己的形象“洗白”。 “根据我们的经验，中国是滥用国际刑警组织规则最老练的国家之一”，英国上级审裁院移民和庇护庭副法官本·基思(Ben Keith)和在伦敦及海牙执业的大律师里斯·戴维斯(Rhys Davies)对美国之音表示。 两人长期处理红色通报、引渡及跨国镇压案件，并合作撰写刚发表的新书
content:
伦敦 —

国际刑警组织(INTERPOL)第94届全体大会将于11月30日至12月3日在香港举行。中国长期以来被指利用国际刑警组织追查政治目标，分析人士担心，中国可能借主办大会的机会，为自己的形象“洗白”。

“根据我们的经验，中国是滥用国际刑警组织规则最老练的国家之一”，英国上级审裁院移民和庇护庭副法官本·基思(Ben Keith)和在伦敦及海牙执业的大律师里斯·戴维斯(Rhys Davies)对美国之音表示。

两人长期处理红色通报、引渡及跨国镇压案件，并合作撰写刚发表的新书《国际刑警组织：法律与实务》（INTERPOL Law and Practice）。

**香港办大会，为中国洗白**

国际刑警组织在香港召开大会期间，将选举档案控制委员会(Commission for the Control of INTERPOL's Files, CCF)的全部七名成员。该委员会负责处理个人对自身数据的查询，也是唯一有权裁决并删除或修改红色通报(Red Notice)申请的机构。

基思说，他担心北京利用香港主办大会的机会，为自身形象“洗白”。“我们非常担心，中国正试图利用国际刑警组织为自己的声誉洗白。”他说。

香港警方近年对多名身处海外的民主活动人士、律师及倡议者发出国安法通缉令，部分案件附带100万港元悬赏。英国政府的香港半年报告说，截至2025年底，香港警方已对34名海外人士发出涉及国家安全罪名的通缉令。

基思把这些悬赏形容为“极其阴险”。他说，这不仅是提供现金线索，也是在鼓励他人寻找方法，把目标带回中国。

英国资深大律师、前香港大律师公会主席夏博义(Paul Harris SC)也对美国之音说，他对大会在香港举行“非常担忧”。

他说：“这是不合适的，因为中国已经违反《中英联合声明》，并以政治罪名监禁香港人。”

英国政府批评香港的海外通缉及悬赏是企图恐吓在英国合法行使言论自由的人士。

香港政府则表示，有关人士涉嫌危害国家安全，当局是在依法追捕逃犯，并非因为其政治立场或言论采取行动。香港政府也表示，《香港国安法》保障人权和自由，绝大多数居民及访港人士不会受到影响。

**政治案件披上刑事外衣**

戴维斯说，中国已成为国际刑警组织中的重要力量。他认为，一些由中国提出的红色通报表面涉及普通刑事罪名，实际上却带有政治动机。

他特别提到中国的“猎狐行动”和“天网行动”。北京将这些行动称为“追逃追赃及反腐败工作”，但基思说，他们接触了部分被中国当局锁定的目标，其中包括异议人士、记者及曾经批评中国政府的人。

基思还说，中国当局有时会扣留或威胁当事人在华亲属，再要求身处海外的目标回国“协助调查”；检察人员也可能向目标保证，回国后不会受到处罚。

中国政府表示，“猎狐”和“天网”旨在追捕涉嫌腐败及其他犯罪的外逃人员，并否认有关行动构成跨国镇压。中国外交部此前对国际调查记者同盟(ICIJ)表示，“中方严格遵守国际法及各国主权”。

戴维斯借用法律界的一个说法，把红色通报称为“独裁者的狙击步枪”，可以跨越国界，精准锁定个人。

他说，即使当事人没有旅行计划，红色通报仍可能导致银行终止服务、声誉受损及长期心理压力。

人权观察(Human Rights Watch)及其他人权机构多次指责中国滥用红色通缉令系统，将其作为打压海外异议人士、维权维稳以及强迫流亡公民回国的工具。

戴维斯认为，红色通报最隐蔽之处，是它为政治追捕披上一层法律外衣。请求国把指控提交国际刑警组织后，其他成员国的警务机关可能因为加入了这一体系而采取行动。

**国际刑警组织如何审查通报**

国际刑警组织章程第三条禁止该组织介入政治、军事、宗教或种族性质的活动。

该组织表示，所有红色通报均须经过专门工作组审查，已经发布的通报也会持续接受核查。当事人可以向档案控制委员会申请查阅或删除资料。

国际刑警组织此前回应国际调查记者同盟时表示，它拥有“稳健且持续接受评估”的审查制度，但最初决定只能依据提出申请时掌握的资料作出。

两名律师承认，国际刑警组织近年来加强了审查。然而，他们认为，如果政治案件被包装成诈骗、腐败或其他普通刑事案件，仍可能通过初步审查。

基思和戴维斯强调，国际刑警合作对于打击严重跨国犯罪不可或缺。但真正的问题是，当一项刑事指控进入全球警务系统后，谁能及时区分正常执法与政治追捕，以及谁来保护被错误锁定的人。

美国之音已就香港主办国际刑警组织全体大会和相关争议，分别向香港警务处和中国驻英国大使馆请求置评。截至发稿，尚未收到回复。

title: The next play

content:
For most of Gabe Norwood’s adult life, basketball dictated the rhythm of his world: practices, games, flights, seasons, championships, losses and the constant preparation that comes with being a professional athlete. For his wife, Lei, it meant building a life around that rhythm too.

Now, with Gabe’s retirement from the Philippine Basketball Association (PBA), the Norwoods are entering a season unlike any they have had before. Their schedule is different, their priorities are shifting, and for the first time in years, they have more freedom to decide what comes next.

“It feels exciting, unfamiliar, and a little surreal all at once,” Lei says. “Basketball dictated so much of the rhythm of our lives for so many years. Now there’s a little more freedom to ask, ‘What do we want this next chapter to look like?’ Not just for Gabe, but for all of us.”

*   [Diplomats, public servants honored at Asia’s Modern Hero Awards 2026](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/11/the-sunday-times/filipino-champions/diplomats-public-servants-honored-at-asias-modern-hero-awards-2026/2443069)

For Gabe, the transition does not mean leaving basketball behind. The game has been part of his life for as long as he can remember, and his connection to it reaches beyond his years as a player.

“The playing part ended,” he says. “The relationships, the lessons, the love for the game, those don’t end.”

Retirement has brought both a sense of finality and gratitude. Looking back, Gabe thinks about the teammates, coaches, fans, organizations and the national team that became part of his journey. There are things he misses, but above all, he feels fortunate to have experienced it all.

For Lei, watching him retire was equally emotional.

“It was truly a bittersweet ride,” she says. “I was beyond proud of him and all that he has accomplished. Full of gratitude for what has been and excited for what is to come.”

*   ![Image 1: 10 special non-working days declared for Oct](https://miopia.newsroom.bi/statics/i/ps/manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/09/1252382.jpg?width=113&crop=113:85)
[10 special non-working days declared for Oct](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/09/regions/10-special-non-working-days-declared-for-oct/2442158)

The sadness of seeing an era end comes with an appreciation for everything basketball has given their family. And perhaps that is the best way to understand the Norwoods today. They are not leaving one life behind. They are carrying everything they learned from it into whatever comes next.

[![Image 2: Over the years, Gabe and Lei Norwood have navigated marriage, children, championships, losses, injuries, adventures, career changes, moves and all the ordinary complications that come with building a family. COVER AND INSIDE PHOTOS COURTESY OF GABE AND LEI NORWOOD](https://manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/10/1254138.jpg)](https://manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/10/1254138.jpg)
Over the years, Gabe and Lei Norwood have navigated marriage, children, championships, losses, injuries, adventures, career changes, moves and all the ordinary complications that come with building a family. COVER AND INSIDE PHOTOS COURTESY OF GABE AND LEI NORWOOD

## **Growing together**

Gabe and Lei have evolved alongside his career. The couple they were at the beginning is very different from the couple they are today.Over the years, they have navigated marriage, children, championships, losses, injuries, adventures, career changes, moves and all the ordinary complications that come with building a family.

They have learned that marriage means making room for each other to change while continuing to grow together. Gabe says they understand each other better now: when to communicate, when to listen and when to give each other space. Through it all, they have learned to see themselves as teammates.

That mindset became especially important during the difficult stretches of a professional sports career. As the couple points out, people see the games, but they do not always know what it takes to get there. The physical work, the recovery, the travel and the pressure to perform year after year.

At home, Lei carried a different kind of responsibility.

*   ![Image 3: ‘No simple living for the Dutertes’](https://miopia.newsroom.bi/statics/i/ps/manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/11/1254518.jpeg?width=113&crop=113:85)
[‘No simple living for the Dutertes’](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/11/news/no-simple-living-for-the-dutertes/2443173)

“When you’re traveling or focused on the season, somebody still has to make everything at home work,” Gabe says. “She gave me the ability to focus on my job because I knew our family was taken care of.”

It is a sacrifice he understands even more now.

There were certainly moments when basketball tested their marriage. Absences, fatigue, the uncertainty before the frustration after all came with the territory.

They worked through those moments by communicating and reminding themselves that basketball was Gabe’s job, not the foundation of their entire family.

“Basketball was my job, but my marriage and family were bigger than the job,” Gabe says.

For Lei, a lasting marriage depends on remembering what matters beyond the circumstances of any particular season. For Gabe, it has meant learning to process challenges without bringing them through the front door. Over time, they have become better at moving through difficult seasons together. Faith has also anchored them.

[![Image 4: Through many seasons, Gabe and Lei have committed to living a life that is authentic to who they are.](https://manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/10/1254139.jpg)](https://manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/10/1254139.jpg)
Through many seasons, Gabe and Lei have committed to living a life that is authentic to who they are.

## **At home, he’s just Gabe**

Away from the cameras and arenas, Lei describes Gabe as very different from the competitive athlete people know. He is low-key, funny and extremely patient. He does not need to be the loudest person in the room.At home, he is simply Gabe.

There are the dad jokes, teasing the boys, lots of eating, sports on television and, inevitably, a reason to turn something into a competition. This is the version of Gabe his family knows best, and now they get to see more of him.

Retirement has changed the rhythm of their household, though it has not necessarily meant slowing down. The family moved, their boys entered new stages of their own lives, and everyone had to establish new routines. In some ways, they are still figuring out what normal looks like.

What excites them most are the ordinary things: family dinners without someone rushing off to practice, more weekends together, being present for school events and holidays without checking a basketball schedule first. There is also more room for travel and adventures.

“The little things you miss during a season become the things you appreciate the most,” Gabe says.

For their children, the transition has been surprisingly simple. They knew their father was a professional athlete, but they also knew him as Dad. Now, Dad is around more.

“I want them to see that your job can change without changing who you are,” Gabe says.

That lesson extends beyond basketball to the kind of home they want their boys to remember. Lei hopes they remember parents who showed up, made home a safe place and taught them kindness, discipline, resilience, humility, integrity and faith.

For Gabe, character matters most. He wants his sons to know that they can pursue their own paths without feeling pressured to become versions of their parents. He wants them to understand what it means to work hard, show respect and be a good teammate, whether in sports, work, marriage or life in general.

[![Image 5: Gabe during his last season of the PBA PHOTO FROM INSTAGRAM/GNORWOOD5](https://manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/10/1254140.jpg)](https://manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/10/1254140.jpg)
Gabe during his last season of the PBA PHOTO FROM INSTAGRAM/GNORWOOD5

## **Beyond the jersey**

Retirement raises questions about identity as well as the future. It is not so much, "What will you do next?" as "Who are you now?"

For Gabe, the answer comes easily: he is a husband and a father first.

He remains competitive, curious and still deeply connected to basketball. But without the demands of preparing his body for the next game, he now has the opportunity to explore other sides of the sport.

He wants to continue mentoring younger players and learn more about basketball operations and the business side of the game. Coaching, player development, scouting, media or some combination of those paths could become part of his next chapter.

“The jersey was a big part of my life, but it was never all of me,” he says.

Lei is experiencing her own rediscovery. With more room to focus on her interests in food, marketing and storytelling, she is thinking about what she wants to build in this season of her life.

And for the first time, there is more opportunity to build side by side. The Norwoods do not have a perfectly mapped-out plan, but they have conversations, ideas and passions they are excited to pursue individually and together.

Their biggest shared dream may be less about one specific project and more about freedom.

The freedom to experience new places as a family and make decisions based on what feels right for them rather than what the season requires.

There is also the freedom to create and give back.

“Building something together that lasts beyond basketball would be pretty special,” Gabe says.

[![Image 6: Despite his many successes in the PBA, Gabe firmly believes the best is ahead.](https://manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/10/1254141.jpg)](https://manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/10/1254141.jpg)
Despite his many successes in the PBA, Gabe firmly believes the best is ahead.

## **A different definition of success**

Ask Lei what she hopes life looks like five years from now, and her answer has little to do with status. She wants their family to feel rooted and their boys to thrive on whatever paths they choose. She wants Gabe doing meaningful work while she continues developing her own pursuits.

She imagines a home filled with family, friends, cooking and laughter, with people gathered around the table.

“Success for me at this point looks a lot like peace and purpose,” she says.

For Gabe, success means work with a sense of purpose, continued learning and the flexibility to enjoy life with his family. It is a striking evolution for someone whose career was once measured by points, wins and championships.

Now, legacy means something much more personal, too. Gabe hopes former teammates remember him as someone they could count on and that younger players remember he helped them.And no matter how busy and demanding the life on the hard court had become, he wants his family to remember he was still there for them.

As a family, Lei hopes they will be remembered for welcoming people, living out their faith and using whatever success they achieve to serve others and pay it forward.

Above all, she hopes people remember how much they love being a family.

[![Image 7: The new chapter has enabled both Lei and Gabe to establish new routines with their three boys.](https://manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/10/1254142.jpg)](https://manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/10/1254142.jpg)

title: Lai's WWII remarks warn of China's bid to reshape world order: Analysts - Focus Taiwan
summary: Taipei, Oct. 10 (CNA) A senior official said Saturday that President Lai Ching-te's (賴清德) emphasis on preserving the historical facts of World War II in his National Day address highlighted concerns over Beijing's efforts to undermine the p
content:
Taipei, Oct. 10 (CNA) A senior official said Saturday that President Lai Ching-te's (賴清德) emphasis on preserving the historical facts of World War II in his National Day address highlighted concerns over Beijing's efforts to undermine the postwar international order.

Lai delivered his National Day address as Taiwan marked the 115th anniversary of the founding of the Republic of China (ROC), the country's formal name, declaring that "distortions" of World War II history must not be tolerated, a point he was making for the first time as president.

## Concerns over WWII history distortion

In speaking about geopolitical challenges facing Taiwan, Lai said he welcomed U.S.-China dialogue to manage competition and reduce the risk of conflict, while stressing that regional peace and stability require a correct understanding of how history unfolded.

"There must be no tolerance for distorting the history of World War II. There must be respect for the right of the people of Taiwan to exist," Lai said.

"And above all, democracies in the Indo-Pacific must join forces to ensure the status quo of peace and stability in the region is not changed," he continued.

The remarks came after Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) and U.S. President Donald Trump recalled U.S.-China cooperation during World War II at their meeting in Washington late last month.

During World War II, China was governed by the Republic of China (ROC), which fought alongside the United States. The ROC government relocated to Taiwan after the war. The People's Republic of China (PRC), led by Xi, was established in 1949, four years after the war ended. From 1895-1945, Taiwan was a colony of Japan and many Taiwanese were conscripted to serve in the Japanese military.

## Risks to international order

By pointing to Beijing's "distortion" of World War II history, Lai cautioned against the risks posed by its attempts to overturn existing international rules and disrupt the status quo, a senior official who wished to remain anonymous told CNA.

Taiwan's commitment to maintaining the status quo is not only about defending the country's right to exist, but also about upholding the postwar principle that peace and freedom should not be coerced through violence or threats, the official said

Wang Hung-jen (王宏仁), a political science professor at National Cheng Kung University, said Beijing has long promoted a narrative portraying today's China as having fought side by side with the U.S. in World War II, as Xi recently did during his meeting with Trump.

Against this backdrop, Lai's emphasis on "distortions of World War II history" in his National Day address was significant, he said.

Beijing's distortion of WWII history could also distort the interpretation of wartime documents, affecting how Taiwan's sovereign status is viewed, Wang noted.

Another Presidential Office official said Lai's support for U.S.-China dialogue to reduce risks, as well as his call for Beijing to return to a rules-based international order, were also noteworthy.

Lai took the opportunity to tell the international community that Taiwan supports dialogue, while stressing that any peaceful arrangement regarding Taiwan must respect its people's right to choose their future, the official told CNA.

## Cross-strait stance unchanged

On cross-strait relations, Wang said that Lai's remarks were consistent with his administration's previous position and did not represent a change in policy.

Wang said Lai stressed the need to maintain peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait, called for defense reforms and stronger resilience across society, and signaled that Beijing should not use gray-zone tactics or military coercion against Taiwan.

Lin Tzu-li (林子立), a political science professor at Tunghai University, said that given the current international situation, maintaining the Taiwan Strait status quo is key to cross-strait stability.

By reiterating the need to maintain peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait in the address, Lai implicitly endorsed a "no independence, no unification" stance, countering Beijing's repeated claims that Taiwan is responsible for disrupting the cross-strait status quo, Lin said.

## Biblical metaphors

In the address, Lai used several biblical metaphors to describe Taiwan as "a city upon a hill," "the salt of the earth" and "the light of the world," which political scholars interpreted in different ways.

According to the Presidential Office official, the "city upon a hill" reflects Taiwan's aspirations for its future, while "the salt of the earth" embodies democracy and self-defense as ways to maintain peace and provide stability in a turbulent region.

The "light of the world" reflects Taiwan's contributions to the international community through its economic development, technological advances and other areas, the official said.

Kuo Yu-jen (郭育仁), vice president of the Institute for National Policy Research, said "city upon a hill" is a distinctive U.S. political phrase referring to the idea of a society serving as a model for others, famously used by former President Ronald Reagan and other U.S. presidents.

Its use in Lai's National Day address underscored the shared founding values between the Republic of China (Taiwan) and the U.S., as well as Taiwan's ties with other democracies, Kuo said.

The wording shows how Taiwan sees its role in the world and its aspiration to serve as a model, while contrasting with China's political system, Wang said.

Lin said Lai's use of "city upon a hill" was meant to inspire confidence among Taiwanese, pointing to Taiwan's democratic and economic performance despite China's threats and challenges facing Western countries, including rising populism, limited economic growth and mounting debt.

(By Yeh Su-ping, Lee Ya-wen, Wen Kuei-hsiang, Lai Yu-chen, and Shih Hsiu-chuan)

title: El Niño will intensify, then peak in December
summary: **GENEVA, Switzerland —**El Niño will intensify even more before peaking in December, the United Nations said on Thursday, warning it could be among the strongest witnessed since 1950. The naturally occurring weather phenomenon is set to br
content:
**GENEVA, Switzerland —**El Niño will intensify even more before peaking in December, the United Nations said on Thursday, warning it could be among the strongest witnessed since 1950.

The naturally occurring weather phenomenon is set to bring higher temperatures to much of the planet, the UN’s weather and climate agency said, with its impact compounding the effects of man-made climate change.

“El Niño will continue to intensify ahead of its forecast peak in December,” the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said in its monthly Global Seasonal Climate Update.

“It is likely to bring above-average temperatures to much of the globe and shift rainfall patterns, increasing the risk of drought and floods in different regions.” El Niño warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns.

It typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months.

Conditions oscillate between El Niño and its opposite La Niña, with neutral conditions in between.

**‘Strengthening rapidly’**

“Sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific are forecast to increase to record levels during October-November-December 2026, reflecting the strengthening of the El Niño event which will drive weather patterns and impact economies, ecosystems and communities across the globe,” the WMO said.

*   ![Image 1: Virata: Martial law pillar](https://miopia.newsroom.bi/statics/i/ps/manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/08/1252091.jpg?width=113&crop=113:85)
[Virata: Martial law pillar](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/09/opinion/columns/virata-martial-law-pillar/2441990)

The forecast is based on consensus across 13 leading national and international meteorological centers.

“El Niño is firmly established and strengthening rapidly,” said WMO chief Celeste Saulo.

“WMO forecasts indicate a near-100 percent likelihood that it will persist through February 2027, potentially being one of the strongest since at least 1950.” Saulo explained that El Niño does not add new heat to the planet, but releases heat being stored in the ocean.

“The ocean it’s drawing from is the warmest we’ve ever measured it. There is simply more heat available to release,” she said.

*   ![Image 2: Robredo, Baste Duterte lead contrasting 2028 scenarios – survey](https://miopia.newsroom.bi/statics/i/ps/manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/07/1250224.jpg?width=113&crop=113:85)

The index, which measures sea surface temperature anomalies across the central-eastern equatorial Pacific — the region at the heart of El Niño — increased from 1.6 degrees Celsius above normal in June to 2.5 C above normal in August.

For October-November-December, the anomaly is forecast to reach approximately 3.7 C above normal.

This would be the highest since observations began, eclipsing the previous record of 2.6 C set in 2015–2016.

The last El Niño contributed to making 2023 the second-hottest year on record and 2024 the all-time high at around 1.55 C above the 1850–1900 preindustrial average.

While El Niño usually peaks between November and February, the resulting spike in temperatures typically comes later.

This El Niño is already hitting some regions hard, including in Central America, where animals and crops are dying from drought.

title: TikTok gave teens, children placebo safety feature in experiment, New York alleges
summary: TIKTOK ran an experiment on thousands of users who tried to turn on a safety feature on the platform, giving them non-functional versions of the tool, according to allegations in New York’s lawsuit against the company unsealed on Wednesday.
content:
TIKTOK ran an experiment on thousands of users who tried to turn on a safety feature on the platform, giving them non-functional versions of the tool, according to allegations in New York’s lawsuit against the company unsealed on Wednesday.

In the so-called “ghost” or placebo experiments, TikTok selected thousands of users, including teens and children, who opted to use safety features like “Algo Refresh,” a tool designed to reset recommendations for users seeking to escape unwanted or potentially harmful content. According to the lawsuit, those users believed they had activated the feature, but their feeds did not change, unlike users who got the fully working version.

The newly unsealed allegations are part of New York Attorney General Letitia James’ lawsuit against the company, one of more than two dozen brought by states accusing TikTok of designing its platform to addict children and of misleading users about its safety. Many documents in state cases across the country have been sealed or heavily redacted as TikTok has sought to keep details about its operations from public view.

*   [Pentagon says the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/09/world/americas-emea/pentagon-says-the-firing-squad-execution-of-fort-hood-shooter-nidal-malik-hasan-will-be-livestreamed/2442298)

The lawsuit claims TikTok assures users that safety is a top priority and that its platform is appropriate for kids and teens, while knowingly preventing some groups of users from accessing certain safety tools, including users who had specifically sought to avoid unwanted or potentially harmful content.

“We continuously make improvements to our platform which means that, like most companies, we regularly test new products and features to validate the experience and understand how they work in the real world,” a TikTok spokesperson said in a statement.

The company has broadly denied New York’s allegations in court filings and has said that keeping young users safe is a priority.

In September, TikTok settled the first state lawsuit set for trial, agreeing to pay Alabama up to $300 million and change how its platform functions for teens in the state.

Ms. James, a Democrat, originally sued in 2024. The claims about the tests were included in an updated, sealed version of New York’s complaint filed at the end of August and later ordered unsealed by a judge.

*   ![Image 1: Robredo, Baste Duterte lead contrasting 2028 scenarios – survey](https://miopia.newsroom.bi/statics/i/ps/manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/07/1250224.jpg?width=113&crop=113:85)

**EMPLOYEE FLAGGED TEST**Internally, a product manager for Digital Well Being at TikTok, said doing placebo tests on the Algo Refresh feature was problematic and that users might find it misleading, the lawsuit alleges.

“This feature is about algorithm transparency and control,” the person wrote in an internal chat, according to the lawsuit. “A placebo group completely conflicts with that.”

Ultimately the company did the tests repeatedly on thousands of users in 2023, comparing users who did not get the feature with those who did, to study how long users stayed on the site and the impact on ad revenue, the lawsuit alleges.

The lawsuit also alleges that TikTok misled consumers about how “Algo Refresh” worked, telling them it would reset the algorithm that recommended videos to them when it was only a temporary change. The TikTok spokesperson said the allegations mischaracterize how “Algo Refresh” works.

The unsealed portions of the lawsuit also allege that TikTok conducted a separate set of experiments, which were previously revealed in a report by Bloomberg. In them, TikTok randomly selected users and turned off safety features on their accounts that limited their exposure to harmful content. A teen boy in New York who was part of the test committed suicide after he was shown content about self-harm and suicide, Bloomberg reported.

Internal reviews showed the boy had been shown an “onslaught” of content about suicide and self-harm, the lawsuit said.

title: Four astronauts return to Earth after eight months in space
summary: CAPE CANAVERAL, Florida — Four astronauts returned to Earth from the International Space Station on Thursday after hurrying there eight months ago to replace an ailing colleague and his crew. SpaceX brought the U.S., French and Russian flye
content:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Florida — Four astronauts returned to Earth from the International Space Station on Thursday after hurrying there eight months ago to replace an ailing colleague and his crew.

SpaceX brought the U.S., French and Russian flyers back with a splashdown in the Pacific off the coast of Los Angeles.

NASA’s Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, France’s Sophie Adenot and Russia’s Andrey Fedyaev departed the orbiting lab on Wednesday, eager to reunite with their families after a lengthy separation. Their replacements arrived three weeks late because of capsule repairs, stalling this crew’s homecoming.

*   [Pentagon says the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/09/world/americas-emea/pentagon-says-the-firing-squad-execution-of-fort-hood-shooter-nidal-malik-hasan-will-be-livestreamed/2442298)

They couldn’t wait to feel the breeze on their faces, hit the shower and, for Adenot at least, plunge back into water sports. Her 237 days in orbit set an endurance record for the European Space Agency.

“We are so excited to be back on Planet Earth after an incredible mission on the International Space Station,” Meir radioed moments after splashing down. While still in orbit, she said the crew had “a lot of mixed, swirling emotions” and would miss the “extraordinary views of our home planet.”

By signing up with an email address, I acknowledge that I have read and agree to the [Terms of Service](https://manilatimes.net/terms-of-service "Terms of Service") and [Privacy Policy](https://manilatimes.net/privacy-policy "Privacy Policy").

All four were out of their capsule within an hour, waving and pumping their fists in the air aboard SpaceX's recovery ship. After a helicopter ride to shore, they were going to head for Houston.

Meir and her crew left the planet in February to replace four station occupants who were sent home early after one of them — NASA's Mike Fincke, now retired — fell ill. It was NASA's first medical evacuation in 65 years of human spaceflight.

The new foursome watched with pride two months later as the Artemis II astronauts flew around the moon. They also celebrated the United States’ 250th birthday up there, with Meir joining the Boston Pops with her piccolo for a Fourth of July concert.

*   ![Image 1: Robredo, Baste Duterte lead contrasting 2028 scenarios – survey](https://miopia.newsroom.bi/statics/i/ps/manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/07/1250224.jpg?width=113&crop=113:85)
[Robredo, Baste Duterte lead contrasting 2028 scenarios – survey](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/08/news/robredo-baste-duterte-lead-contrasting-2028-scenarios-survey/2441041)

Meir took part in four spacewalks, while Adenot ventured outside three times for maintenance and upgrades to the 28-year-old outpost.

In the middle of all the work, the astronauts found time for fun, throwing a dance party last month and holding regular cooking demonstrations complete with aprons and a chef's toque.

Meir presented a how-to video for curly-haired spacewomen like herself, while Hathaway kept his bushy mustache — a space rarity — groomed to perfection. He grew the naval aviator-style mustache before rocketing into orbit as a way to honor his Navy ties, and found it no harder to maintain in weightlessness than on Earth. Some ground controllers grew mustaches in solidarity.

**Will his mustache disappear now that his mission is over?**

*   ![Image 2: LTO identifies rider in hit-and-run incident involving 'It's Showtime' host](https://miopia.newsroom.bi/statics/i/ps/manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/07/1249307.jpg?width=113&crop=113:85)

“It’s kind of become a little bit of my brand up here,” Hathaway said in August, “so I don’t know if it’ll go away right away or I’ll end up keeping it for a while.”

Seven astronauts remain aboard the space station, representing the U.S., Russia and Canada. The outpost has welcomed 298 visitors from 26 countries since the doors swung open in 2000, by NASA's count.

*   ![Image 3: Virata: Martial law pillar](https://miopia.newsroom.bi/statics/i/ps/manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/08/1252091.jpg?width=113&crop=113:85)

SpaceX is now gearing up for a space station supply run next week. Elon Musk's company will launch more than 6,000 pounds (2,700 kilograms) of cargo, including the last of a series of solar panel additions, toilet pump, spacewalking suit, and fresh fruit and other goodies.

Beijing claims most of the strategic waterway despite an international ruling that its assertion has no legal basis, and confrontations between Philippine and Chinese ships have in some cases led to collisions resulting in injuries and damage.

In September, Manila monitored 101 Chinese navy and coast guard ships around Philippine-garrisoned Thitu Island and Second Thomas Shoal, as well as off Sabina Shoal and Chinese-controlled Scarborough Shoal.

title: South Korean diplomacy: the wheels are coming off
summary: By **Mason Richey** Since President Lee Jae Myung entered office in June 2025, I have mostly complimented his administration’s foreign policy. Alas, the wheels are coming off. Before we get to the current situation — with Seoul flailing on
content:
By **Mason Richey**

Since President Lee Jae Myung entered office in June 2025, I have mostly complimented his administration’s foreign policy. Alas, the wheels are coming off. Before we get to the current situation — with Seoul flailing on U.S., Ukraine and North Korea issues — let’s review the trajectory until now.

When Lee took office, he faced a difficult diplomatic environment. Above all, Seoul was under competing pressures from Washington and Beijing. The U.S. under President Donald Trump was increasingly demanding of allies — including Seoul — in the realms of security and economics. Meanwhile China remained a tricky economic partner for South Korean industry and a regional security actor with inscrutable goals on North Korea. Upgrading other bilateral relations was important, both per se and as means for creating more autonomy vis-à-vis the U.S. and China. To this end, Seoul continued to enhance strategic partnerships — e.g., with Japan, Europe, Australia, Singapore and Canada — while emphasizing relations with Global South states with significant commercial or resource profiles.

An important multilateral diplomatic calendar also loomed — a mid-June G7 summit, late-June NATO summit, September U.N. General Assembly, October APEC summit hosted in Gyeongju and December G20 meeting.

The Lee administration largely acquitted itself well, notably on key bilateral issues and the APEC summit. South Korea stood firm as a U.S. ally while patiently resisting excessive U.S. trade and investment demands. Seoul’s trade relations with Beijing stayed on track, and China even removed controversial facilities from the China-South Korea Provisional Maritime Zone. Entente with Japan continued apace, to the surprise of many, given the contentious history of Seoul-Tokyo relations under prior progressive presidents. Outreach to other strategic partners and the Global South established a conveyor belt of memoranda of understanding on economic relations, supply chains, critical resources and other cooperation areas that may mitigate some of the risks Seoul experiences in being caught between Washington and Beijing.

APEC in Gyeongju was successful, both multilaterally and in terms of bilateral meetings surrounding it. The most important was a Trump-Lee summit that — in principle — established a U.S-South Korea trade and investment agreement and opened the door to a South Korean nuclear-powered submarine deal that includes potential rights for Seoul to develop uranium enrichment and spent nuclear fuel reprocessing capabilities.

However, the end of 2025 marked the high point of Lee’s diplomacy, and it has been mostly a downhill slide ever since. In January 2026, the Trump administration began voicing displeasure at Seoul’s implementation of the trade and investment deal. In January and February, U.S.-South Korea discord over the treatment of online delivery platform Coupang began disrupting progress in other areas, including security and defense. Also in February a kerfuffle emerged over the scheduling of U.S.-South Korea-Japan trilateral air exercises. Spring and summer were marked by the effect of the U.S. war against Iran, which both affected South Korea’s economy and occasioned Trump to coerce Lee into joining the war. This reached a climax with an angry social media post in which Trump insulted Lee and South Korea, praised North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, curtailed U.S.-South Korea military exercises and again pressured Seoul to enter the Iran conflict. All this was accompanied by growing influence of the “autonomy” faction of South Korea’s progressive foreign policy apparatus, which began to crank up obsequious, ineffective outreach to Pyongyang. They also added a wrinkle by attempting — for reasons involving commercial relations, natural resources, arctic shipping and North Korea — to get the Lee administration to accommodate Putin’s Russia, thus irritating European and Canadian partners.

Currently the diplomatic wheels are off the rails. Washington and Seoul publicly dispute the status of South Korean investment into an Alaska LNG project — a deliverable for the U.S.-South Korea trade and investment deal. Consequently Trump is threatening to punish Seoul financially. The submarine deal may also be endangered. The transfer to South Korea of North Korean POWs held by Ukraine has devolved into a rhetorical fight between Seoul and Kyiv over whether the POWs’ repatriation should have been announced. Regardless of which side is right, Seoul would have been better served to keep the argument quiet. A North Korean land mine that exploded in the DMZ, injuring South Korean soldiers, has backfooted Lee’s administration. In demanding a North Korean apology while also downplaying the incident as an “unfortunate accident,” Seoul is incoherently both making it a big deal and providing Pyongyang with cover. Unsurprisingly, the media report that the National Security Council’s “autonomy” and “alliance” factions are deeply divided over the response.

How did Lee’s diplomacy go from hero to zero? Beyond intra-government ideological rifts, domestic politics play a role. Lee’s weakened poll numbers are causing ruling party frustration, with the “autonomy” faction using increased influence to underline South Korean sovereignty as an appeal to base supporters of the Democratic Party of Korea.

This probably won’t work domestically. It’s definitely failing diplomatically. The next risk is that the administration doubles down and gins ups problems with Japan. In that case, the train will likely be not only off the rails, but over the cliff.

_Mason Richey is a professor of international politics at Hankuk University of Foreign Studies and president of the Korea International Studies Association._

 Attendees gather at the Global South Modernization Forum in Cairo, Egypt, on Wednesday. XINHUA

CAIRO — The 2026 Global South Modernization Forum was held in Cairo on Wednesday under the theme "The Rise of Artificial Intelligence: Opportunities and Challenges for Modernization in the Global South."

More than 100 experts and scholars from nearly 30 countries and regions attended the forum.

Participants said innovation in AI technology presents enormous opportunities while also posing governance challenges.

At the 18th BRICS Summit earlier this month, President Xi Jinping put forward important initiatives to empower new industrialization with AI and promote open-source and inclusive AI development, outlining a direction for AI development that serves the common good, they said.

Modernization in the Global South is at a crucial stage of overcoming development constraints, addressing capacity gaps and transforming growth drivers, they said, calling for effective use of AI to continually strengthen the internal drivers of development.

Participants said AI is a shared asset of all humanity and urged Global South countries to seize this historic opportunity to use AI to empower a wide range of industries and improve people's well-being.

They called for improving global AI governance, practicing genuine multilateralism, bridging the AI divide and ensuring that development and security reinforce each other.

They also urged greater exchanges and mutual learning in AI, a commitment to open-source development, openness, cooperation and sharing, and deeper theoretical and practical research to ensure that AI better benefits humanity.

The forum was jointly hosted by the State Council Information Office of China, the Party School of the Communist Party of China Central Committee (National Academy of Governance), the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, Peking University, Renmin University of China and Cairo University.

The event featured four parallel forums. "The Rise of the Global South: An Atlas of Academic Research on Modernization in the Global South" and "Top 10 Buzzwords in Global South Modernization Research of 2026" were released at the forum.

Academic exhibitions, youth exchanges and think tank seminars were also held before and after the forum.
