title: Xi’s Purge and the War Over Taiwan
summary: Executive Summary: Central Military Commission (CMC) Vice Chairman Zhang Youxia’s expulsion from the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) was politically motivated; Chairman Xi Jinping’s purge of the PLA high command is best explained by his dissa
content: Executive Summary: Central Military Commission (CMC) Vice Chairman Zhang Youxia’s expulsion from the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) was politically motivated; Chairman Xi Jinping’s purge of the PLA high command is best explained by his dissatisfaction with senior officers’ assessments of an operation against Taiwan and their willingness to act on Xi’s orders. The Fujian-based generals Xi once trusted most, as well as the leadership of the Equipment Development Department and Rocket Force, and Zhang himself shared a professional caution about a cross-Strait war. Xi appears to have read their warnings as cowardice and resistance to the 2027 military readiness goal. The purge shows political will emphasized over military professionalism. Military conflict is less likely in the short term while new officers enter their posts, but gray-zone pressure will likely escalate. A leadership consisting of compliant subordinates makes war increasingly likely over time. Editor’s note: Jiang Lin is a former Lieutenant Colonel in the People’s Liberation Army and served as a reporter for the PLA Daily for 27 years. Central Military Commission (CMC) Vice Chairman Zhang Youxia’s (张又侠) time as Xi Jinping’s number two at the top of the Chinese military came to an end at the beginning of 2026. It was only in late September, however, that he was finally expelled from the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). Zhang, whose political failings were put front and center in the official announcement of his purge, is now set for a military prosecution ( Xinhua , September 21; China Brief , September 23). The official record divulges little information about the precise nature of Zhang’s crimes—political or otherwise. Part of what makes it so difficult to uncover the facts of his case is that the official record itself is unreliable. The Party’s pronouncements follow a logic of their own, and truth is far from a necessary criterion. The initial notice announcing that Zhang was under investigation was followed by an editorial in the PLA Daily that accused Zhang of being involved in five offenses. These included gravely betraying the trust and heavy responsibilities placed on him by the Party Central Committee and the CMC, severely trampling upon and undermining the CMC Chairman responsibility system, and seriously fueling political and corruption problems ( PLA Daily , January 25). The seriousness of these offenses indicated that corruption alone could not have been the root cause of the accusations. As the September announcement now suggests, Zhang’s crimes were ultimately political in nature. Mass Purges are a Response to Political Crimes Xi is not the first to remove disagreeable generals before forging ahead with hostilities. In 1938, for example, Adolf Hitler used the Blomberg–Fritsch affair—a scandal that was partly real and partly concocted—to reshuffle his high command and accrue more direct power over the military. Xi is also not the only PRC leader to do so, either. In 1962, Mao elected to attack India, not long after a shake up of the PLA high command following the dismissal of Peng Dehuai (彭德怀), his top military officer throughout the 1950s ( Foreign Affairs , July 18, 2025). The Party leadership’s most prominent purge of senior People’s Liberation Army (PLA) officers for political crimes took place between June 1989 and mid-1992, following the Tiananmen Square Massacre, when the CMC purged or sidelined key generals who had initially opposed the intervention, replaced six of the seven military region commanders, and engineered a complete turnover of PLA representation on the Central Committee ( People’s Daily , November 10, 1989; CSIS , February 24).  [1] Some research indicates that an estimated 3,500 PLA officers were purged for disobeying orders (Wall Street Journal, October 9, 1991).  [2] Only political reasons could have driven such a large purge. General Secretary Xi Jinping’s similarly dramatic purge appears likewise to have been motivated by political factors. In his case, the most likely explanation for his actions is dissatisfaction over both the readiness and willingness of senior officers to stage operations targeting Taiwan. Unification with Taiwan has been of central importance to Xi since he first came to power. From the start, his principal political objective, which he referred to as the “China dream” (中国梦), had subsuming Taiwan as its main military component. Responsibility for that component of Xi’s agenda falls principally on the PLA. The enormous reforms he launched to both the military and other Party and state institutions during his first term, and his successful efforts to amend the constitution and allow for indefinite tenure as state president, were intended to mobilize the entire system toward the achievement of this primary political objective.  [3] The massive purges seen throughout the PLA in recent years very likely relate to what Xi views as a lack of meaningful progress toward attaining this goal, as others have argued ( China Brief , January 26; AEI , January 28; CSIS , February 24). They began in the early days of Xi’s PLA reforms with the removal of those who opposed his agenda, such as the CMC vice chairs Guo Boxiong (郭伯雄) and Xu Caihou (徐才厚) ( The Diplomat , April 7, 2016). These were followed by the discovery of corruption issues within the Equipment Development Department (EDD) and the Rocket Force during efforts to improve capabilities for a Taiwan scenario. The larger-scale purge that occurred subsequently was driven more by political and military strategy than by issues with reform and corruption. Since 2022, 36 PLA generals and lieutenant generals have been formally purged, while another 65 high-ranking officers have disappeared from public view or may have faced purges ( CSIS , February 24). Of the seven members of the CMC present at the end of 2022, besides Xi Jinping only one remains. Xi Seeks Less Cautious Generals The purge of Zhang and other senior figures most likely represented a clash between Xi’s political strategy and a military community that was cautious about a potential war over Taiwan. When the absolute authority of a Leninist party comes into conflict with the physical realities of modern, professional warfare, this is the only possible resolution if the regime is to persist (China Brief, January 26 , February 11 ). Many believe that former CMC vice chairman He Weidong (何卫东) and officers from the former 31st Group Army were Xi’s most trusted allies in the PLA ( The Diplomat , October 20, 2025). Based in Fujian, Xi came to know them during his nearly 20 years working in the province. If they had been involved in corruption alone, Chinese political tradition indicates that they would likely have received only light punishment, not the unusually harsh treatment that ended up being administered. Those closest to the Taiwan Strait best understand the hard military realities, unlike the political officers in Beijing. They are aware of Taiwan’s strong defensive advantages, such as its difficult terrain, dense anti-ship missiles, and air defenses. They also realize that huge air and sea superiority, as well as long supply lines, would be needed to land large forces successfully, and that U.S. and Japanese intervention, however brief, would cut off any PLA troops who managed to make it ashore. In other words, their caution comes from professional judgment ( China Brief , March 20). When Xi demanded the PLA complete its preparation to attack Taiwan by 2027, the generals’ realistic assessments of high costs and risks sounded like fear and a lack of determination by Xi ( U.S. Department of Defense , November 29, 2022). Although Xi promoted these former Fujian subordinates because he thought they understood the Strait and would obey his command, he expected them to build a fast, powerful force using modern brigades that could quickly disable Taiwan. In a system that demands absolute loyalty, their subsequent claims of immature technology or a lack of readiness was reinterpreted as double-dealing and deliberate deception. Xi concluded that the generals never intended to fight and used professional concerns mainly to mask cowardice and protect themselves. This sense of betrayal was deeper than ordinary corruption, so no graceful exit was allowed ( PLA Daily , October 18, 2025). The final target, Zhang Youxia, shared key traits with the purged Fujian-faction generals on Taiwan strategy issues. As one of the few commanders who had actually led troops in battle, he had a deep, instinctive caution about the brutality of war and the gap between theory and real combat effectiveness ( ISDP , January 30). When frontline Fujian generals—who had spent years war-gaming a Taiwan Strait landing—warned against hasty action based on professional judgment, Zhang agreed and supported them as a fellow professional soldier. Their shared caution about war became a common professional language ( China Brief , January 26). They may have seen some of Xi’s goals, including tight force-building timelines, as unrealistic, and resisted them on professional military grounds. Analysts have speculated that part of Zhang’s downfall could be attributed to his long stint as head of the CMC EDD, which appears to have been a locus of a high degree of corruption ( Global Security/Zhang Youxia , accessed October 1). A more likely reason why this could be a contributing factor to his demise, however, is that the department fully adhered to Zhang’s cautious stance, and many senior officials who were later purged, such as Li Shangfu (李尚福), were subordinates that Zhang had promoted during his tenure there. This led to a situation—that for Xi was unacceptable—in which officials in charge of weapons development (the EDD and Rocket Force), frontline combat preparation (Eastern Theater Command and Fujian faction), and overall military oversight (Zhang himself) developed a strong shared understanding of tactical pragmatism with regard to a possible Taiwan Strait war. Together, they were seen as systematically using technical excuses and equipment shortcomings to resist Xi’s unification strategy passively. A strong indicator of this is Zhang’s assertion, in the pages of the PLA Daily in late 2025, that 2035, not 2027, would be the year by which the military would acquire all-domain operational capabilities ( People’s Daily , November 12, 2025; China Brief , January 26). Conclusion Xi’s purge appears to be a decisive victory of political will over military professionalism. The removal of seasoned veterans who valued professional caution about war could lead to replacements who are less likely to push back on Xi’s demands ( CSIS , February 2024). This could propel the Taiwan Strait situation along a more dangerous path. Though Xi’s purge reduces the short-term probability of a kinetic conflict, as promoted officers familiarize themselves with their new billets, gray-zone warfare is likely to continue to escalate. The greatest danger is that the information cocoon created by submissive subordinates, coupled with Xi’s arbitrary exercise of power, creates the conditions that make war across the Taiwan Strait increasingly likely once the new PLA leadership team is formed. Notes [1] As a victim of that purge, one of us can verify that it was indeed politically motivated ( NYT , May 28, 2015; NYT Chinese Edition , May 29, 2019; NYT Chinese Edition , June 3, 2019). Numerous generals involved in defying the martial law order were sentenced, dismissed, or demoted—such as Xu Qinxian (徐勤先), commander of the 38th Army ( The Guardian , December 24, 2025), He Yanran (何燕然), Commander of the 28th Army ( CND , December 31, 2025), Li Lianxiu (李连秀), Commander of the People’s Armed Police Force ( RFA , June 9, 2023), and Xu Feng (许峰), Commander of the 116th Division of the 39th Army ( DW , June 4, 2018). [2] Chong-Pin Lin. “China’s Restive Army.” Wall Street Journal , October 9, 1991. [3] For analysis of Xi’s structural reforms to the military over the last decade, see: Miller, Frank, Tung Ho, Kenneth Allen, and Arran Hope, eds. The People’s Liberation Army as Organization Volume 3.0 . Washington, D.C.: The Jamestown Foundation; Vienna: Exovera, 2025. The post Xi’s Purge and the War Over Taiwan appeared first on Jamestown .

content: 李承鹏（大眼哥）   X @dayangelcp · Oct 2, 2026 我的油管第11期：《 中美历史恩怨合订本——十大美好瞬间和十大交恶时刻 》。 历史每天都很正确，就是不能看合订本。郭德纲老师说，凡事就怕同行衬托。别看宴会上你侬我侬唱你问，我爱你，有多深……你爱我有多深，得看合同签几分。 历史就这么诡异，当年要是乒乓球运动员科恩没上错大巴，老毛晚上安眠药剂量再大一点，基辛格表演肚子疼没成功……中美指不准啥时候才能建交，老百姓指不准啥时候才能看上电视、冰箱。 1979年大年初一，邓小平在飞往美国的专机上说：回头看这几十年，凡是和美国搞好关系的国家，都富起来了。 在肯尼迪中心，200名美国孩子用中文合唱《我爱北京天安门》……你看，美国早就让孩子唱中文歌接待中国元首了。邓小平竟然还跑上台去亲吻孩子，用洋范儿动作争取西方世界的接纳。你很难把这温馨一幕跟十年后下令广场开枪的屠夫联想起来。 卡特说“送10万人来！”邓小平马上给美国送去一大批留学生，其中就有王沪宁…… 邓小平戴上女骑手献上的白色牛仔帽，向全场挥帽致意。临别时他对卡特说：“我们不怕美国的制度，美国也不必怕我们。” 但对美国制度骨子里的恐惧很快暴露，四年后中美交恶，因为19岁的网球女子运动员——胡娜出逃，寻求政治庇护。坊间狗血传说，邓小平怒斥里根，其中一条是拐骗了我的干女儿。 中美价值观迥异，现实需求却是刚需。里根放宽对华技术出口，承诺执行“一个中国”政策，中国再次掀起赴美浪潮。这一年，一位年轻的中国县委书记随农业考察团来到小城马斯卡廷。他衣着整洁、每次准时，很有好奇心，住进了当地一户农民家。他，就是习近平…… 老布什在长城饭店举行答谢宴会，邀请了中国异见知识分子方励之夫妇，但方励之夫妇在路上被警察堵住了。“六四”发生，枪声和坦克履带声打碎了幻想……老布什带头全面制裁中国，中美关系再次降到冰点。 中美就像一场虐恋。克林顿称：只要中国经济发展了，民主就水到渠成。1997年，正式邀请江泽民访美，在夏威夷，老江愉快地弹起夏威夷吉他……蜜月又回来了。中美总是规律性的一会儿蜜月，一会儿交恶。 1998年6月，克林顿访华，在人民大会堂的全球记者会上，在中央电视台全程直播中，全国人民都看见了——克林顿公开表示：“六四事件中使用武力、造成人命损失是错误的”，他还力挺达赖……而江泽民竟然在央视全程直播中，跟美国总统碰撞六四、西藏、台湾这些极敏感的话题，这是中国元首史上唯一一次。 惊喜不惊喜，意外不意外。所以，当看到小白们因为这次会谈上唱了中国歌就激动不已，我这老登真想拍着您的肩膀说：年轻人，图漾图森破…… 两天后，克林顿去北大与学生辩论自由和人权问题，央视竟然播出画面。克林顿引用胡适的话说：个人争取自由，也是在为国家争取自由。北大中文系女生马楠反驳……几年后她移民美国，嫁给美国人。 经历过那个时代的我，也被这段历史给惊呆了，中国元首竟然跟美国总统在央视直播辩论六四、西藏，人权。美国总统竟可以窜访北大……回首往事，恍若隔世。就请问：您怀不怀念那个时代，而那个时代，正是中美之间最好的时代。 结论是：一定要和美国搞好关系，和美国关系好的时候，就是中国最开放的时代。 点击进入： —————————————————— 李承鹏（大眼哥） @dayangelcp · 5h 寓言般的画面是：马斯克，黄仁勋，库克，苏姿丰和她老公，与美国总统、中国元首坐一张桌吃饭。你能想像马云、马化腾、雷军、潘石屹跟习近平坐在一张桌上吃饭？ 要啥自行车？让你活着就是皇恩浩荡。当年马云挥斥方遒跟马斯克对谈。五年后，马云消失，马斯克成了世界首富，马斯克问：马云在哪儿…… 马斯克公开骂川普，还当世界首富，还是川普座上宾……任志强写了一封内部信，就判了十八年，生死不明…… 据说一批中国企业家到了华盛顿，没等到通知，稍息、立正，就地解散，从“随行商界代表团”变成“自由行”，跟旅游团大妈打卡去了。而川普用空军一号拉着一群商人到北京吃国宴，又拉着他们在白宫吃国宴，中国商人跟元首一张桌吃饭？ 这还叫社会主义吗，红旗还要不要打？美国商人跟总统吃饭时，中国商人正想着补税和外逃，想着从香港还是越南走更安全，后备厢够不够大，女朋友能不能装下…… 制度DNA差异。商业立国，谁本事大谁上桌。领导立国，让谁上桌才能上桌，鱼头冲谁，霍金见着领导，渐冻症也得好了，站起来“我先干了，领导您随意”。 中国经济能不能好起来，你的生活能不能好起来，取决于中美关系能不能好起来。 点击进入： https:// youtu.be/4vg_xrPIQRs?si =ORQKc4R5TyEUG1CV

content: 一、事件回顧與我們的關切 2026年9月23日至25日，中國國家主席習近平訪問華盛頓期間，白宮及周邊地區聚集了不同政治立場的抗議者與支持者。9月24日，現場不同人群之間發生多次衝突，警方對部分涉事人員採取了逮捕等執法措施。公開報導顯示，當日下午至少有數人因涉嫌襲擊警員、普通襲擊及其他違法行為被捕。（WJLA相關報導） 在這一背景下，我們尤其關注9月24日下午白宮外和平抗議活動期間發生的衝突事件。 根據本人在現場所見，在政府依法劃定的和平抗議區域及公共場所舉行的新聞發布會期間，和平抗議者遭到疑似由中共統戰系統組織或動員的對立陣營人員干擾，現場一度發生衝突，導致相關活動受到干擾並一度中斷。 對於上述情況，有必要由獨立、具權限的執法及監督機構依法調取、保存和核實現場錄影、照片、警方執法記錄、逮捕報告以及其他相關證據，以查明事件的完整經過。 更加值得關注的是，在衝突發生之後，部分和平抗議者遭到警方逮捕，而現場其他涉嫌首先實施暴力、襲擊他人或擾亂活動秩序的人員是否也受到同等標準的調查和追責，目前仍有必要進一步核實。 我們認為，任何對執法部門公正性的質疑，都不應僅僅停留在政治立場或個人判斷層面，而應當通過現場錄影、警方記錄、逮捕報告、現場指揮記錄以及相關證人證言等證據予以查明。 如果和平抗議者因行使美國憲法第一修正案所保障的言論、和平集會及請願權利而受到不當對待，這是值得認真調查的問題；如果現場確有人實施暴力、襲擊或其他違法行為，無論其政治立場、國籍或組織背景如何，都應依法承擔相應責任。 這不僅關係到個別抗議者的權利，也關係到美國法治、公民自由以及執法機關公信力的基本原則。 二、跨國鎮壓不應跨越美國國界 近年來，美國政府及執法部門已公開關注外國政府針對美國境內人士實施的跨國鎮壓行為。 美國司法部及聯邦執法部門公布的一系列案件表明，外國政府及其代理人可能通過威脅、騷擾、跟蹤、脅迫、暴力甚至情報活動，試圖影響或壓制生活、工作於美國的異議人士和政治活動人士。 美國司法部近期涉及中華人民共和國政府海外警察站及相關人員的案件，也表明跨國鎮壓並非一個抽象的安全概念，而是美國執法機關已經實際處理的法律與國家安全問題。 因此，我們對近期華盛頓發生的相關事件表示嚴重關切。 我們特別希望有關部門依法調查以下問題： 第一， 現場是否存在有組織、有預謀的暴力行為； 第二， 是否存在外國政府、相關組織或個人對美國境內和平抗議活動進行指揮、協調、資助、威脅或其他形式非法干預的證據； 第三， 在衝突發生之後，不同政治立場的涉事人員是否受到一致、平等並符合正當程序的執法對待； 第四， 是否存在針對海外異議人士的長期跟蹤、恐嚇、騷擾、網絡攻擊或其他形式的跨國鎮壓行為，以及這些行為是否與本次事件存在任何關聯。 我們同時強調：不能因為某一事件涉及中國政府或海外民主運動，就預設任何一方已經構成犯罪。所有具體指控都應以證據為基礎，由美國司法及執法機構依法調查、認定。 同樣，我們也不能因為目前缺乏立即可見的證據，就忽視外國政府可能利用美國境內組織、個人或社會矛盾，實施影響、恐嚇和壓制的現實風險。 三、執法公正與第一修正案權利必須得到保障 美國憲法第一修正案所保障的言論自由、新聞自由、和平集會及請願權，是美國民主制度的重要基礎。 無論一個人支持中國共產黨、反對中國共產黨，支持民主運動，還是持有完全不同的政治立場，只要其行為受到美國法律保護，就應當受到平等的法律保護。 同樣，任何人也不能以「政治立場」為理由，獲得實施暴力、襲擊他人或破壞公共秩序的豁免。 因此，我們認為，華盛頓特區此次事件應當成為檢視相關執法程序及保障公民權利的重要契機。 公眾有權了解： 當日現場執法的具體標準和法律依據是什麼； 警方如何認定誰是衝突的實施者、參與者以及受害者； 不同涉事人員是否接受相同的調查及證據審查標準； 現場是否存在任何可能影響執法判斷的不正當因素； 對被捕人員採取的後續法律措施是否符合適用法律和正當程序； 如果涉及移民執法措施，相關部門是否依法進行了獨立、充分和一致的法律審查。 這些問題不是為了保護某一個政治陣營，而是為了保護美國法律本身。 法律不能因一個人的政治立場而改變。第一修正案也不能因一個人的政治觀點而失去應有的法律保護。 四、對「跨國鎮壓」問題應當保持理性與警惕 近期圍繞民運人士界立建等人的事件以及相關內部紛爭，也提醒我們，必須以更加理性、審慎和基於證據的方式，看待海外民主運動內部存在的複雜關係。 我們既不能把所有內部矛盾、個人衝突和組織紛爭簡單歸結為「中共滲透」，更不能因為擔心被批評為「陰謀論」，就忽視外國情報機構可能利用社會分裂、輿論操縱、恐嚇、威脅以及暴力手段打擊海外異議人士的客觀風險。 判斷一個事件是否涉及跨國鎮壓，應當依靠事實和證據，包括但不限於資金流向、通訊記錄、人員關係、組織指揮鏈、威脅記錄，以及其他依法取得的相關證據。 我們反對沒有證據的政治指控，也反對對真實存在的安全風險視而不見。 美國真正需要建立的，是一套以證據、法律和正當程序為基礎的跨國鎮壓調查、預警與應對機制。 五、四點核心敦促與訴求 基於上述關切，我們敦促美國政府、國會以及相關執法和監督機構採取以下措施： 建立跨部門調查機制 我們敦促美國司法部及相關聯邦和地方執法機構，對2026年9月23日至25日期間華盛頓特區相關抗議活動中發生的暴力及衝突事件進行全面調查，並審查其中是否存在外國政府或相關代理人實施跨國鎮壓、威脅、騷擾或其他非法干預的證據。 調查應依法進行，並在不影響刑事調查、個人隱私及合法國家安全利益的前提下，適時向公眾公布調查進展及結論。 呼籲國會舉行公開聽證 我們呼籲美國國會相關委員會，根據其法定權限，就以下問題進行監督和審查： 白宮及周邊地區在相關日期的安全部署； 美國特勤局及華盛頓特區警察局的現場執法程序； 相關衝突發生前後的指揮與協調機制； 被捕人員的執法及後續處理情況； 不同政治陣營的涉事人員是否受到不同的執法標準對待； 外國政府及其代理人是否試圖在美國境內影響、恐嚇或壓制和平抗議活動。 如有必要，應邀請相關執法機構、法律專家、人權組織以及事件親歷者作證，以便國會及公眾更全面地了解事實。 對現場執法程序及涉嫌選擇性執法問題進行獨立審查 我們敦促相關監察及監督機構對本次事件進行獨立審查，重點核查： 是否存在執法標準不一致； 是否存在不適當的現場指揮； 是否存在未得到充分調查的暴力行為； 是否存在因政治立場而產生的執法偏差； 是否存在任何不當干預執法決定的情況。 如果調查證明執法人員存在違法、失職或其他不當行為，應依法追究相關責任。 如果調查證明相關執法決定符合美國法律及現場安全需要，也應向公眾說明事實依據，以增進社會對執法機構的理解與信任。 建立防範跨國鎮壓的長期機制 我們敦促美國政府進一步完善針對外國政府跨國鎮壓行為的預警、報告、調查及執法機制。 尤其應當： 為受到外國政府威脅、跟蹤和騷擾的美國居民及其他合法居留人士提供明確的舉報渠道； 加強聯邦與地方執法機構之間的信息共享； 對涉及暴力、威脅、脅迫及非法外國代理活動的案件依法調查； 對和平集會活動提供明確、平等的安全保障； 防止任何外國政府利用美國境內組織和個人，非法壓制美國境內的言論及政治活動； 同時確保相關措施不被濫用於壓制合法的言論、集會、新聞報導或政治表達。 六、我們的原則 我們提出這些訴求，不是為了要求美國政府支持某一個政治組織，也不是要求執法機關根據某種政治立場決定誰是「好人」或「壞人」。 我們要求的，只有一個基本原則： 法律面前，人人平等。 和平抗議者不應因為表達不同的政治觀點而受到暴力威脅；任何人也不應因為政治立場不同而成為暴力攻擊的對象。 無論一個人來自中國、香港、台灣、美國或其他國家，無論其政治立場為何，只要身處美國，就應當受到美國憲法和法律的保護。 同樣，任何人在美國境內實施暴力、威脅、脅迫、騷擾，或者代表外國政府從事違法活動，也都應當依法承擔相應責任。 我們相信，美國的力量不僅來自軍事和經濟實力，更來自憲法、法治、自由以及獨立的司法和執法制度。 如果美國不能保障一個人在街頭和平表達自己政治觀點的權利，那麼第一修正案的意義就可能受到損害；如果外國政府能夠通過恐嚇和暴力，把政治迫害延伸到美國本土，那麼美國的法治和國家主權也將面臨嚴峻挑戰。 因此，我們再次呼籲美國政府、國會及相關執法機構： 徹查事實，公開透明； 平等執法，依法追責； 保障第一修正案權利； 防止跨國鎮壓蔓延； 維護美國憲法與法治尊嚴。 和平表達不應成為罪行。 追求民主與自由不應成為罪證。 在美國，任何人都不應因為自己的政治觀點，而受到外國政府或其代理人的恐嚇與迫害。 讓事實說話，讓法律說話，讓憲法保護每一個人的自由。 姚戈 2026年9月30日

content: ——从政治运动、饥荒与文革，到疫情封控与权力集中 作者：赵燕涛 编辑：吕聪 1949年10月1日，中国共产党在北京宣布中华人民共和国成立。 七十七年过去了。 但如果我们要理解1949年以后中国发生的一切，就不能只从1949年开始。 我们必须把时间拉回到抗日战争时期。 抗日战争期间，中国共产党在华北等敌后地区建立根据地，发展武装力量，开展大规模游击战争。 游击战争给日军造成了军事压力，但与此同时，敌后地区也成为战争和日军报复的重要空间。 扫荡、报复、屠杀，最终承受巨大代价的，不只是军人，也包括大量普通中国平民。 而对于中国共产党来说，抗战也是一个扩大根据地、发展组织、扩大政治影响的重要历史阶段。 与此同时，中国共产党并不是完全孤立地发展起来的。 共产国际和苏联方面长期与中共保持政治、组织、经济以及军事方面的联系和支持。 这些国际关系，同样是理解中国共产党后来取得政权的重要历史背景。 1945年抗日战争结束。 国共内战再次爆发。 1949年，中国共产党取得全国政权。 然后，中国进入了一系列规模巨大的政治运动。 土地改革。 反右运动。 大跃进。 人民公社。 文化大革命。 计划生育。 这些运动，深刻改变了无数中国普通人的命运。 土地改革时期，大量地主遭到财产没收、批斗和处决。 阶级身份开始成为决定一个人命运的重要因素。 1957年反右运动以后，大量知识分子因为发表不同意见而受到政治迫害。 然后，是大跃进。 全民炼钢。 人民公社。 粮食产量层层虚报。 政治口号取代了经济规律。 最后发生的，是大规模饥荒。 学术研究对于具体死亡人数存在不同估计，但毫无疑问，这是一场造成巨大非正常死亡的历史灾难。 我的家族，也有人在那场饥荒中饿死。 对别人来说，它可能只是历史书上的一个数字。 对我们家来说，那是一个永远回不来的亲人。 然后，是文化大革命。 批斗。 抄家。 武斗。 政治迫害。 知识分子遭到打击。 普通家庭被卷入政治斗争。 而在一些地方，暴力甚至发展到了令人难以想象的程度。 1968年，广西武宣发生严重的集体暴力和杀戮，甚至出现了食人事件。 人被杀害。 尸体被肢解。 甚至出现了人吃人的惨剧。 这不是文学故事。 这是曾经真实发生过的历史。 后来，是长期实行的计划生育政策。 强制执行过程中，一些家庭承受了巨大的痛苦，也留下了长期的人口结构问题。 再后来，是新冠疫情。 疫情本身是一场公共卫生危机。 但疫情期间采取的治理方式，同样值得历史检验。 封城。 封控。 健康码。 大规模核酸。 一轮又一轮的全民检测。 一些地方甚至长期实行常态化核酸。 当核酸检测成为维持正常生活的必要条件时，它也形成了规模巨大的经济活动。 问题因此出现了： 如此巨大的公共资源投入，到底有多少真正用于保护人民？ 公共财政应该接受什么样的监督？ 检测机构、地方政府和相关利益链条之间，又应该接受什么样的审查？ 我们不能简单地把所有财政问题都归咎于核酸，也不能把养老基金的问题直接说成是被核酸“掏空”。 但有一点非常明确： 老百姓辛苦工作一辈子缴纳的养老保障资金，必须受到严格监督。 因为那是普通中国人的养老钱。 不是任何机构可以随意支配的钱。 而今天，我们还必须面对另一个更加根本的问题： 谁来监督权力？ 谁来约束权力？ 谁来保护普通人的权利？ 2018年，中国修改宪法，删除了国家主席、副主席“连续任职不得超过两届”的规定。 2023年，习近平获得第三个国家主席任期。 于是，一个问题摆在每一个中国人面前： 如果最高政治权力可以长期延续， 谁来真正限制权力？ 谁来真正监督权力？ 七十七年的历史，不应该只有一种声音。 土地改革中的死亡。 反右运动中的沉默。 大跃进和饥荒中的饥饿。 文化大革命中的暴力。 广西武宣发生的食人惨剧。 计划生育留下的家庭创伤。 疫情时期的封控与核酸。 以及今天仍然存在的言论审查和政治控制。 这些，都应该被记住。 因为历史不是宣传口号。 历史也不是某一个政党的私人记忆。 历史属于每一个曾经生活在这片土地上的普通人。 那些已经死去的人，应该被记住。 那些曾经遭受迫害的人，应该被记住。 那些因为一句话、一个身份、一个家庭背景而改变命运的人，也应该被记住。 一个真正成熟的国家，不应该害怕人民讨论自己的历史。 一个真正有尊严的社会，不应该害怕人民追问权力。 我们希望有一天： 人民可以自由表达。 法律可以真正约束权力。 公共资金可以受到公开监督。 政治权力可以受到制度制衡。 一个普通人的命运，不再因为政治标签而被决定。 七十七年过去了。 历史还没有结束。 中国人民对自由、尊严、法治和民主的追求，也不应该结束。

title: Taiwan receives its first US-made F-16V fighter jets
summary: Taiwan received its first two US-made F-16V fighter jets on Friday, as the island democracy upgrades its military capabilities to deter a potential Chinese attack. The warplanes are part of an $8 billion deal for 66 F-16Vs approved during U
content: Taiwan received its first two US-made F-16V fighter jets on Friday, as the island democracy upgrades its military capabilities to deter a potential Chinese attack. The warplanes are part of an $8 billion deal for 66 F-16Vs approved during US President Donald Trump’s first term and scheduled for delivery this year. F-16V fight jet. Photo: Wang TIng-yu via Facebook. The arrival of the aircraft comes as Taiwan awaits Washington’s approval of a separate $14 billion arms package that Trump paused after Chinese objections. China claims Taiwan is part of its territory and has threatened to use force to seize it. The two F-16Vs, made by US defence contractor Lockheed Martin, touched down under a clear sky at Taiwan’s air force base in Taitung, on the island’s southeast coast. The jets had been expected in early September after making refuelling stops in Hawaii and Guam. Local media reported that the planes had turned back to Hawaii shortly after taking off for Guam. No official explanation was given. Dozens of locals, some equipped with binoculars and long-lensed cameras, gathered near the air base’s perimeter fence to watch the highly anticipated arrival of the jets. Kimi Chi, a salesman from the central city of Taichung, had travelled through the night to be able to photograph the aircraft landing in Taitung. He was philosophical about the delays, saying “good things take time.” “In terms of hardware capabilities, there will definitely be an improvement,” the 37-year-old told AFP. “But what we are actually lacking the most right now is pilots. Of course, I hope the government can provide better additional allowances for these military pilots.” Former Air Force serviceman Eric Chan, 57, marvelled at the improvements made to the F-16 over the past 30 years and said the fighter jets based in Taitung will “play a very important defensive role” against China. “The threat from the CCP has always been there so we definitely need to strengthen our defence capabilities,” Chan told AFP, referring to the Chinese Communist Party. Delivery delays The United States is Taiwan’s most important security backer and biggest arms supplier. But bottlenecks have slowed delivery of critical weapons. Taiwan’s Defence Minister Wellington Koo. Photo: Ministry of National Defense (Taiwan). Taiwan’s Defence Minister Wellington Koo said previously it would be “challenging” for all the F-16Vs to be delivered this year, despite Lockheed Martin ramping up production. On Friday, Koo said more F-16Vs would be delivered to Taiwan “before the end of the year”, but did not say how many. “At present, I think aircraft are gradually moving through the production line, and there are also aircraft that have passed the tests,” Koo said. “As for when they will fly back, we will coordinate further with the US side.” Trump has stalled signing off on the record $14 billion weapons purchase by Taipei, calling it in May a “very good negotiating chip” in dealings with China, which raised fears that Taiwan’s security could be traded away. Experts believe approval for the package is unlikely before the G20 summit in the United States in December where Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Trump are expected to meet for the fourth time this year. A US official said recently it was increasingly likely the $14 billion worth of arms, which include the Patriot air defence system, would be broken up into smaller amounts to temper China’s response.

title: National Day: China Celebrates 77 Years with Pride, Patriotism and Confidence in the Future
summary: China’s National Day marks the anniversary of a political proclamation, not an ancient dynasty. At 3 p.m. on October 1, 1949, Mao Zedong stood at the Tiananmen rostrum in Beijing and announced the establishment of the People’s Republic of C
content:
China’s National Day marks the anniversary of a political proclamation, not an ancient dynasty. At 3 p.m. on October 1, 1949, Mao Zedong stood at the Tiananmen rostrum in Beijing and announced the establishment of the People’s Republic of China. The proclamation followed decades of war, foreign invasion and civil conflict. The Nationalist government had already retreated to Taiwan, leaving the Communist Party in control of mainland China. The date became the republic’s national day and, 77 years later, remains one of the most important dates on China’s political calendar.

This year’s anniversary began before dawn in Tiananmen Square, where crowds gathered for the traditional flag-raising ceremony. The Chinese flag was raised as the national anthem was played, followed by the release of white doves. The ceremony provided the familiar imagery of National Day: the flag, the square and thousands of citizens gathered at the symbolic heart of the Chinese state.

#### **A republic transformed**

The China that emerged in 1949 was overwhelmingly rural, poor and exhausted by years of conflict. The decades that followed were marked by dramatic political and economic upheaval, including the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution. The decisive change came after Mao’s death, when Deng Xiaoping and other leaders began introducing economic reforms that gradually opened China to foreign investment, international trade and market forces while preserving Communist Party rule.

People & Society

Those reforms changed the country’s trajectory. Agricultural production expanded, special economic zones attracted foreign capital, manufacturing grew rapidly and millions of people moved into cities. China’s entry into the World Trade Organization in 2001 accelerated its integration into the global economy. What began as a low-cost manufacturing story eventually developed into something much larger: China became a central part of global supply chains and a major market in its own right.

The transformation is visible in the country’s infrastructure and technology. High-speed rail connects major cities, Chinese companies compete internationally in electric vehicles and batteries, and the country has become a major producer of solar equipment, telecommunications technology and advanced industrial products. The next phase is increasingly focused on artificial intelligence, semiconductors, robotics and other technologies that Beijing considers strategically important.

#### **China’s economy enters a new phase**

The economic picture in 2026 is more complicated than the extraordinary expansion of the previous decades. China’s economy grew 4.7 percent in the first half of the year, according to the National Bureau of Statistics, with services growing 5.2 percent and manufacturing 5.5 percent. Information technology and related services were among the faster-growing parts of the economy.

But China is also dealing with a weaker property sector, changing demographics and the need to stimulate domestic consumption. The government is therefore trying to shift the emphasis from sheer expansion towards higher-quality growth, technological capability and greater economic resilience. That transition is at the centre of the country’s 15th Five-Year Plan, covering 2026 to 2030.

For the rest of the world, the implications are considerable. China’s manufacturing strength, enormous consumer market and technological ambitions mean that decisions made in Beijing can affect commodity producers in Africa, factories in Europe, technology companies in the United States and supply chains across Asia.

#### **China and the wider world**

China’s rise has been particularly visible across Africa. It has become a major trading partner for many African countries and an important participant in infrastructure, telecommunications, energy, construction and industrial projects. The relationship is evolving, however. African governments are increasingly interested in manufacturing, technology, agricultural value chains and investment that can create jobs and strengthen domestic production rather than simply importing finished goods.

China’s Belt and Road Initiative has expanded that international footprint across Africa, Asia, the Middle East, Europe and Latin America. Supporters see the initiative as a major source of infrastructure and connectivity; critics have raised questions about debt, transparency and the long-term economic returns of some projects. For African policymakers, the central issue is increasingly how to secure greater economic value from one of the world’s most important bilateral relationships.

#### **The United States and Taiwan**

China’s growing influence has also produced a more difficult relationship with the United States. Trade, advanced technology, artificial intelligence, semiconductors, critical minerals and military power have all become part of a broader strategic competition between Washington and Beijing. Yet the two economies remain deeply connected, making the relationship one of competition and interdependence rather than simple separation.

Taiwan remains the most sensitive issue. Beijing considers the island part of China and opposes Taiwanese independence, while Taiwan maintains its own elected government and political system. The dispute has become a major point of tension between China and the United States and remains one of the most closely watched security issues in Asia.

#### **National Day in 2026**

The anniversary comes during China’s extended National Day holiday, which runs from October 1 to October 7. The period is one of the country’s biggest annual travel seasons, with millions of people moving by rail, road and air to visit family and tourist destinations.

The holiday also comes as Beijing seeks to encourage domestic consumption. China’s enormous internal market has become increasingly important as policymakers attempt to reduce dependence on property investment and strengthen household spending. The sheer scale of holiday travel offers a useful, if imperfect, snapshot of consumer confidence and economic activity.

The political message of the anniversary has also been clear. At the National Day reception in Beijing on September 30, President Xi Jinping placed emphasis on economic resilience, technological innovation and the country’s longer-term development agenda. The government is now looking beyond the extraordinary growth that defined much of the reform era towards a more technologically sophisticated and self-reliant economy.

Executive Branch

#### **Seventy-seven years later**

The distance between the China of 1949 and the China of 2026 is extraordinary. The country that emerged from civil war as a poor and largely agrarian state is now a nuclear power, permanent member of the UN Security Council, manufacturing giant and one of the principal centres of global trade, technology and investment.

Discover more

That transformation has changed the choices available to developing countries and altered the strategic calculations of the world’s established powers. For Africa, China’s continued rise presents opportunities in trade, infrastructure, technology and investment, but also requires governments to negotiate partnerships carefully and pursue greater local value creation.

At 77, China’s National Day is therefore both a celebration of the past and a statement about the future. The question is no longer whether China has become a global power. It has. The more consequential question is how Beijing will use that power, how Washington and other major capitals will respond, and what China’s next stage of development will mean for a world already being reshaped by its rise.

Happy National Day to the People’s Republic of China.

title: HRC63: Hong Kong defenders highlight transnational repression as States renew concerns over China - ISHR
summary: The September session drew renewed attention to restrictions on civic space in China, the human rights situation in Tibet and the Uyghur region (Xinjiang), and the use of Hong Kong’s national security laws against activists at home and abro
content:
The September session drew renewed attention to restrictions on civic space in China, the human rights situation in Tibet and the Uyghur region (Xinjiang), and the use of Hong Kong’s national security laws against activists at home and abroad.

Through the testimony of Hong Kong defenders accompanied by ISHR, the Council also heard directly how repression can cross borders and extend to their families.

### **Carmen Lau: ‘Speaking before you today carries real risks’**

Exiled Hong Kong human rights defender **Carmen Lau** addressed the Council about the risks she continues to face as a result of her human rights advocacy. Lau is among the exiled Hong Kong activists subject to arrest warrants and HK$1 million bounties imposed by Hong Kong authorities.

She told the Council that repression had followed her to the United Kingdom, where her neighbours received letters containing sexually explicit AI-generated deepfakes of her and urging them to hand her over to the Chinese embassy. She also described constant online harassment and rape threats intended to intimidate and silence her.

> Speaking before you today carries real risks. I live with a credible fear of surveillance, harassment, and abduction because of my human rights advocacy. We urge the High Commissioner and Member States to condemn these acts through concrete action and call for an end to the extraterritorial weaponisation of Hong Kong’s national security laws.

Carmen Lau

### **Anna Kwok: ‘The UN and Member States should also do their utmost to respond’**

Hong Kong human rights defender **Anna Kwok** addressed the Council during its annual dialogue on the UN Secretary-General’s report on reprisals. Kwok, who is also subject to a HK$1 million bounty, spoke about the imprisonment of her 70-year-old father in Hong Kong, which she characterised as retaliation aimed at her work abroad.

> I speak to you today as a target of transnational repression and reprisals for my human rights advocacy, including my engagement with the UN. When States do their utmost to silence activists abroad, including for cooperating with the UN, the UN and Member States should also do their utmost to respond to it.

Anna Kwok

Kwok also pointed to a landmark [joint statement](https://ishr.ch/latest-updates/over-130-human-rights-experts-issue-global-call-for-states-to-end-transnational-repression/) on transnational repression by over 130 UN human rights experts issued a day earlier. The statement provides a roadmap for action, calling on States to prevent and investigate transnational repression, hold perpetrators accountable, strengthen protection for people at risk, and prevent the misuse of international law enforcement and other cross-border mechanisms.

### **Governments renew scrutiny of China’s human rights record**

During Council discussions, States continued to press China to act on recommendations already made by the UN. Four years after the UN Human Rights Office published its report finding possible crimes against humanity in the Uyghur region, [France](https://events.ohchr.org/PublicEvent/DownloadOralStatement/52841?eventHeaderId=197), the [United Kingdom](https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/un-human-rights-council-63-uk-statement-for-the-item-2-general-debate) and [Canada](https://events.ohchr.org/PublicEvent/DownloadOralStatement/52614?eventHeaderId=197) again called for follow-up, amid continuing calls for the High Commissioner to provide a substantive update on China’s implementation of the Office’s recommendations. The EU, in a [statement](https://www.eeas.europa.eu/delegations/un-geneva/hrc63-eu-statement-hrc63-item-4-human-rights-situations-require-councils-attention_en) joined by Albania, Montenegro and Liechtenstein, also called for implementation of recommendations from the UN Human Rights Office and other UN human rights mechanisms, as did the [Netherlands](https://events.ohchr.org/PublicEvent/DownloadOralStatement/55036?eventHeaderId=197), [Czechia](https://events.ohchr.org/PublicEvent/DownloadOralStatement/54864?eventHeaderId=197) and [Sweden](https://events.ohchr.org/PublicEvent/DownloadOralStatement/55064?eventHeaderId=197).

> Four years after the UN Human Rights Office concluded that serious violations in the Uyghur region may constitute crimes against humanity, the lack of substantive public follow-up is no longer tenable. High Commissioner Türk has a responsibility to follow up on his Office’s recommendations and publicly assess and report on the extent to which China has implemented them.

Lee Chung Lun, ISHR programme officer

As High Commissioner Volker Türk [appealed](https://www.ohchr.org/en/statements-and-speeches/2026/09/high-commissioner-turk-updates-human-rights-council-human-rights) for an ‘urgent U-turn’ on tightening restrictions on the rights of Tibetans and expressed deep concern at detention facilities and violations in the Uyghur region,China’s new **Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress** emerged as another significant focus of scrutiny for governments. Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom, the EU, Switzerland, the Netherlands, Ireland and Germany raised concerns about its potential impact on cultural, linguistic and religious rights, particularly for Tibetans, Uyghurs and Mongols.

The situation in Hong Kong also remained a major concern, with States drawing attention both to repression inside the territory and to efforts to target defenders abroad. The [EU](https://www.eeas.europa.eu/delegations/un-geneva/hrc63-eu-statement-hrc63-item-4-human-rights-situations-require-councils-attention_en) raised the repressive use of national security legislation, while [Japan](https://events.ohchr.org/PublicEvent/DownloadOralStatement/55014?eventHeaderId=197), [Ireland](https://events.ohchr.org/PublicEvent/DownloadOralStatement/55015?eventHeaderId=197), [Austria](https://events.ohchr.org/PublicEvent/DownloadOralStatement/55144?eventHeaderId=197), Germany and [Denmark](https://events.ohchr.org/PublicEvent/DownloadOralStatement/54406?eventHeaderId=197) raised concerns over fundamental freedoms, civic space and media freedom. Echoing [calls](https://www.ohchr.org/en/press-releases/2026/09/hong-kong-sar-sentences-against-three-activists-regrettable) by High Commissioner Türk for the quashing of sentences against **Chow Hang-tung, Lee Cheuk-yan and Albert Ho**, t he [United Kingdom](https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/un-human-rights-council-63-uk-statement-for-the-item-4-general-debate) highlighted recent convictions under the National Security Law, including those of leaders of the **Hong Kong Alliance** and **Joshua Wong**, and again called for the release of **Jimmy Lai**.

### **China remains at heart of UN debates on reprisals and transnational repression**

In the latest Secretary-General’s annual report on reprisals, China’s cross-border targeting of activists continued to draw concern. During the Council’s [debate](https://ishr.ch/latest-updates/human-rights-council-reprisals-debate-highlights-growing-trend-of-transnational-repression/) over the Secretary-General’s reprisals report, [Liechtenstein](https://events.ohchr.org/PublicEvent/DownloadOralStatement/55304?eventHeaderId=197) raised specific concern over the cases of **Anna Kwok** and **Carmen Lau**, while the [United Kingdom](https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/un-human-rights-council-63-uk-statement-for-the-interactive-dialogue-on-the-secretary-generals-report-on-cooperation-with-the-united-nations) also highlighted Lau’s situation. [Norway](https://events.ohchr.org/PublicEvent/DownloadOralStatement/54855?eventHeaderId=197) separately identified China among States where journalists in exile have reportedly faced patterns of transnational repression.

The Council’s reprisals debate also kept attention on pressure against defenders inside Hong Kong. [Belgium](https://events.ohchr.org/PublicEvent/DownloadOralStatement/55543?eventHeaderId=197), speaking for the Benelux countries, and Germany urged the immediate release of **Chow Hang-tung**, while Australia, speaking for Canada and New Zealand, called for the release of pro-democracy activists in Hong Kon g.

ISHR urges States to sustain and increase coordinated pressure on China to respect human rights and end repression and restrictions against human rights defenders. We also call on the UN Human Rights Office and independent experts to continue and strengthen monitoring and reporting on the country.

## Author

Lee Chung Lun

Lee Chung Lun is a programme officer at ISHR. He supports Chinese, Uyghur, Tibetan, and Hong Kong human rights defenders in their advocacy at the United Nations.

The public session of the 89th session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (ACHPR) will be held in Dakar, Senegal, from 12 to 21 October. The public session will be preceded by a training session organised jointly by ISHR, Front Line Defenders and Defend Defenders on 6, 7 and 11 October, and the NGO Forum, organised by ACDHRS from 8 to 10 October.

On 28 September, a delegation from the Government of Sierra Leone presented its fourth report under the Universal Periodic Review to the Human Rights Council. Of the 310 recommendations received, Sierra Leone 'took note' of 39 and accepted 271, of which 19 on the protection of human rights defenders and their working environment.

On 25 September, a delegation from the Government of Niger presented its report to the Human Rights Council as part of the fourth cycle of the Universal Periodic Review. Of the 265 recommendations received, Niger took note of 11 and accepted 254, including 23 relating to the protection of human rights defenders and their working environment.

title: Cyber based influence campaigns 21st  - 27th September 2026 Report: Insights and Analysis by CRC
summary: ### [Introduction] Cyber-based hostile influence campaigns are aimed at influencing target audiences by promoting information and/or disinformation over the internet, sometimes combined with cyber-attacks which enhance their effect (hence f
content:
### [Introduction]

Cyber-based hostile influence campaigns are aimed at influencing target audiences by promoting information and/or disinformation over the internet, sometimes combined with cyber-attacks which enhance their effect (hence force **Cyfluence**, as opposed to cyber-attacks that aim to steal information, extort money, etc.) Such hostile influence campaigns and operations can be considered an epistemological branch of Information Operations (IO) or Information Warfare (IW).

Typically, and as customary during the last decade, the information is spread throughout various internet platforms, which are the different elements of the hostile influence campaign, and as such, connectivity and repetitiveness of content between several elements are the main core characteristics of influence campaigns.

**Hostile influence campaigns, much like Cyber-attacks,**have also become a tool for rival nations and corporations to damage reputation or achieve various business, political or ideological goals. Much like in the cyber security arena, PR professionals and government agencies are responding to negative publicity and disinformation shared over the news and social media.

We use the term **cyber based**hostile influence campaigns, as we include in this definition also cyber-attacks aimed at influencing (such as hack and leak during election time), while we exclude of this term other types of more traditional kinds of influence such as diplomatic, economic, military etc.

During the 21st to the 27th September 2026, we observed, collected and analyzed endpoints of information related to **cyber based**hostile influence campaigns (including Cyfluence attacks). The following report is a summary of what we regard as the main events. Some of the mentioned campaigns have to do with social media and news outlets solemnly, while others leverage cyber-attack capabilities.

### [Contents]

**_Facebook_**

*   [Singapore Police Data Helps Meta Disrupt Scam Networks](https://www.cyfluence-research.org/post/cyber-based-influence-campaigns-21st-27th-september-2026-report#viewer-v1rop45819)

**_X_**

*   [US Backs Musk's Challenge to EU's First DSA Fine](https://www.cyfluence-research.org/post/cyber-based-influence-campaigns-21st-27th-september-2026-report#viewer-wxm0872808)

**_Tiktok_**

*   [AI-Fabricated Anti-Immigration Rallies Circulate on TikTok](https://www.cyfluence-research.org/post/cyber-based-influence-campaigns-21st-27th-september-2026-report#viewer-2pm0v73540)
